How to read this glossary

Term type · subject area

  2. Critical comment, with the yellow bar: what the term means for animals, from a vegan and antispeciesist point of view.

3Rs

acronym · Reducing and Ending the Use of Animals

The principle of Replacement, Reduction and Refinement in animal experimentation: replacing animals with other methods whenever possible, using the smallest number of animals, and reducing as far as possible the pain and stress of those used.

It was proposed by the British scientists William Russell and Rex Burch in the book The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique (1959). Today it is written into laws such as the 2010 European directive, which states full replacement of animals as its ultimate goal, and Brazil's Arouca Law. Critics say that, in practice, refinement and reduction get more attention than replacement.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Three Rs, Replacement, Reduction and Refinement
See also
Replacement methods, Arouca Law, Animal model, Animal experimentation, Animal Use Ethics Committee (CEUA)
Example
"The ethics committee asked the project to explain, in light of the 3Rs, why it would not use cell cultures and how it would reduce the number of mice."

A life worth living

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

The idea that welfare should not only avoid suffering but ensure that the animal's life, overall, has more good experiences than bad ones; used by the UK's farm animal welfare council since 2009.

The concept forces us to ask whether an animal's life has a positive balance, not only whether they were spared some pain. Many intensively farmed animals would hardly pass this test. At the same time, sentientists point out that a good life doesn't justify taking it early: death is also a harm.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Life worth living
Antonyms
Life not worth living
See also
Welfare range, Harm of death, Five Domains, Animal welfare
Example
“A hen kept in a small cage may have a life that is not worth living, even though she is well fed.”

Abolitionism

noun · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

A movement to abolish an institution considered unjust; in the historical sense, the movement to end the enslavement of people, above all Black people, in the 18th and 19th centuries; in animal ethics, the current that advocates ending the use of animals as property, rather than reforms that merely regulate that use.

The original meaning is the fight against slavery. In Britain, campaigners such as Olaudah Equiano, who had been enslaved, and William Wilberforce helped end the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of the empire in 1833; in the United States, Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman were among its best-known figures, and slavery was abolished in 1865. In Brazil, the movement included Luiz Gama, who had been enslaved and, as a lawyer, helped free hundreds of people, and led to the Golden Law of 1888, which made Brazil the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery. Many abolitionists, especially Black abolitionists, also fought racism, which is why abolitionism is seen as part of the history of anti-racist struggle; but not all of them did, and the end of slavery came without reparation or integration, which helps explain inequalities that persist. Today the word also names prison abolitionism, which advocates replacing prisons with other responses. In animal ethics, the term was adopted deliberately, especially by the legal scholar Gary Francione from the 1990s, to argue for ending the property status of animals and to criticize welfarism. This analogy with human slavery is controversial, and using it calls for respect for the word's origin.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal abolitionism
Antonyms
Welfarism, Reformism
See also
Abolitionist veganism, Animal slavery, Welfarism, Reformism, Animals as property
Example
"For those who defend abolitionism, making cages bigger is not enough: what must end is the status of animals as property."

Abolitionist veganism

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A strand that emphasizes ending animals' status as property as its central axis, critical of welfarism.

This strand is associated with the legal scholar Gary Francione, who defends veganism as a moral baseline and vegan education as the main strategy, and criticizes welfare reform campaigns and single-issue campaigns. Critics accuse it of purism and say it rejects concrete gains for animals alive today.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Abolitionist vegan approach, Francione-style veganism
Antonyms
Pragmatic veganism, Welfarism
See also
Abolitionism, Welfarism, Pragmatic veganism, Neo-welfarism
Example
“Abolitionist veganism rejects campaigns for bigger cages, since it calls for the end of all exploitation rather than its reform.”

Absent referent

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A concept from the author Carol J. Adams: the animal who became food is made absent from the plate, by words and packaging that hide that there was a living individual and a death.

Words like "steak" and "chicken" separate the food from the animal. Rebuilding the link between what we eat and who was killed is a common awareness strategy. See The Sexual Politics of Meat (1990).

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Erasure of the animal, Missing referent
See also
Objectification, Commodification, Euphemism, Meat
Example
“Calling a steak ‘red meat’ is a case of absent referent: the name erases the animal that once existed.”

Absolute poverty

noun phrase · Intersectionality and Social Justice

The condition of those who lack the minimum for basic needs, such as food, shelter, health care and education; since 2025 the World Bank has measured it with an extreme poverty line of 3 dollars per person per day.

Robert McNamara, president of the World Bank in the 1970s, described it as a condition beneath any reasonable definition of human decency, and Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), starts from it for the pond argument. By World Bank estimates, about 800 million people lived below that line in 2025, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa; the book's figures, from around 1990, are out of date. Singer also links the topic to animals: much of the world's grain and soy becomes feed, and hunger is mainly a problem of distribution, not production. That is why the charge that defending animals diverts resources from the poor does not hold, since not eating animals does not compete with helping humans, although critics point out that poverty has political causes that no change of diet solves on its own.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Extreme poverty
Antonyms
Absolute affluence
See also
Pond argument, Demandingness objection, Effective altruism, Food justice
Example
“He pointed out that fighting absolute poverty and no longer eating animals do not compete with each other.”

Action

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

Any deliberate conduct of a moral agent, evaluated ethically by its consequences, intentions or conformity to rules.

Under the equal consideration of interests, actions that cause avoidable suffering to sentient beings are subject to the same moral scrutiny applied to actions that affect humans.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
conduct, act
Antonyms
Omission
See also
Omission, Decision, Choice, Moral agent, Consequentialism
Example
"For consequentialism, what makes an action right or wrong is the outcome it produces for all affected beings, human or not."

Organized action in defense of a cause, here the animal cause.

Active and organised engagement in defence of a political or social cause, including the animal cause.

Activist burnout

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

Physical, emotional and mental exhaustion in people devoted to a cause, leading to loss of energy, cynicism and often to leaving activism.

A study of social justice and human rights activists (Chen and Gorski, 2015) pointed to common causes such as neglecting self-care, the emotional weight of the cause and conflict among activists. In animal advocacy, frequent exposure to images of suffering and the feeling that change is slow add to this. The World Health Organization treats burnout as a work-related phenomenon, not as a disease. Looking after yourself is part of sustaining activism over the long term. See Activist fatigue, Vicarious trauma and Learned helplessness.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
activist exhaustion, activist fatigue
See also
Activist fatigue, Vicarious trauma (secondary traumatic stress), Learned helplessness, Activism
Example
"After years of watching slaughterhouse footage, the volunteer reached activist burnout and had to step away from the NGO to recover her health."

Argument in the guide →

Activist fatigue

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

Accumulated tiredness in people who take part in campaigns, debates and actions for a long time, with falling motivation and energy.

It is milder and more common than burnout, but can lead to it without rest. A related concept is compassion fatigue, described among professionals who care for people in distress: the capacity to care diminishes after long exposure to others' pain. Breaks, support from others and realistic goals help prevent it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
activist weariness, campaign fatigue
See also
Activist burnout, Vicarious trauma (secondary traumatic stress), Activism, Activism (militancy)
Example
“After years of weekly vigils, she felt activist fatigue and decided to take a break to regroup.”

Ad hoc reply

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A reply or hypothesis made up only to save a claim from an objection or a counterexample, with no independent reason in its favor.

The Latin phrase means "for this", and criticism of ad hoc hypotheses is common in the philosophy of science, for example in Karl Popper. A reply is not ad hoc just because it came after the objection: it is ad hoc when it would have no support if the objection did not exist and when it explains nothing beyond the case it needs to save. Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), applies the test to replies to the argument from marginal cases: those who say only rational beings have rights must account for babies and people with profound cognitive disabilities, and rules such as "those who belong to a normally rational species count" often look tailor-made to include these humans and exclude animals. It is what this guide's commitment to parsimony asks us to avoid.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
ad hoc hypothesis, ad hoc explanation
See also
Argument from marginal cases, Counterexample, Begging the question, Reflective equilibrium
Example
“Saying babies count because they belong to a rational species looks like an ad hoc reply: the rule was made up only to include them.”

Adoption

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The act of taking on the responsible, permanent care of an animal, usually a rescued or abandoned one, instead of buying it.

The slogan "adopt, don't shop" rests on the idea that each purchase encourages commercial breeding, while shelters and rescuers have animals waiting for a home. Adoption solves one animal's situation, but not the cause of abandonment; for that reason it usually comes with neutering and responsible-care campaigns.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
pet adoption
Antonyms
abandonment, buying animals
See also
Rescue, Animal rescuers (Brazil's "protetores de animais"), Castration, Fostering (temporary adoption), Pet shop
Example
"Instead of buying a puppy in a shop, the family went to an adoption fair and took home a dog rescued from the street."

Affirmative action

noun phrase · Intersectionality and Social Justice

Measures, usually temporary, that seek to correct historical inequalities affecting discriminated groups, giving them more access to opportunities.

The best-known example in Brazil is quotas in public universities, which the Supreme Federal Court ruled constitutional in 2012 and which became mandatory in federal universities by law that same year. The underlying idea is that treating equally those who start from very unequal situations can keep the inequality in place. This connects with the principle of equal consideration of interests: equal consideration doesn't mean identical treatment, but giving the same weight to what each one needs.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Positive discrimination, Affirmative policies
See also
Intersectionality, Representation, Equal consideration, Justice
Example
“The debate on affirmative action shows how treating everyone identically can preserve unequal starting points.”

Afro-veganism (or Black veganism)

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A strand that centers Black experiences and racial critique within the vegan movement, questioning its predominantly white history.

Two works mark this strand: the anthology Sistah Vegan (2010), edited by A. Breeze Harper, with writings by Black vegan women, and Aphro-ism (2017), by the sisters Aph Ko and Syl Ko. They criticize the idea that veganism is a thing for white and wealthy people and connect the oppression of animals to racism, without treating the two kinds of suffering as equal.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Black vegan movement
See also
Intersectionality, Intersectional veganism, Animal slavery, Vegan movement, Food colonialism / vegan decoloniality
Example
"At the Afro-veganism meeting, the speakers discussed how Black food culture, often plant-based, has been erased from the public image of veganism."

noun · Plant-Derived Products

Agribusiness

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The set of economic activities tied to large-scale agriculture and livestock farming, from production to processing and marketing.

It brings together distinct activities: veganism opposes livestock farming and fishing, which are part of agribusiness, but not agriculture, which is also part of it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
agro-industry, agri-industry
See also
Agropecuária (agriculture and livestock), Agriculture, Industrial livestock farming, Livestock industry, Subsidies
Example
"Agribusiness accounts for a large share of the country's exports, and debate grows over how much of it depends on raising animals for slaughter."

Agriculture

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

The cultivation of plants, such as grains, legumes, fruit and fibers, for human food, animal feed or other uses.

Veganism does not oppose agriculture, but the exploitation of animals. Part of agriculture serves to feed animals raised for consumption, and crop production also has impacts that deserve attention.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
crop farming, cultivation
See also
Agropecuária (agriculture and livestock), Agribusiness, Livestock farming, Veganism, Feed
Example
"The family lives from agriculture: they grow beans, corn and vegetables on small plots, without raising any animals for sale or slaughter."

Agropecuária (agriculture and livestock)

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The combination of crop farming and livestock farming, that is, growing plants and raising animals.

The term joins two distinct activities, and veganism treats each differently: it opposes raising and using animals, but not growing plants.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
farming, agriculture and animal husbandry
See also
Agriculture, Livestock farming, Agribusiness, Zootechnics (animal science)
Example
"The farm is devoted to mixed agriculture and livestock: part of the land grows soy and corn, and part is pasture for cattle."

Alienation

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The distance between people and the real consequences of what they do, produce or consume; in everyday use, also a lack of awareness of what is happening around one.

The concept has philosophical roots and gained prominence with Karl Marx, who in the 1844 Manuscripts described the alienation of workers from the product of their labour. In the consumption of animal products, alienation is made easier by physical and informational distance: animals are kept far away, in closed sheds, death happens out of sight, and meat reaches the shop in pieces that don't look like an animal. The less visible the suffering, the easier it is to keep practices that, seen up close, many people would reject. One caution: calling someone "alienated" tends to sound like an insult and close the conversation; showing what is hidden works better than labelling those who haven't seen it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
disconnection, estrangement, detachment
Antonyms
awareness
See also
Absent referent, Carnism, Cognitive dissonance, Apathy, Euphemism
Example
"Because meat reaches the shop on clean trays with no trace of the animal, alienation from what happens in slaughterhouses persists."

Altricial and precocial animals

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A classification of animals by their degree of development at birth or hatching: precocial animals are born relatively mature and mobile, while altricial animals are born underdeveloped and depend on parental care.

Classic examples are foals and ducklings, which are precocial, and songbird chicks and human babies, which are altricial; Augustine, Lika and Kooijman (2019) show that this is a continuum, not two boxes. The distinction matters in the debate about wild animal suffering because it is sometimes said that young animals who die early do not yet feel anything. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that being immature is not the same as not being sentient, and that most small animals with many offspring are precocial, that is, they must fend for themselves from very early on. The empirical question, however, remains open: for many larvae and fish fry it is not known when sentience begins.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
altricial-precocial spectrum, nidicolous and nidifugous
See also
Sentience, Population dynamics, r and K reproductive strategies, Wild animal suffering
Example
"A foal, a precocial animal, stands within hours, while a sparrow chick, an altricial animal, hatches without feathers and depends on its parents for everything."

Altruism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A disposition to act for the benefit of others, even when it brings no advantage to the one who acts, or has some cost.

The term was coined in the 19th century by the philosopher Auguste Comte, as the opposite of egoism. In biology, it also describes animal behavior that helps others, such as warning the group about a predator. In animal ethics, altruism shows up when someone changes habits or devotes time and resources to beings who will never repay them. But the defense of animals doesn't depend on altruism: not causing avoidable harm is a duty, not a generous gesture.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
selflessness, benevolence, generosity
Antonyms
egoism, selfishness
See also
Effective altruism, Egoism (egocentrism), Charity, Compassion, Empathy
Example
"She spent the weekend caring for rescued cats without expecting anything in return, a gesture the neighbours described as pure altruism."

Political or ethical objection →

Analogy

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

An argumentative resource that compares distinct situations because they share relevant characteristics.

Comparisons between animal exploitation and human oppressions, such as slavery, are used by antispeciesists to highlight common structures of domination, but they are also criticized for potentially minimizing the specificity and gravity of the historical human suffering involved.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
comparison, parallel
Antonyms
disanalogy
See also
Argument, Fallacies, Animal slavery, Animal Holocaust, Argument from relevance
Example
"By comparing the confinement of pigs to that of enslaved people, the speaker used an analogy that many listeners found disrespectful of human history."

Anarchism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A political current that rejects hierarchies and unjustified forms of domination, including the State, and proposes organizing society through voluntary association and self-management.

Part of anarchism includes animals: Élisée Reclus defended vegetarianism, and veganarchism, a term coined by Brian A. Dominick (1995), unites veganism and anarchism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Antonyms
statism
See also
Veganarchism, Green anarchism, Socialism, Liberalism, Dominionism
Example
"For anarchism, no hierarchy is valid without justification, and some anarchists extend this rejection to the domination humans exercise over other animals."

Political or ethical objection →

Anesthesia

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A medical procedure to suppress the sensation of pain during interventions; its use (or absence) in livestock procedures is a central topic in welfare debates.

Several routine procedures in livestock farming are allowed without anaesthesia when performed on very young animals. In the European Union, castration and tail docking of piglets require anaesthesia only after the seventh day of life; in Brazil, the 2020 pig welfare rule of the Ministry of Agriculture requires anaesthesia for tail docking only after the third day and gives farms until 2030 to make it mandatory for all surgical castration. Beak trimming, disbudding and hot-iron branding are also usually done without anaesthesia. Even with local anaesthesia, pain can last for days after the procedure, which is why veterinary bodies also recommend analgesics.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Castration, Tail docking, Beak trimming, Pain, Disbudding
Example
"Even with local anaesthesia, the vet also prescribed an analgesic, because the pain of the procedure can last for days after the effect wears off."

Animal

noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

A multicellular living being of the kingdom Animalia, capable of movement and, in most cases, possessing a nervous system; a biological term that includes humans, although it is popularly used to refer only to nonhumans.

This everyday separation between "humans" and "animals" reinforces, in common language, a moral hierarchy between species that biology itself does not support.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
critter, creature, beast
See also
Nonhuman animal, Living being, Sentient being, Speciesism, Zoology
Example
"When someone says they treat animals well, it is worth asking whether that includes hens and fish, because in everyday speech the word usually leaves humans out."

Animal advocacy

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

Legal and political work aimed at defending the interests and rights of animals before courts, legislators and public bodies.

Part of this advocacy seeks not only to improve conditions of exploitation, but to recognize animals as subjects of rights of their own, and not merely as objects of indirect protection.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
legal advocacy for animals, animal law practice
See also
Animal law, Animal habeas corpus, Animal legal personhood, Institutional activism, Lobby
Example
"The organization hired an animal advocacy legal team to take a cruelty case at a breeding facility to court and ask for custody of the animals."

Animal behavior

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The scientific study (ethology) of animals' actions and reactions, used as indirect evidence of their mental states.

In practice, it is the main source of empirical evidence for inferring suffering and welfare in species whose subjectivity cannot be directly verified.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal conduct, animal ethology
See also
Ethology, Stereotypic behavior, Animal emotions
Example
"Studying animal behavior, the team noticed that hens scratch and dust-bathe when they have space, but not in cages."

Animal cloning

noun phrase · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

Producing an animal genetically identical to another, from the genetic material of a body cell of the original animal.

The first mammal cloned from an adult cell was Dolly the sheep, born in 1996 at the Roslin Institute in Scotland after hundreds of attempts. The technique still has a low success rate: many embryos fail to develop, and many animals are born with health problems or die young. It is used in research, in animal farming, in conservation programs and, commercially, to "clone" pet dogs and cats, which requires surrogate mothers and many animals undergoing procedures.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Artificial reproduction, Animal model, Genetic engineering
Example
"Dolly the sheep, born in 1996, became the most famous example of animal cloning, and her short life raised doubts about clone welfare."

Animal cognition

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The study of the mental capacities of non-human animals, such as memory, planning and problem solving.

Recent discoveries in this area have revealed, in several species, capacities once attributed exclusively to humans, which weakens criteria for moral exclusion based on supposed cognitive inferiority.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
comparative cognition, animal intelligence
See also
Animal consciousness, Animal emotions, Ethology
Example
"Research in animal cognition shows that crows make tools and plan for the future, contradicting the idea that only humans think."

Animal confinement

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A farming system in enclosed, restricted spaces (e.g., CAFO, Concentrated Animal Feeding Operation).

According to a 2019 Sentience Institute estimate, about 74% of farmed land animals worldwide and almost all farmed fish live on factory farms; in the United States, the share reaches 99%. Confinement makes it possible to produce more with less space and labour, but it prevents basic behaviours such as walking, scratching, rooting or caring for young. It also concentrates manure and favours the spread of disease, which leads to heavy antibiotic use.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
factory farming confinement, intensive confinement
See also
Factory farm, Industrial livestock farming, Antimicrobial resistance
Example
"In animal confinement, thousands of chickens share a closed shed, and the high density promotes disease that leads to routine antibiotic use."

Animal consciousness

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

An extension of the concept of consciousness applied specifically to non-humans; it discusses whether, and to what degree, different species have their own subjective experience and how this can be scientifically inferred.

Given scientific uncertainty on this topic, a sentientist perspective tends to adopt the precautionary principle: granting moral consideration whenever there is a reasonable probability of consciousness, rather than demanding absolute certainty before acting.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal mind, non-human consciousness, consciousness in animals
See also
Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, Sentience, Animal cognition
Example
"Research on animal consciousness gained strength when scientists recognized that mammals, birds and octopuses have neural structures linked to experience."

Animal cruelty

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

The act of inflicting unnecessary suffering on an animal; a legal and moral category central to the first protection laws of the 19th century, predating the very concept of 'animal rights'.

The criterion of 'necessity' used to define cruelty tends, in practice, to exclude the suffering caused by legalized industries such as livestock farming, which reveals the limits of this concept when not accompanied by a broader reflection on the moral status of animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal abuse, maltreatment, animal mistreatment
Antonyms
Compassion
See also
Environmental Crimes Law (animal abuse), Zoosadism, Suffering
Example
"The court convicted the owner of animal cruelty after finding the dog chained, thin and without water for days."

Animal emotions

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

Affective states, such as fear, anger, joy, grief or the urge to play, experienced by nonhuman animals and studied by ethology and affective neuroscience.

For a long time science avoided talking about emotions in animals, partly because of the legacy of Descartes, who saw animals as machines. Charles Darwin had already devoted a book to the expression of emotions in humans and animals, in 1872. The neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp, who coined the term affective neuroscience, identified basic emotional systems in ancient brain regions that mammals share. Knowing that an animal can feel fear or joy changes the moral question: avoiding physical pain is not enough.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal affect, emotional lives of animals
See also
Animal-machine, Positive experiences, Suffering, Animal cognition
Example
“A female elephant’s grief over the body of a companion is cited as evidence that animal emotions are complex.”

Animal entertainment

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The use of animals in circuses, zoos, water parks and similar venues.

More than 40 countries ban or restrict the use of wild animals in circuses, according to a survey by the organization Four Paws, and in Brazil there are state and municipal laws to that effect. Training for shows can involve punishment, and the animals spend much of their time in small spaces and in transport. Dolphins and orcas in marine parks are also criticized, and countries such as Canada and France have restricted by law the keeping of cetaceans in captivity.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal shows, animal-based amusement
See also
Zoo, Rodeo, Bullfighting, Animal fighting
Example
“More and more cities ban circuses with animals, since they consider that animal entertainment does not justify confinement and coercive training.”

Animal ethics

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The philosophical field devoted to the moral status of nonhuman animals and to how they ought to be treated.

Its development has been central to exposing speciesism as a moral bias as arbitrary as racism or sexism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
ethics of animals, animal-related ethics
See also
Ethics, Practical ethics, Animal rights, Welfarism
Example
“In an animal ethics course, the class discussed whether raising pigs for food can be justified.”

Animal experimentation

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The use of animals in scientific research, product safety testing, teaching and the production of biological substances, such as vaccines and antibodies.

An estimate published in 2019 calculated that about 190 million animals were used in laboratories worldwide in 2015, mostly mice, rats, fish and birds. Experimentation is regulated by laws that require justification and pain control, but allow procedures that cause severe suffering. Supporters point to contributions to medicine; critics question how well the results transfer to humans and advocate animal-free methods.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal research, animal testing
See also
3Rs, Animal model, Arouca Law, Replacement methods
Example
“Before approving the project, the committee asked whether animal experimentation was truly necessary or whether a validated alternative existed.”

Animal exploitation

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An umbrella term for any instrumental use of animals for human benefit.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal use, animal instrumentalization
Antonyms
animal liberation
See also
Instrumentalization, Animals as property, Happy exploitation, Animal liberation
Example
“Animal exploitation ranges from dairy to the circus: any use in which the animal serves as a means to a human end.”

Animal fighting

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Forced confrontation between animals (roosters, dogs) for entertainment and betting, usually illegal.

In Brazil, the Supreme Federal Court struck down several state laws that authorized cockfighting, such as Rio de Janeiro's in 2011, holding the practice to be cruelty prohibited by the Constitution. In the United States, taking part in animal fighting is a federal crime. Even so, clandestine fights continue to be uncovered, and cockfighting is legal and popular in countries such as the Philippines.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal fight
See also
Animal cruelty, The Link, Vaquejada, Animal entertainment
Example
“Police broke up a clandestine fight and rescued injured roosters, bred only to fight.”

Animal habeas corpus

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

A legal instrument used in test cases to challenge the captivity of animals (e.g., great apes), without going into the names of specific cases.

Its use reflects an attempt to break with the logic that only humans can be subjects of a legal instrument historically reserved for the protection of individual liberty.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Habeas corpus for animals, Nonhuman habeas corpus
See also
Animal legal personhood, Animals as property, Animal law, Jurisdiction
Example
"An animal protection group filed an animal habeas corpus petition seeking to move a chimpanzee kept alone in a zoo to a sanctuary."

Animal Holocaust

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

An expression used by part of the animal movement to describe the industrial-scale killing of animals, compared with the Holocaust.

The comparison appears in the work of the Jewish writer Isaac Bashevis Singer, who called the life of animals "an eternal Treblinka", and in Charles Patterson's book Eternal Treblinka (2002). It is highly controversial: Jewish organizations and part of the animal movement itself reject it, considering that it trivializes the genocide of people. PETA's "Holocaust on your plate" campaign was banned in Germany, and the European Court of Human Rights upheld the ban in 2012. The guide discusses this controversy in the argument "Comparing animal farming to slavery or the Holocaust is offensive".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal genocide
See also
Animal slavery, Slaughter, Animal exploitation, Slaughterhouse
Example
"By using the expression animal Holocaust, the speaker sparked debate, as many listeners found the comparison offensive to human victims."

Argument in the guide →

Animal language

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

Forms of communication used by nonhuman animals, such as vocalisations, gestures and chemical signals, studied to understand the cognition of different species.

Findings in this area have progressively narrowed the gap that was once assumed to exist between human communication and that of other species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Language, Animal cognition, Animal behavior, Animal emotions
Example
"Researchers study animal language by recording monkeys' alarm calls, which vary with the type of predator."

Animal law

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals · Animal Law and Legislation

The branch of law that studies rules about non-human animals: their legal status, their protection and disputes over their use.

It is a field of study and practice, like environmental or consumer law, not a moral position: one can study animal law without holding that animals have rights. An important part of the field, however, argues for going beyond protection against cruelty and recognizing animals as subjects of rights, breaking with their status as property. Not to be confused with animal rights, which are the rights animals themselves would have.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
law on animals, animal protection law
See also
Animal rights, Animal protection legislation
Example
"The law school created an Animal law course, covering everything from anti-cruelty statutes to the debate over animals' legal personhood."

Animal legal personhood

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

A debate about recognising animals as subjects of rights, and not merely property. It is defended by antispeciesist jurists as a necessary paradigm shift to break with the historical reduction of animals to the status of property.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Nonhuman legal personhood, Legal personhood for animals
Antonyms
Animals as property
See also
Animal habeas corpus, Animals as property, Animal law, Great Ape Project
Example
“A court recognized a chimpanzee as a rights-holder, opening the way to discussing animal legal personhood.”

Animal liberation

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

Both a philosophical concept and the tactic of directly rescuing animals from exploitation.

The expression became known through the book Animal Liberation (1975) by Peter Singer, who took the name from the Black and women's liberation movements. Singer's argument is utilitarian and rests on equal consideration of interests, not on rights. As a tactic, the expression also names the Animal Liberation Front.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal emancipation
Antonyms
Animal exploitation, Animal enslavement
See also
Direct action, Rescue, Speciesism, Total liberation
Example
"The book 'Animal Liberation' popularised the idea that animals' interests deserve equal consideration regardless of species."

Animal model

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An animal used in research to represent a biological process or a human disease, such as mice genetically altered to develop a type of cancer.

The choice of species often follows the Krogh principle, from the Danish physiologist August Krogh: for each problem there is an animal in which it can be studied most conveniently. Being convenient doesn't guarantee that the result holds for humans. Most drugs that pass preclinical testing fail in human trials, through lack of efficacy or safety problems, and differences between species are one of the causes discussed. Supporters point out that animal models have contributed to medical advances; critics advocate methods based on human biology. In 2022, the United States stopped requiring animal tests for approving new drugs.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Research animal
See also
Animal experimentation, Replacement methods, 3Rs, Guinea pig
Example
"The mouse was chosen as an animal model to study diabetes, but critics question whether the results apply to people."

Animal nutrition

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The field that studies the nutritional needs of non-human animals and how to meet them through feeding.

In animal farming, it focuses on making animals grow and produce more at the lowest cost, measuring feed conversion, how much feed becomes meat, milk or eggs. This conversion reveals an inefficiency: the animal spends most of what it eats on living, and only part becomes food for people. The same field also serves welfare, when it looks after the health of companion, rescued and sanctuary animals, and it is the field that studies whether foods without animal ingredients meet the needs of dogs and cats.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Nutrition, Feed, Vegan pet food, Zootechnics (animal science)
Example
“Before changing the dog's diet, her guardian consulted a veterinarian specializing in animal nutrition to make sure the diet was complete.”

Argument in the guide →

Animal population control

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A set of methods for reducing the number of animals in a population, ranging from killing (culling, hunting, poisoning) to non-lethal methods such as neutering and contraception.

For stray dogs and cats, trap-neuter-return (TNR) is an alternative to capture and killing. In wild animals, contraceptive vaccines are already used, for example in wild horses in the United States. From a sentientist point of view, non-lethal methods are preferable when they work, and the question is not only how many animals there are, but how they live and die. Killing is often defended as cheaper or faster, but in many cases the population grows back. For wild animals, Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) defends sterilization without consent only when three conditions are met: a high probability that the offspring would have lives of extreme suffering, a high probability of reproduction and no less harmful means that is equally effective; he also notes that sterilizing females is more efficient, since one male can fertilize many females. He distinguishes these cases from those of humans living in poverty, where the obstacle is social, but critics see in the comparison an echo of eugenic policies of forced sterilization, and reproductive justice and ecofeminism reject the principle.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
population management
See also
Castration, Invasive alien species, Pests, Sterile insect technique
Example
"The animal population control program replaced culling with mass neutering, reducing the number of stray cats without resorting to killing."

Animal protection legislation

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

The body of laws and rules that protect animals against cruelty and regulate their use, in areas such as farming, transport, slaughter, research and entertainment.

Most of this legislation is welfarist: it limits how animals are used, but doesn't ban using them. Some rules go further and recognize animals as sentient beings, such as the Treaty of Lisbon in the European Union.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal welfare law, Animal cruelty statutes
See also
Animal law, Statute, Sentience in law, Welfarism
Example
"The new animal protection legislation banned short chains for dogs and set fines for those who keep them."

Argument in the guide →

Animal protein

noun phrase · Animal-Derived Products

Protein derived from animal tissues or secretions, distinct from plant protein in amino acid composition.

It is common to hear that plant protein is "incomplete" and that foods must be combined in the same meal. The 2016 position of the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics is that a variety of plant foods eaten over the course of the day supplies all the essential amino acids, without the need to combine them at each meal. Rice and beans, a common dish in Brazil, is an example of such a combination.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal-derived protein
Antonyms
Plant protein
See also
Plant protein, Nutrition, Vegan diet, Meat
Example
“Many believe only animal protein sustains muscles, but vegan athletes show that beans, tofu and lentils work too.”

Animal psychology

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The study of the mind and behavior of non-human animals, such as perception, learning, memory, emotions and social relationships; also called comparative psychology.

For a long time the field was shaped by behaviorism, which studied only observable behavior and avoided talk of mind, often with experiments that caused suffering, such as the learned helplessness experiments on dogs. Today, together with ethology and the science of animal cognition, it provides much of the evidence that many animals feel fear, pleasure and stress, learn, and have complex social lives. There is also an applied side, which deals with behavior problems in companion and captive animals. Not to be confused with the psychology that studies humans' relationship with animals, such as the meat paradox.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Comparative psychology
See also
Animal cognition, Ethology, Animal emotions, Morgan's canon
Example
“Animal psychology experiments showed that crows solve puzzles and plan actions in advance.”

Argument in the guide →

Animal rescuers (Brazil's "protetores de animais")

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

In Brazil, people who rescue, treat, neuter and rehome abandoned or at-risk animals, above all dogs and cats, often on their own; called independent rescuers when they work without an organization.

The Portuguese term, literally "animal protectors", can be confusing, because "protecting animals" could include all of them, but in Brazilian usage it usually refers to companion and street animals. The tradition goes back a long way: the União Internacional Protetora dos Animais (UIPA) was founded in São Paulo in 1895. Today much of the work is done by individuals, mostly women, who take animals into their homes, pay for vet care and food out of their own pockets and organize adoption fairs, at a high financial and emotional cost. The closest English terms are animal rescuer or independent rescuer, and someone who takes animals in temporarily is a foster carer; "animal protection" in English usually covers all animals, including those raised for food. Being a rescuer doesn't imply being vegan, and many rescuers eat meat; the reverse also holds, because veganism doesn't replace caring for the animals who already need help. Both kinds of work start from the same concern, and each can learn from the other.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Independent rescuers
See also
Rescue, Adoption, Fostering (temporary adoption), Foster carer, Castration, Pet
Example
“An animal rescuer took in twelve rescued cats at home, paying with donations for the neutering and vaccination of each one.”

Animal rights

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

Rights that non-human animals would have, in the moral or legal sense, such as not being killed, confined or used as property.

The theory of animal rights took shape with the philosopher Tom Regan, in The Case for Animal Rights (1983), for whom animals who are subjects-of-a-life have intrinsic value and cannot be treated as mere resources. It differs from welfarism, which accepts using animals as long as suffering is reduced. Not to be confused with animal law, the branch of law that studies rules about animals: one thing is the field of study, another is the thesis that animals have rights.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
rights of animals, nonhuman animal rights
See also
Animal law, Rights, Intrinsic value, Abolitionism
Example
“For those who defend animal rights, a pig should not be treated as a resource, even if the law still classifies it as a commodity.”

Argument in the guide →

Animal slavery

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

An expression used by part of the animal movement to describe the condition of animals treated as property: bought, sold, confined, forced to work or to breed, and killed when they stop being profitable, compared with human slavery.

The comparison was developed in Marjorie Spiegel's book The Dreaded Comparison (1988), and is discussed critically by Black authors such as Aph Ko and Syl Ko. Those who defend it compare structures, such as ownership of bodies and the denial of interests, and don't claim the suffering is equal. Those who criticize it point out that it can erase the history and the consequences of the enslavement of Black people, which are still present. The guide discusses this controversy in the argument "Comparing animal farming to slavery or the Holocaust is offensive" and in "Stop saying".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
enslavement of animals, animal servitude
Antonyms
animal liberation
See also
Animal Holocaust, Animals as property, Animal liberation, Instrumentalization
Example
“For these activists, treating animals as property that can be bought and sold is animal slavery, comparable to practices humanity has already condemned.”

Argument in the guide →

Animal theory of mind

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The capacity to attribute mental states to oneself and to others; studied in primates, corvids and cetaceans as an indication of cognitive complexity. Evidence of theory of mind in many species reinforces the idea that cognitive complexity is not exclusively human, undermining one of the traditional arguments of speciesism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Theory of mind in animals
See also
Animal cognition, Animal emotions, Animal consciousness, Critical anthropomorphism
Example
“Experiments suggest that ravens hide food when they notice another raven watching, which fuels the debate on animal theory of mind.”

Animal traction

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The use of an animal's physical strength to pull loads or vehicles.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal power, Draft work
See also
Beast of burden, Animal-drawn cart (carroça, Brazilian usage), Riding, Animal exploitation
Example
“Horses pulling carts in city streets work under strong sun, and the debate on animal traction calls for alternatives for the cart drivers.”

Animal trafficking

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The illegal trade in wild or domestic animals, often involving capture, transport and cruel conditions.

In Brazil, Renctas, a network against wildlife trafficking, has estimated since its first report in 2001 that about 38 million wild animals are taken from nature each year, most of them birds, and that most die during capture or transport; the figure is old and its method is poorly documented. In international trade, the CITES convention regulates the sale of endangered species. Trafficking supplies mainly the pet market, as well as collectors, traditional medicine and food, and it increases the risk of zoonoses.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Illegal wildlife trade, Wildlife trafficking
See also
CITES, Pet shop, Zoonosis, Extinction
Example
“The seizure of dozens of birds in cramped boxes showed how animal trafficking causes suffering and risks spreading disease.”

Animal training

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The process of training an animal to perform specific behaviors through conditioning; coercive methods are debated ethically.

Methods range from rewards, such as food and play, to punishment, such as leash jerks and shock or prong collars. A study by Ana Catarina Vieira de Castro and colleagues, published in 2020, observed dogs at training schools in Portugal and associated aversive methods with more signs of stress and more pessimistic responses, and several veterinary bodies recommend reward-based training. In circuses, rodeos and other shows, training serves behaviours the animal would not perform on its own, and the criticism goes beyond the method: it questions the use itself.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Animal entertainment, Rodeo, Positive education, Domestication, Animal cruelty
Example
"The trainer swapped the shock collar for treats and praise, and the dog learned to obey without signs of fear or stress."

Animal Use Ethics Committee (CEUA)

proper noun · Animal Law and Legislation

A committee that reviews and approves, or rejects, an institution's research and teaching projects involving animals; in Brazil, mandatory under the Arouca Law, with equivalents in other countries, such as IACUCs in the United States.

The committee must check whether the use of animals is justified, whether the number of animals is the minimum needed and whether pain will be controlled. Studies of committees of this kind point to limits: they are generally made up mostly of researchers from the institution itself, and they rarely reject projects. Including outside members, such as representatives of animal protection societies, is one way of balancing this review.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
IACUC, animal ethics committee, animal care and use committee
See also
Arouca Law, 3Rs, Animal experimentation
Example
"Before starting the experiments with mice, the researcher had to submit the project to the CEUA, which requires justifying animal use and seeking alternatives."

Animal welfare

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

The state of an animal as regards their health, what they feel and their ability to live according to their nature; also the scientific and ethical field that assesses and seeks to improve that state, especially in animals under human care.

The scientist David Fraser described three ways of thinking about welfare: biological functioning (health, growth), affective states (what the animal feels) and natural living (being able to express their behaviors). The three don't always go together: a broiler chicken can grow fast and be in pain. For a sentientist ethics, what the animal feels is central. Animal welfare as a science is not the same as welfarism, the political position that accepts the use of animals as long as they are treated well.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal well-being, welfare of animals
See also
Five Domains, Coping, Welfarism, Five Freedoms, Environmental enrichment
Example
"The farm enlarged the pens and added perches to improve animal welfare, but the hens are still raised for slaughter."

Animal-assisted therapy

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The use of animals, such as dogs, horses and cats, in health treatment, rehabilitation or education, under professional supervision.

There is evidence of benefits for some people, such as reduced anxiety, although many studies are small. The ethical question is the animal's side: they need rest, the ability to refuse contact and not to be exposed to constant stress. Practices such as therapy with captive dolphins are criticized because they depend on capturing or confining animals who suffer in those conditions.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
AAT, Pet therapy, Zootherapy
See also
Companion animal, Animal welfare, Animal entertainment, Human-animal bond
Example
“The hospital invited trained dogs for weekly visits to hospitalized children, but the staff also checked whether the animals were stressed by the routine.”

Animal-drawn cart (carroça, Brazilian usage)

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A vehicle pulled by animals, used to carry goods or people.

In Brazil, carts are widely used by waste pickers and other low-income workers, and the horses suffer from overloading, long working days, lack of rest and traffic accidents. Several cities have passed laws banning animal-drawn vehicles, such as Recife and Belo Horizonte, where the ban took effect in 2026, but enforcement runs into the lack of alternatives for cart drivers. For that reason, replacement proposals usually combine removing the horses with motorized or electric vehicles and income support for the workers.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
horse cart, donkey cart, animal-drawn wagon
See also
Animal traction, Beast of burden, Intersectionality
Example
"In many Brazilian cities, cart drivers who rely on the cart for work were supported with projects to replace it with motor vehicles and rehome the horses."

Animal-machine

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A view associated with the philosopher René Descartes, in the 17th century, that animals are mindless automata whose cries and movements are merely mechanical reactions, without feeling.

This idea helped justify experiments on living animals with no concern for pain, and shaped Western science for centuries. Historians debate how far Descartes himself denied all sensation to animals, but the doctrine associated with him was used in exactly that way. Today it is rejected by biology and neuroscience.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal automatism, beast-machine
See also
Evolutionary continuity, Animal emotions, Vivisection, Sentience, Animal cognition
Example
"On the animal-machine view, a dog's cry under the scalpel would be just the creaking of a gear, an idea that current science rejects."

Animalism (in the sense of animal advocacy)

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A generic term for the set of ideas, movements and practices aimed at defending animals, ranging from welfarism to abolitionism.

Because it covers positions as different as welfarism and abolitionism, the term is criticized by stricter antispeciesists for blurring relevant strategic and ethical differences between these currents.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal cause, animal protection movement, animal rights movement
See also
Activism, Vegan movement, Animal liberation, Animal rights, Animal ethics
Example
"Animalism brings together those who ask for larger cages and those who want to abolish animal use, and the strategies of these currents do not always coincide."

Animals as persons

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

A legal and philosophical proposal to recognize certain animals as nonhuman persons, subjects of basic rights, and not mere objects.

Restricting this proposal only to species with high cognitive complexity is criticized by sentientists, who argue that the capacity to suffer, not intelligence, should be the relevant criterion for recognizing basic rights.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
nonhuman persons, nonhuman personhood
Antonyms
Animals as property
See also
Animal legal personhood, Animal habeas corpus, Animals as property, Great Ape Project, Animal rights
Example
"The lawyer argued that the chimpanzee should be treated as a person and not as a thing, and asked the court to recognize her right to liberty."

Animals as property

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

The predominant legal status of animals in most legal systems, which classifies them as movable goods that can be possessed, bought and sold.

It is the central target of the abolitionist critique, which argues that, as long as animals are legally property, their fundamental interests can always be legally subordinated to the economic interests of their owners.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animals as chattel, animals as goods
Antonyms
Animals as persons
See also
Objectification, Commodification, Animal legal personhood, Abolitionism, Animal law
Example
"Because the law treats the dog as property, in a divorce it is divided like an asset, without anyone asking whom it would prefer to live with."

Anthropocentric environmentalism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

An environmentalist view that protects the environment because it matters to human beings, which gives it instrumental value.

It already recognizes that individuals matter, people, so it has to explain why it would leave out the other animals who also feel.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
instrumental environmentalism, anthropocentric environmental ethics
Antonyms
ecocentrism
See also
Anthropocentrism, Instrumental value, Sentientist environmentalism, Holistic environmentalism, Environmentalism (moral)
Example
"He argues for protecting the forest because it regulates the climate and supplies water to cities, a typical argument of anthropocentric environmentalism."

Anthropocentric speciesism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A variant of speciesism that specifically privileges the human species as the supreme criterion of value, distinct from broader forms of species-based discrimination.

It is the most common form of speciesism, present in most cultural and institutional practices that treat human interests as automatically superior to those of any other species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
human supremacy, human-centered speciesism
Antonyms
antispeciesism
See also
Speciesism, Anthropocentrism, Moral anthropocentrism, Indexical speciesism
Example
“When a law protects any human interest above every animal interest, critics see anthropocentric speciesism.”

Anthropocentrism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

The view that places the human being as the center and measure of moral value.

It is the worldview that antispeciesism and sentientism most directly contest, because it assigns moral value on the basis of species, and not of the capacity to suffer.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
human-centrism, human-centredness
Antonyms
Biocentrism, Ecocentrism, Sentiocentrism
See also
Moral anthropocentrism, Anthropocentric speciesism, Biocentrism, Ecocentrism, Sentiocentrism
Example
"Saying that a forest is only worth what it gives to humans, and not the beings who live in it, is a typical anthropocentric position."

Beyond veganism →

Anthropomorphism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

The attribution of human characteristics, emotions or intentions to nonhuman animals; it can be a useful tool of empathy or a source of interpretive error, depending on the scientific context.

Categorically rejecting any attribution of mental states to animals, out of fear of anthropomorphism, can fall into the opposite bias: systematically underestimating the mental life of other species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
anthropomorphization, humanizing animals
Antonyms
anthropodenial
See also
Critical anthropomorphism, Morgan's canon, Animal emotions, Ethology, Animal cognition
Example
"Saying the cat was embarrassed because it knocked over the vase may be anthropomorphism, since it may merely have reacted to its owner's tone of voice."

Anti-ableist veganism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A current that links animal liberation to that of people with disabilities and criticizes the use of cognitive ability as a measure of worth.

Sunaura Taylor, in Beasts of Burden (2017), is a reference.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Disability-aware veganism
See also
Intersectionality, Intersectional veganism, Speciesism, Oppression
Example
“Anti-ableist veganism reminds us that many disabled people have dietary restrictions and that the movement must be accessible to them.”

Anti-vegan

noun · Activism and the Movement

A person who opposes veganism, often actively; also the adjective for what goes against veganism, such as a speech, a campaign, a law or a joke.

Not to be confused with non-vegan: someone who isn't vegan isn't anti-vegan for that reason. An anti-vegan is someone who rejects veganism, mocks vegans or works against the cause, for example with campaigns to restrict vegan products. The hostility is measurable: in a 2017 study, the psychologists Cara MacInnis and Gordon Hodson found that vegans were rated as negatively as, or more negatively than, several other social groups. This guide treats anti-vegan arguments in their strongest version, with what they get right and where they fail, because answering those who disagree well is more useful than dismissing them.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
vegan-basher, vegaphobe
Antonyms
Vegan
See also
Anti-veganism, Non-vegan, Carnist, Vegan, Critical thinking
Example
"The columnist, openly anti-vegan, wrote an article attacking those who refuse meat, but ended up answering critics with arguments that readers found weak."

Anti-veganism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

The set of positions, discourses, campaigns and measures that oppose veganism, as a philosophy or as a practice.

It ranges from jokes and stereotypes to industry campaigns and rules that hinder vegan products, such as the 2017 ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union that reserved names like "milk" and "cheese" for animal products. The most common anti-vegan arguments are nutritional, cultural and economic. The nutritional ones have lost ground: bodies such as the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics consider well-planned vegan diets appropriate at all stages of life, though some call for more caution in childhood.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
veganphobia, vegaphobia, vegan-bashing
Antonyms
Veganism
See also
Anti-vegan, Non-vegan, Carnism, Veganism, Vegan movement
Example
"Jokes about annoying vegans online are a mild form of anti-veganism, while campaigns to discredit the vegan diet without evidence are a more serious case."

The anti-vegan line of reasoning →

Antienvironmentalism

noun · Activism and the Movement

Organized opposition to environmental protection policies and movements, often in the name of economic growth, which includes denying or downplaying problems such as climate change.

Not every criticism of an environmental measure is antienvironmentalism: someone starting from sentientism, for example, questions measures that harm animals without denying environmental problems.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
environmental denialism
Antonyms
Political environmentalism
See also
Political environmentalism, Post-truth, Pseudoscience, Lobby, Environmentalism (ecologismo)
Example
"The campaign accused scientists of exaggerating deforestation data, a discourse typical of antienvironmentalism tied to economic interests."

Antimicrobial resistance

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The ability of bacteria and other microorganisms to survive drugs that used to kill them, which makes infections harder to treat.

One of the causes is the mass use of antibiotics in animal farming, often to prevent diseases favored by confinement or to speed up growth. Estimates published in the journal Science in 2019 indicate that about three quarters of the antimicrobials sold worldwide are used in farmed animals. The World Health Organization considers resistance one of the greatest threats to global health, and the European Union banned the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in 2006. It is a public health argument that adds to the ethical one. The main driver of resistance in human infections, however, is use in medicine itself, and no one knows precisely how much comes from animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Antibiotic resistance
See also
Superbug, Industrial livestock farming, Factory farm, Zoonosis
Example
“Routine antibiotic use in healthy animals speeds up antimicrobial resistance, making human infections harder to treat.”

Stop saying →

Antispeciesism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A position and movement that actively opposes speciesism, defending the equal consideration of interests across species.

Not every antispeciesist necessarily defends the end of all use of animals, a position more associated with abolitionism; in the strict sense, antispeciesism is the rejection of moral discrimination based on species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
anti-speciesism
Antonyms
Speciesism
See also
Speciesism, Equal consideration, Sentience, Animal liberation, Veganism
Example
"The activist explained that antispeciesism does not say all animals are the same, but that each one's suffering matters, whatever the species."

Beyond veganism →

Antivivisectionism

noun · Activism and the Movement

The movement that opposes vivisection and, more broadly, experimentation on animals; organized mainly from the 19th century in the United Kingdom.

The Irish writer Frances Power Cobbe founded one of the first antivivisection societies in 1875, and in 1876 the United Kingdom passed the first law regulating experiments on animals. The movement brought together many women and had links with women's suffrage. Today part of it calls for an end to all experimentation and part for gradual replacement by animal-free methods.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
antivivisection, anti-vivisection movement
See also
Vivisection, Animal experimentation, Replacement methods, Animal model, 3Rs
Example
"The nineteenth-century English antivivisection society organized petitions against surgery on live dogs in medical schools and called for protective laws."

Apathy

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

Emotional or motivational indifference in the face of another's suffering.

In relation to animals, it tends to work as a psychological mechanism that sustains exploitative practices despite the intellectual recognition that they cause suffering.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
indifference, unconcern
Antonyms
Empathy
See also
Empathy, Compassion, Selective outrage, Alienation, Activist fatigue
Example
"Faced with a video of a slaughterhouse, he shrugged and changed the subject, and his friend regretted that apathy in the face of others' suffering."

Aquaculture

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The farming of aquatic animals in captivity, with its own welfare issues that are little regulated.

In 2022, according to the FAO, aquaculture overtook capture fisheries for the first time as the main source of aquatic animals, with about 51% of production. A study published in 2023 estimated that about 124 billion farmed fish were killed for food in 2019, not counting shrimp and other crustaceans. Most die by asphyxiation in air or on ice, without stunning, and welfare laws usually protect fish far less than mammals and birds. Farming in dense tanks and net pens also brings disease and parasites and, for carnivorous species such as salmon, the use of wild fish in feed.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
aquafarming
See also
Fish farming (pisciculture), Fishing, Industrial fishing, Seafood, Animal welfare
Example
"Salmon aquaculture in net pens is growing, and with it debates about overcrowding, disease and the use of wild-caught fish in feed."

Aquafaba

noun · Plant-Derived Products

The liquid left from cooking chickpeas or other legumes, used as a vegan substitute for egg white because of its foaming properties.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
chickpea brine, chickpea water
See also
Banana biomass, Plant-based, Grains (lentils, quinoa), Vegan diet
Example
"Whipped to stiff peaks, aquafaba replaced the egg white in the meringue, and nobody at the party realized the dessert was vegan."

Arbitrariness

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The absence of a consistent rational justification for a distinction or decision.

It is identified as the central feature of speciesism: species, taken alone, is not a morally relevant criterion for justifying a difference in treatment.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
capriciousness
Antonyms
justification
See also
Logical consistency, Moral consistency, Justification, Double standard, Speciesism
Example
"Protecting dogs and cats but eating pigs, with no relevant difference between them, is for many philosophers a case of moral arbitrariness."

Argument

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A structured set of premises that support a conclusion.

The strength of an argument about the moral status of animals should be assessed by its logical validity and the evidence that supports it, and not by the familiarity or comfort its conclusion provides.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
reasoning, line of reasoning
See also
Fallacies, Logic, Critical thinking, Direct argument, Indirect argument
Example
"A good argument shows its premises and conclusion clearly, so that anyone who disagrees knows exactly which step to contest."

Argument from marginal cases

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The thesis that criteria used to exclude animals from moral consideration, such as rationality or language, would also exclude humans with severe cognitive disabilities, revealing an inconsistency in speciesism.

Because it exposes this inconsistency, many philosophers consider it one of the hardest challenges to answer for those who defend cognitive criteria as the basis for the moral exclusion of animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
argument from species overlap, argument from marginal humans
See also
Argument from relevance, Edge cases, Speciesism, Equal consideration, Rationality
Example
"If rationality justifies protecting only humans, the argument from marginal cases asks what to do about babies and people with severe cognitive disabilities."

Argument from potential

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The argument that a being who does not yet have certain capacities, such as reason and self-awareness, but can develop them, already deserves the protection of those who have them.

It is used against abortion and to explain why human babies would have a status that animals lack. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), replies that being a potential X does not confer the rights of an X: a prince is a potential king and does not thereby have a king's rights, and whoever destroys an acorn does not destroy an oak. He also notes that potential is a matter of degree, as in vitro fertilization shows. From an antispeciesist point of view, the argument does not explain why capacities an animal already has should count for less than capacities another being will only have in the future, and it leaves unanswered the humans who lack that potential, whom common morality protects without hesitation. Defenders such as John Finnis and Robert George hold that a human being has, from conception, the rational nature from which their rights derive, and Don Marquis, in "Why Abortion Is Immoral" (1989), replaces potential with the loss of a valuable future, a criterion that, as he himself acknowledged, may also apply to some animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Potentiality argument
See also
Argument from marginal cases, Self-conscious and merely conscious beings, Moral status, Edge cases
Example
“By the argument from potential, a baby deserves protection for what it may become, but the argument does not explain why what the pig already is should count for less.”

Argument from relevance

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The thesis that only morally relevant characteristics, such as the capacity to suffer, justify a difference in treatment; species, in itself, is not one of those characteristics.

It is one of the central arguments used to characterize speciesism as morally unjustified discrimination, analogous to racism and sexism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
relevance argument, argument from moral relevance
See also
Argument from marginal cases, Equal consideration, Speciesism, Sentience, Arbitrariness
Example
"By the argument from relevance, skin colour does not justify treating someone worse, and neither does species alone, since neither changes the capacity to suffer."

Arouca Law

proper noun · Animal Law and Legislation

Brazilian Law 11,794 of 2008, which regulates the use of vertebrate animals in scientific research and teaching, created the National Council for the Control of Animal Experimentation (CONCEA) and made Animal Use Ethics Committees mandatory.

It is named after the public health doctor and congressman Sérgio Arouca, author of the original bill. The law regulates experimentation rather than banning it: it requires institutions to be accredited, projects to receive ethical approval and attention to alternative methods. Critics argue that it legitimized practices that had been challenged in court, and supporters say it brought rules where there were almost none before.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Law 11.794/2008, Brazilian animal experimentation law
See also
Animal Use Ethics Committee (CEUA), Animal experimentation, 3Rs, Replacement methods
Example
"A research laboratory may only use animals in its studies if the project is approved under the Arouca Law."

Artificial insemination

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The mechanical introduction of semen into a female's reproductive tract without natural mating, a standard practice in modern livestock farming.

Semen is collected from males with an artificial vagina or, in some cases, by electroejaculation, and placed in the restrained female. The technique allows a few selected males to sire thousands of offspring, which speeds up selection for productivity. In commercial turkeys, selection has gone so far that the males, too heavy, have difficulty mating, and practically all reproduction depends on insemination.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
AI, Artificial breeding
Antonyms
Natural mating, Natural service
See also
Forced mating, Artificial selection, Rape rack, Artificial reproduction
Example
"On the dairy farm, cows undergo artificial insemination again and again throughout their lives, so that they become pregnant and keep producing milk."

Artificial reproduction

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Any assisted reproduction technique (artificial insemination, in vitro fertilization) used to control the genetics and productivity of animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Assisted reproduction
Antonyms
Natural reproduction
See also
Artificial insemination, Artificial selection, Forced mating, Animal cloning
Example
“In artificial reproduction of dairy cows, semen is collected from selected bulls and injected into females without any courtship.”

Artificial selection

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Deliberate human choice of desired genetic traits in animals through controlled breeding.

Selection for productivity has changed animals' bodies: according to a 2014 study by Martin Zuidhof and colleagues, broiler growth increased by more than 400% between 1957 and 2005, and rapid growth is associated with leg and heart problems. Dairy cows produce far more milk than the calf needs, which is associated with more mastitis and hoof problems, and laying hens lay about 300 eggs a year, far more than the wild ancestral species. In dogs, selection for appearance has produced hereditary diseases.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Selective breeding, Genetic improvement
Antonyms
Natural selection
See also
Pedigree, Artificial insemination, Domestication, Genetic engineering
Example
“Artificial selection in broiler chickens produced birds that gain weight so fast that many struggle to walk.”

Artivism

noun · Activism and the Movement

The use of art as a tool for activism and awareness-raising.
