Synonyms and related uses
art activism, activist art
See also
Activism, Protest, Street activism, Digital activism, Social movement
Example
"The group practised artivism by painting a huge canvas of cattle faces in the city centre, drawing attention to life inside slaughterhouses."

Autonomy

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The capacity of an agent to govern themselves and make their own decisions.

Although often used to deny moral status to animals because of their supposed lack of rational autonomy, this requirement is contested by antispeciesists, who point out that autonomy is not a prerequisite for having interests that deserve consideration: human babies and people with certain severe cognitive disabilities also lack it.

self-governance, self-determination
Antonyms
heteronomy, paternalism
See also
Preference autonomy, Freedom, Paternalism, Consent, Moral agent
Example
"The patient has autonomy to refuse a treatment, but a laboratory animal can neither consent to nor refuse what is done to it."

Battery cages

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Stacked, overcrowded cages used to confine laying hens, with extremely restricted space.

Each hen usually has less space than a sheet of letter-size paper, unable to spread her wings, nest, scratch or dust-bathe. The European Union banned conventional cages from 2012, but allows slightly larger "enriched" cages. Many companies, including in Brazil, have committed to buying only cage-free eggs, but cage-free systems still have problems, such as overcrowding and the culling of male chicks.

Synonyms, example and related terms

battery systems, stacked cages
Antonyms
cage-free, free range
See also
Animal confinement, Free range, Beak trimming, Poultry farming
Example

Beak trimming

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Partial cutting of the beak of birds (usually laying hens) to reduce aggressive pecking caused by the stress of confinement.

The cut is made on chicks, with a hot blade or, increasingly, with infrared, and it affects innervated tissue; studies record signs of pain, especially with the hot blade. The practice treats the symptom, not the cause: pecking comes from stress, overcrowding and lack of materials for scratching. Some countries, such as Norway, have banned it for decades, which shows that hens can be kept without beak trimming, although the pecking problem does not disappear with the ban alone.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
beak cutting, debeaking
See also
Battery cages, Cannibalism (in confinement), Anesthesia
Example
"Laying hens raised in cages undergo debeaking as chicks, with a hot-blade cut to the beak so they do not injure each other by pecking."

Beans

noun · Plant-Derived Products

A protein-rich legume, a dietary staple in many cultures, including Brazilian cuisine.

Synonyms and related uses

See also
Soy, Pea, Plant protein, Rice
Example

Bear bile farming

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The keeping of bears, mainly Asiatic black bears, in small cages for the periodic extraction of bile from the gallbladder, used in the traditional medicine of some Asian countries.

Extraction is done through catheters or open wounds in the abdomen, and the bears may spend years confined, with pain, infections and stereotypic behaviors. The active substance in bile, ursodeoxycholic acid, can be produced without animals, and there are plant alternatives within traditional medicine itself. The practice remains legal in China. Vietnam banned it in 2005, and South Korea approved the end of bear farming for bile from 2026.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
bear bile extraction farm, bear farm
See also
Animal confinement, Stereotypic behavior, Animal trafficking, Animal cruelty
Example
“Photos of bears in tiny cages at a bear bile farm led the government to restrict the activity.”

Beast of burden

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An animal, such as a donkey, mule, horse or ox, used to carry loads or pull carts; figuratively, a person made to do the heavy work without recognition.

Donkeys and mules still carry loads and pull carts in many regions, often with wounds, excessive weight and little water and rest. In recent years they have also been slaughtered in large numbers for the trade in skins used in ejiao, a traditional Chinese medicine product, which has led several countries to restrict this trade. English has a whole family of figurative expressions from working animals: "workhorse", "pack mule", "work like a dog", "treated like a beast of burden". Brazilian Portuguese says "burro de carga". They all show how normalized animal exploitation is: saying a person is "treated like a beast of burden" denounces an abuse against them, but assumes the same treatment is normal for the animal.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
pack animal, draft animal, workhorse
See also
Animal traction, Speciesist term, Objectification, Riding, Harness
Example
"The pack donkey climbed the hill with bags of cement on its back, and residents grew used to seeing it as normal."

Beekeeping

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The keeping of bees to produce honey, wax, propolis and other products, with its own debates about insect sentience and the impact of commercial production.

In commercial beekeeping it is common to clip the queen's wings to stop the swarm from leaving, artificially inseminate queens, replace the queen frequently and substitute sugar syrup for the honey removed. Research gathered, for example, in the book The Mind of a Bee (2022), by the biologist Lars Chittka, suggests that bees have complex learning and emotion-like states, which makes it plausible that they are sentient, although the question remains open. There are also studies indicating that large numbers of European honeybee hives can compete with native bees for flowers. Most definitions of veganism, such as the Vegan Society's, exclude honey.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
bee farming, beekeeping practice
See also
Honey, Propolis, Xenospeciesism, Insectivory, Sentience
Example
"Many vegans avoid honey on the view that beekeeping treats bees as a production source, although the sentience of these insects is still debated."

Begging the question

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A fallacy in which the argument assumes, in one of its premises, the very conclusion it should prove, often in other words.

It is also called circular reasoning, and the Latin name is petitio principii; Aristotle already described it. The argument may even be valid, but it gives someone who doubts the conclusion no new reason to accept it. Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), shows that the mistake appears on both sides of the debate: "we have a right to eat animals" and "animals have a right to life", said with no further reason, only repeat that eating animals is permissible or that killing them is wrong. The same happens when moral worth is defined by the very trait one wants to use to exclude animals, such as having a human soul or belonging to the human species. The way out is to say why the right exists, for example through sentience or the interests of whoever would hold it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
circular reasoning, petitio principii
See also
Fallacies, Validity, Hidden premise, Rights
Example
“Saying that eating animals is permissible because we have a right to eat them is begging the question: the premise just repeats the conclusion.”

Fallacies →

Benefit

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

What leaves a being better off than they would otherwise be, either by giving them something good, such as pleasure, health or companionship, or by preventing something bad.

In bioethics, the principle of beneficence asks us to act for the good of others, and it is one of the four principles proposed by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress in 1979, alongside respect for autonomy, non-maleficence and justice. In the debate about animals, the question is often whether the benefits of a use outweigh the harms it causes. Often the benefit to humans is small, such as taste or convenience, and the harm to animals is enormous, such as a life of confinement and death.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
advantage, gain, good
Antonyms
Harm, Detriment
See also
Harm, Maleficence, Interest, Positive experiences, Pleasure
Example
"For the breeder, confinement brings the benefit of lower costs, but the harm to the animal, a life of confinement followed by death, is far greater."

Benefit of the doubt

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

A decision rule according to which, when there is real doubt about whether an avoidable act would seriously harm someone, one should act as if it would, rather than take the risk.

In Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), Peter Singer illustrates it with the hunters' rule: someone who sees something moving in the bushes and does not know whether it is game or another hunter does not shoot. He applied it to the doubt about which animals are self-conscious: since it is hard to know, and killing such a being would be serious, it should be given the benefit of the doubt, which, Singer says, is enough to condemn much of the killing of animals. The same logic applies to doubt about the sentience of fish, crustaceans and insects, and lies behind the precaution defended by Jonathan Birch in The Edge of Sentience (2024), for whom a realistic possibility of sentience already calls for proportionate measures. Critics say the rule, applied without limit, would paralyze action, since almost anything may affect some being of uncertain sentience; the usual answer is to weigh the probability and severity of the harm against the cost of avoiding it, which, in the case of food, is low.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Hunter's rule, Precautionary principle (on sentience)
See also
Nociception, Sentience, Self-conscious and merely conscious beings
Example
"If we do not know whether the octopus suffers, the benefit of the doubt says not to cook it alive."

Bias

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A systematic tendency of thought that distorts judgment in a predictable way, usually without the person noticing.

Biases aren't stupidity or bad faith: everyone has them, because the brain uses shortcuts. Some come up a lot in conversations about animals, such as confirmation bias, status quo bias and the cognitive dissonance of the meat paradox, which leads people to think the animals we eat feel less. Knowing your own biases helps you talk more honestly. The guide has a page with the most common biases about animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Tendency, Partiality
Antonyms
Impartiality
See also
Fallacies, Cognitive dissonance, Cognitive biases, Impartiality
Example
“Our proximity bias makes us feel more compassion for a dog than for a pig, although both are capable of suffering.”

Biases →

Biocentric egalitarianism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

The thesis that all living beings, or all natural entities, have equal intrinsic value, with neither species nor the capacity to feel making any difference in value.

Arne Næss spoke in 1973 of a biospherical egalitarianism "in principle"; Bill Devall and George Sessions, in Deep Ecology (1985), presented biocentric equality as the intuition that all organisms and entities in the ecosphere have an equal right to live and flourish; and Paul W. Taylor, in Respect for Nature (1986), gave the idea its most developed philosophical form, treating each organism as a teleological center of life with equal inherent worth. Taylor drew a consequence favorable to animals: since raising them for food requires destroying far more plants, respect for nature would call for a vegetarian diet. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), replies that a plant pursues its own good only in a metaphorical sense, as a river seeks the sea, that being part of an interconnected whole does not prove intrinsic value, let alone equal value, and that the thesis clashes with strong intuitions, such as that a gorilla counts for more than a weed. From a sentientist point of view, equating the value of a pig with that of a yeast dilutes the consideration owed to those who feel, and Taylor's rules for conflicts still allow destroying organisms and habitats for the sake of non-basic human interests.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Biocentric equality, Biospherical egalitarianism
Antonyms
Sentientism, Anthropocentrism
See also
Biocentrism, Reverence for life, Deep ecology, Sentientism
Example
"Under biocentric egalitarianism, an oak and a dog would have the same intrinsic value."

Biocentrism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

The view that extends moral value to all life, sentient or not.

It diverges from sentientism by also including organisms without the capacity to feel, such as plants, in the sphere of direct moral consideration, a relevant point of disagreement between the two currents.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
biocentric ethics, life-centred ethics
Antonyms

See also
Sentiocentrism, Ecocentrism, Anthropocentrism, Living being, Naturocentrism
Example
"On biocentrism, a tree has moral value of its own, even though it feels nothing, so felling it for no reason would already be a wrong."

Bioethicist

noun · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

An expert in bioethics: a person who studies the moral problems of medicine, scientific research and biotechnology, and who often sits on committees that review research and clinical decisions.

Bioethicists serve on ethics committees in hospitals and in human research and, in the case of animals, on committees such as Brazil's CEUAs, which review the use of animals in teaching and research. Most of this work follows the 3Rs principle, replacing, reducing and refining the use of animals, which limits harm without questioning whether the use is just. Some bioethicists go further: Peter Singer, one of the central figures of animal ethics, was for decades a professor of bioethics at Princeton University.

Bioethics

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A branch of applied ethics that investigates moral questions related to the life sciences and health, including animal research, biotechnology and medicine.

Traditionally centered on human dilemmas, bioethics has been pressed by sentientist currents to fully incorporate the interests of nonhuman animals as moral subjects, and not only as means to human ends.

It is from biological evidence, and not from intuitions or cultural traditions, that criteria such as the presence of sentience are usually assessed.

Brambell Report

proper noun · Animal Law and Legislation

A report by a British government committee, published in 1965, on the welfare of animals in intensive farming systems; it was a response to Ruth Harrison's book Animal Machines (1964).

The report argued that every animal should at least be able to turn around, groom itself, get up, lie down and stretch its limbs, and it recognized that animals can suffer mentally. These ideas gave rise to the Five Freedoms, later formulated by the UK's Farm Animal Welfare Council. It is a landmark in the beginning of animal welfare science. "The cattle entered the chute in single file, a narrow corridor that led them to the squeeze chute, where they would be vaccinated."

Bullfighting

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A spectacle involving a confrontation between a bull and bullfighters, usually resulting in serious injury and the death of the animal.

In the Spanish bullfight, the bull is wounded with lances and banderillas before being killed with a sword; in Portugal, killing in the ring is generally prohibited, but the bull is wounded and usually slaughtered afterwards. Bullfighting is still legal in a few countries, such as Spain, Portugal, France (in some regions), Mexico, Peru, Ecuador and Venezuela, and in 2024 Colombia passed a law banning it from 2027. Supporters invoke tradition and culture, an argument that also appears in defence of vaquejada and rodeo.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Corrida de toros
See also
Banderillas, Vaquejada, Cultural relativism, Rodeo
Example
“The city banned bullfighting after a referendum, but defenders of the spectacle argued that it is part of the local culture.”

Burdizzo

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An instrument used for bloodless castration of males, by crushing the spermatic cord without an incision.

"Bloodless" means without blood, not without pain: the clamp crushes the spermatic cord through the skin, and studies record signs of acute and prolonged pain. Like castration with a rubber ring or a knife, burdizzo castration is allowed without anaesthesia in young animals in many countries; in the United Kingdom, for example, in calves and lambs up to a certain age.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
bloodless castrator, emasculatome
See also
Castration, Anesthesia, Intensive livestock farming, Pain
Example
"With the burdizzo, the vet crushed the calf's spermatic cord without cutting, but explained that the procedure also hurts and calls for anaesthesia."

Butter

noun · Animal-Derived Products

A dairy fat obtained by churning cream.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Dairy products, Margarine, Milk, Plant-based cream
Example
"In the vegan cake recipe, he swapped the butter for coconut oil and plant cream, and the result came out soft."

Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness

proper noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

A declaration signed by a group of neuroscientists on July 7, 2012, at the University of Cambridge, stating that humans are not the only beings with the neurological substrates that generate consciousness.

The text states that all mammals and birds, and many other animals such as octopuses, have these substrates. It is neither a law nor a formal consensus of all of science, but it carried great public weight because it came from researchers in the field. In 2024, the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness went further, speaking of a realistic possibility of conscious experience in all vertebrates and many invertebrates.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Cambridge Declaration
See also
Animal consciousness, Subjective experience, Sentience
Example
"The 2012 Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness is cited by those who argue that mammals, birds and other animals have the neural basis for consciousness."

Cannibalism (in confinement)

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An abnormal behavior in which confined animals (such as pigs or birds) bite or peck one another because of stress, boredom or behavioral frustration.

The industry's most common response is not to change the conditions that cause the behaviour but to mutilate the animals: the tip of hens' beaks and piglets' tails are cut off. Research points to lack of space, of straw or other materials for rooting and scratching, and genetic selection for productivity as causes. In the European Union, the law prohibits routine tail docking and requires conditions to be changed first, but the rule is poorly enforced in most countries.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Beak trimming, Tail docking, Environmental enrichment
Example
"In an overcrowded shed, cannibalism among the birds became common, so the farmer trimmed their beaks instead of lowering the stocking density."

Capabilities approach

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A theory of justice that assesses well-being by what each being is able to do and to be, that is, by its real opportunities to exercise the functions proper to its form of life.

It was created by the economist Amartya Sen, starting with the lecture "Equality of What?" (1979), and extended to animals by the philosopher Martha Nussbaum in Frontiers of Justice (2006) and Justice for Animals (2023). It goes beyond pain: a circus bear that doesn't suffer, but lives caged, dressed up and performing tricks, is still deprived of foraging, exploring and living socially as a bear, and that is already a harm. It thus protects more than an accounting of pleasure and pain alone and fits with the idea of telos. Critics point to three problems: defining what flourishing means for each species can be used to justify whatever is natural, predation included; moving sentience out of the centre would open the door to plants and ecosystems, which Nussbaum avoids by requiring sentience; and lists of capabilities help little in settling conflicts of interest.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
capability approach
See also
Telos, Animal welfare, Sentience, Utilitarianism, Justice
Example
"On the capabilities approach, an elephant held in a small enclosure, even if well fed, loses the chance to walk long distances and live in a herd."

Political or ethical objection →

Captive breeding

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The breeding of animals of wild species in zoos, aquariums or conservation centers, generally with the stated aim of maintaining populations of threatened species.

There are success stories with release back into the wild, such as the golden lion tamarin in Brazil and Przewalski's horse in Mongolia. But most animals born in zoos are never released, many belong to species that are not threatened, and surplus animals may be sold or killed. The ethical question is whether the good of the species justifies each individual's life in captivity.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Ex situ breeding, Captive propagation
See also
Zoo, Extinction, Holistic environmentalism, Compassionate conservation
Example
“The zoo announced the birth of a jaguar cub through captive breeding, but the animal will always live in an enclosure.”

Carbonism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A form of substratism that gives less weight to the good of a sentient being because its body is not organic, carbon-based.

It stands to substratism as anthropocentrism stands to speciesism: the particular case that privileges one's own group. If what matters is the capacity to be harmed or benefited, the material the body is made of decides nothing.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
carbon chauvinism, bio-chauvinism
Antonyms
Substrate neutrality
See also
Substratism, Speciesism, Sentience in AI and digital systems
Example
"Saying a digital system could never feel pain just because it is not made of cells would be, for some philosophers, a form of carbon chauvinism."

Carnism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

The belief system that makes eating certain animals seem normal, natural and inevitable, and that hides the fact that it is a choice.

The term was coined by the social psychologist Melanie Joy in 2001 and spread through her book Why We Love Dogs, Eat Pigs, and Wear Cows (2009). The central idea is that eating meat isn't the absence of a position, but a position sustained by justifications Joy summed up as three Ns: normal, natural and necessary. A 2015 study by Jared Piazza and colleagues confirmed these justifications and added a fourth: nice. Carnism also explains why the same culture finds it right to eat pigs and wrong to eat dogs. Some criticize the term as loaded, because it names as an ideology what most people see as a simple habit.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
carnistic ideology, carnist ideology
Antonyms
Veganism
See also
Carnist, Speciesism, Cognitive dissonance, Anti-vegan
Example
"According to the psychologist, carnism explains why we love dogs and eat pigs without feeling any contradiction: the belief that eating meat is normal stays invisible."

Carnist

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A person who, knowingly or not, follows carnism, that is, who eats animals because they consider it normal, natural and necessary; also the adjective for what reflects or sustains carnism, such as an advertisement or a policy.

The word describes a position, not an insult, and hardly anyone calls themselves a carnist: most people have never thought of eating meat as a choice, which is exactly what the concept points out. So using it in a conversation can sound like an accusation and push the other person away; it usually works better to explain an idea than to label someone. Not every carnist is anti-vegan: many people eat meat and respect, or even admire, those who don't.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
adherent of carnism
Antonyms
Vegan
See also
Carnism, Non-vegan, Anti-vegan
Example
"She described herself as a carnist without knowing it: she had never questioned why she eats cow and pig, yet would never eat a dog."

Carnivore diet

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A fad diet that excludes all or almost all plant foods and is based on meat, eggs and sometimes dairy.

It is promoted on social media with stories of improved health, but there are no long-term studies of its safety. The main survey, from 2021, heard from 2,029 followers online, with self-reported data, and the authors urged caution; many participants had high LDL cholesterol. The diet excludes fiber and several plant nutrients. Not to be confused with carnism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
all-meat diet, zero-carb diet
Antonyms
Vegan diet
See also
Carnivorism, Restrictive diet, Healthy diet
Example
"Influencers promote the carnivore diet as miraculous, but nutritionists warn that it excludes fiber and vitamins and lacks long-term studies."
  • doi.org

Carnivorism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

In biology, a diet based mainly on meat, characteristic of animals such as cats; applied to humans, a diet based mainly or entirely on animal products.

Not to be confused with carnism, the belief system that normalizes eating certain animals and not others.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
carnivory, carnivorousness, meat-eating
Antonyms
Herbivory
See also
Carnivore diet, Omnivorism, Herbivory
Example
"The carnivory of lions is biological and necessary; that of humans, who can be well nourished on plants, is a cultural choice."

Carrying capacity

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The maximum population size of a species that an environment can sustain over time, given the available resources, represented in models by the letter K.

The concept appears in the logistic equation, proposed by the Belgian mathematician Pierre-François Verhulst in 1838, in which a population's growth slows as it approaches K. In wild animal ethics, the central point is that the number of offspring born is usually far greater than the carrying capacity, so that in a stable population the surplus dies, generally early. For this reason, providing more food without controlling births may only increase the number of animals that are born and die, which is why proposals such as contraception come up in this debate. Ecologists criticize the use of carrying capacity as a fixed number, since it varies with climate, with other species and over time.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Population dynamics, r and K reproductive strategies, Animal population control
Example
"When the deer population exceeded the forest's carrying capacity, the winter food shortage caused starvation and mass deaths."

Castration

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The surgical removal or disabling of an animal's reproductive organs, used both in livestock production and in population control of pets.

In dogs and cats, neutering is done by veterinarians under anaesthesia and is the main way to reduce the number of abandoned animals. In livestock farming it serves mainly production interests, such as avoiding boar taint in the meat of male pigs and making bulls more docile, and it is often done without anaesthesia on young animals, with a knife, rubber ring or burdizzo. For pigs there is immunocastration, a vaccine that suppresses sex hormones. Germany banned castrating piglets without anaesthesia in 2021, and in Brazil the 2020 pig welfare rule gives farms until 2030 to require anaesthesia and analgesia for all surgical castration.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
neutering, spaying
See also
Burdizzo, Anesthesia, Animal population control
Example
"The city opened a free neutering drive for dogs and cats to reduce unwanted litters and abandonment on the streets."

Catch and release

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A form of recreational fishing in which the fish is hooked, taken out of the water and returned alive.

It is presented as harmless or sustainable, but the hook injures the mouth and sometimes the gills, the struggle and time out of water cause stress, and some fish die after release. Research on pain in fish, such as the biologist Lynne Sneddon's work with trout, shows responses to injury that go beyond reflex. If the fish can feel, injuring them for fun is hard to justify, even when they go back into the water.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Catch-and-release angling
See also
Fishing, Pain, Sentience, Sport hunting
Example
“The angler said he practiced catch and release, but the fish returned to the water was injured and exhausted.”

Categorical imperative

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

In Immanuel Kant's ethics, the supreme principle of morality, which commands acting in a certain way regardless of the desires or ends of the agent.

Kant set it out in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785) in more than one formula. The formula of universal law asks us to act only on a rule we could will to hold for everyone; the formula of humanity asks us to treat humanity, in ourselves and in others, always also as an end and never merely as a means. For Kant, only rational beings are ends in themselves, and duties regarding animals would be indirect: cruelty to them would be wrong because it coarsens those who practice it. Tom Regan, as Nathan Nobis reads him in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), keeps the idea of never treating anyone merely as a means and changes who counts as an end in itself: every subject of a life. Christine Korsgaard, in Fellow Creatures (2018), argues from Kant himself that animals are ends in themselves too.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
formula of humanity, humanity principle
Antonyms
hypothetical imperative
See also
Deontology, Instrumentalization, Subjects-of-a-life, Perfect and imperfect duties
Example
“If the categorical imperative tells us never to treat anyone merely as a means, the question is why that someone would have to be rational, and not just sentient.”

Catupsoy (Brazilian brand)

proper noun · Plant-Derived Products

A Brazilian commercial brand of soy-based plant cream, inspired by requeijão cremoso (a Brazilian creamy spreadable cheese).

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
vegan cream cheese
See also
Plant-based cream, Requei Soy, Soy protein
Example
"At the vegan breakfast, she spread Catupsoy on warm bread, since the soy cream reminds her of the requeijão she ate as a child."

Cellular agriculture

noun phrase · Reducing and Ending the Use of Animals

The production of biological tissues (including "meat") from cell culture, without raising and slaughtering animals.

Besides cultivated meat, the field includes precision fermentation, in which microorganisms produce proteins identical to animal ones, such as whey or egg-white proteins, without cows or hens. Not every cellular agriculture product does away with animals entirely: cultivated meat still starts from animal cells.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
cell-based agriculture, cell ag
See also
Cultivated meat, Technological veganism, Genetic engineering, Plant-based, Meat
Example
"A cellular agriculture startup unveiled a cheese made by precision fermentation, with proteins identical to those in milk but without using cows."

Central nervous system

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The part of the nervous system made up of the brain and spinal cord, sometimes used as a criterion for inferring the presence of sentience in a species.

Adopting this anatomical criterion exclusively risks underestimating the capacity to feel in species with different nervous architectures, such as octopuses and many insects.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
CNS, Brain and spinal cord
Antonyms
Peripheral nervous system
See also
Nervous system, Sentience, Nociception, Animal cognition
Example
“In vertebrates the central nervous system integrates painful information, while octopuses and insects show very different architectures, which makes comparison difficult.”

Cereals (oats)

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

Grains such as oats, used as a base for food and for plant-based drinks.

grains

Plant milk, Grains (lentils, quinoa), Vegan diet
Example
"For breakfast, he cooked oats with fruit and cinnamon, a cheap, fully plant-based meal that keeps energy up for hours."

Charity

noun · Activism and the Movement

Help given voluntarily to those in need, such as donations of money, time or goods, usually without expecting anything in return.

In the animal cause, charity shows up in donations to shelters, sanctuaries and organizations, and in rescues. It is valuable, but there is an important critique: treating animals as objects of charity, rather than as beings with rights, suggests that helping them is an optional favor. For many animal advocates, what animals need is justice, starting with not being exploited. Charity can also be more or less effective, and some organizations assess where donations reduce the most suffering.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
philanthropy, benevolence, almsgiving
See also
Altruism, Effective altruism, Rights
Example
"The association survives on charity: residents donate food and money every month to help feed the dogs and cats rescued from the neighborhood's streets."

Cheese

noun · Animal-Derived Products

A dairy product obtained by coagulating milk, traditionally using rennet of animal origin.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Dairy products, Rennet, Vegan cheese, Milk
Example
“Although it seems harmless, cheese requires cows to be impregnated, separated from their calves and milked repeatedly.”

Children's palate

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

The set of food preferences formed in childhood, relevant to discussions about food education and the transition to plant-based diets.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Healthy eating, Dietary transition, Fast food, Diet
Example
“The school changed its menu and many parents feared rejection, but they found that children's palates adapt well to new flavors with gradual exposure.”

Choice

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The act of selecting one of several alternatives, an expression of the freedom and autonomy of the one who chooses.

Having the freedom to choose does not say whether the choice is just: when there is a victim, the choice no longer concerns only the person making it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
option, decision
Antonyms
imposition, coercion
See also
Decision, Autonomy, Freedom, Personal choice, Consent
Example

Cholesterol

noun · Animal-Derived Products

A lipid substance made by the body itself and present in relevant amounts only in animal foods; plants contain only traces, which do not matter in the diet.

The human body produces all the cholesterol it needs, so there is no need to get it from food. Plants have phytosterols, of similar structure, and only traces of cholesterol, of no dietary importance.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Healthy diet, Nutrition, Vegan diet
Example
"The doctor explained that plant foods contain no cholesterol and that the body's own cholesterol is produced by the liver itself."

Churrasco (Brazilian barbecue)

noun · Animal-Derived Products

A technique for preparing meat grilled over embers, culturally associated with the consumption of beef in South America.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
barbecue, BBQ, asado
See also
Vegan churrasco (Brazilian barbecue), Meat, Carnism
Example
"The Sunday churrasco gathers the family around the embers, a tradition many Brazilians see as part of the country's cultural identity."

CITES

acronym · Animal Law and Legislation

The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, a treaty signed in 1973 and in force since 1975, which controls or prohibits trade between countries in threatened species.

Species are listed in appendices according to their level of threat, and commercial trade in the most threatened is prohibited. The convention protects species, not individuals: an animal of a common species is not protected by it, and the treaty does not deal with suffering in transport or captivity. Even so, it is the main international tool against the trafficking of wild animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Washington Convention, Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species
See also
Animal trafficking, Extinction, Holistic environmentalism
Example
"To legally export crocodile skins, the company needed permits required by CITES, which regulates trade in threatened species between countries."

Civil disobedience

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

A public, deliberate and usually nonviolent breach of a law, carried out on grounds of conscience to protest an injustice or change a law or policy, often accepting the punishment.

The term became popular with Henry David Thoreau's essay (1849), and the most cited definition is John Rawls's, in A Theory of Justice (1971); Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. are the classic examples. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), points out that in a democracy majority rule carries moral weight, and that disobedience is easier to justify when the contested decision does not really express the will of the majority, for example because the public does not know what is going on; acting illegally to publicize an abuse can then be an extension of democratic means. He discusses the 1984 case in which the Animal Liberation Front took from a University of Pennsylvania laboratory videos of brain-injury experiments on monkeys, and separates damage to property, which he examines case by case, from violence against people, which he rejects. There is disagreement about the legitimacy and effectiveness of such actions, and part of the movement prefers open rescue, done openly and accepting the legal consequences.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Civil resistance
Antonyms
Obedience to the law
See also
Direct action, Nonviolence, Protest, Legality
Example
“The group entered the farm openly, filmed everything and waited for the police, in an act of civil disobedience.”

Classical utilitarianism

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The version of utilitarianism that seeks to maximize the total aggregate sum of well-being of all those affected by a decision, without giving additional weight to those who are worse off.

It differs from negative utilitarianism in holding that positive experiences can, in principle, compensate for suffering.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Hedonistic utilitarianism, Benthamite utilitarianism
Antonyms
Negative utilitarianism
See also
Utilitarianism, Negative utilitarianism, Consequentialism, Utility maximisation
Example
“For classical utilitarianism, a pleasurable experience can offset a painful one, so the total balance of happiness is what matters.”

Co-optation

noun · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

Absorbing an opponent, a movement or an idea by offering positions, advantages, recognition or partnerships, so that it stops challenging and starts serving the interests of whoever co-opted it.

In the animal cause, the concern takes several forms: welfare labels and partnerships that make exploitation more acceptable without reducing it, words like "humane" and "sustainable" used in industry marketing, and large meat companies buying or launching plant-based brands. Not all of this is co-optation: talking to companies, supporting reforms and seeing meatpackers sell plant-based products can help animals, and the movement debates when it helps and when it hinders. The useful test is to ask whether the partnership brings the end of exploitation closer or pushes it away, and whether those invited to the table can still say no.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
capture, absorption, assimilation
See also
Political pawns, Lobby, Welfarism, Manipulation
Example
"Critics saw co-optation when the big company began funding the NGO and, in return, earned a welfare label for its farms."

Cochineal carmine

noun phrase · Animal-Derived Products

A natural red dye extracted from dried females of the cochineal insect, used in foods and cosmetics.

It is estimated that about 70,000 cochineal insects are needed to produce one pound (about half a kilo) of dye. On labels it appears as carmine, cochineal, carminic acid or E120, in yogurts, drinks, candy and lipsticks, and many people do not know it comes from insects. In 2012, Starbucks stopped using it in strawberry drinks after customer complaints.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
cochineal, E120, natural red 4, carminic acid
See also
Cruelty-free, Insectivory
Example
"Reading the strawberry yogurt label, she noticed the cochineal carmine dye and understood why the package carried no vegan seal."

Cognitive biases

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Systematic distortions of judgment that affect how animal suffering is perceived. Biases such as cognitive dissonance and conformity bias help explain why widely shared beliefs about the moral value of animals do not always translate into consistent behavior.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Bias, Fallacies, Cognitive dissonance, Critical thinking
Example
“Confirmation bias is one of the cognitive biases that make us accept only the information that fits what we already do.”

Cognitive dissonance

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The psychological discomfort generated by the coexistence of contradictory beliefs, or of beliefs and behaviors.

In animal consumption, it typically appears between loving animals and sustaining practices that harm them, and is often resolved through rationalizations, such as the naturalistic fallacy, rather than through a change in behavior.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
cognitive conflict, belief-behavior discomfort
Antonyms
cognitive consonance
See also
Moral consistency, Moral schizophrenia, Carnism, Disneyfication
Example
“She loves dogs but keeps eating meat; when she notices the contradiction, she feels cognitive dissonance and changes the subject.”

Biases →

Comfort zone

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

A psychological state of familiarity and low risk that tends to resist change. In the context of animal consumption, it is often cited as one of the main psychological obstacles to adopting habits more aligned with the equal consideration of interests across species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Comfort area
See also
Dietary transition, Cognitive dissonance, Paradigm shift, Humane education
Example
“Leaving one’s comfort zone, trading old habits for new recipes, can be the first step toward aligning the plate with one’s values.”

Commodification

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The process of turning a sentient being into a commodity, valued for their exchange value rather than their intrinsic value.

In most of the world's laws, including Brazil's, animals are treated as property that can be bought, sold and inherited, even though some instruments, such as the European Union's Treaty of Lisbon, already recognize them as sentient beings. An animal's price depends on its weight, breed or productivity, not on its interests.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
commoditization, commercialization
See also
Animals as property, Intrinsic value, Objectification
Example
"In the commodification of animals, a hen is measured by the eggs she lays and sold as an input, not seen as an individual."

Political or ethical objection →

Common good

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

The set of conditions that benefit the collectivity.

The systematic exclusion of animals' interests from the definition of what counts as the "common good" is identified by antispeciesists as an arbitrary limitation of this concept to a single species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
public interest, collective welfare
Antonyms
private interest
See also
Justice, Communitarianism, Utilitarianism, Contractualism, Utility maximisation
Example
"Supporters of banning cosmetic tests on animals say it serves the common good, since it reflects ethical values that society shares."

Communitarianism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A current in political philosophy holding that justice and moral values arise from the traditions, practices and shared understandings of each community, rather than from universal, abstract principles.

It gained ground in the 1980s as a critique of John Rawls's liberalism, with Alasdair MacIntyre (After Virtue, 1981), Michael Sandel (Liberalism and the Limits of Justice, 1982), Michael Walzer (Spheres of Justice, 1983) and Charles Taylor. For animals, it cuts both ways: a state that promotes common values can ban cruel practices that liberalism would leave to individual choice, but if the standard is whatever the community already values, vaquejada, bullfighting and factory farming get the seal of tradition. Mary Midgley and J. Baird Callicott tried to include animals through ties of community, which also makes room for putting those close to us first. Critics such as Alasdair Cochrane, in An Introduction to Animals and Political Theory (2010), reply that custom does not justify harm and that protecting animals requires a standard that doesn't depend on majority approval.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Antonyms
Liberal individualism
See also
Contextual universalism and particularism, Mixed community, Cultural relativism, Liberalism
Example
"From the standpoint of communitarianism, a town's values arise from shared life, not from abstract principles valid for all humanity."

Political or ethical objection →

Companion animal

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An animal kept for emotional and social reasons, with no productive purpose (dogs, cats and other pets).

The line between companion and farmed animal is cultural, not biological: dogs are eaten in some countries, guinea pigs are pets in some places and food in others, such as Peru, and pigs can also live as companions. Companion animals receive more affection and legal protection, but they are also bought, sold, bred in large numbers and abandoned.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
pet, house pet
See also
Pet, Carnism, Selective outrage, Farmed animal, Guardian or caregiver
Example
"He treats his dog as a family member but serves bacon at breakfast, and the example is cited to discuss the line between companion and farmed animals."

Compassion

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The capacity to recognize another being's suffering and feel motivated to relieve it.

Although it is an important emotional basis, sentientist currents warn that compassion alone is insufficient and can be applied inconsistently, arguing that it should be accompanied by rational consistency in applying equal consideration of interests.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
pity, sympathy, mercy
Antonyms
Cruelty, Indifference
See also
Empathy, Altruism, Suffering
Example
"Moved by compassion, the neighbor stopped the car, picked up the injured dog from the roadside and took him straight to the vet."

Compassionate conservation

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A current in conservation that defends protecting species and ecosystems without causing unnecessary harm to individual animals.

A landmark of the movement is the collection Ignoring Nature No More (2013), edited by the ethologist Marc Bekoff, and its principles are usually summed up as "first, do no harm", "individuals matter", inclusivity and peaceful coexistence. Arian Wallach and colleagues (2018) defended the approach in the journal Conservation Biology, and Matt Hayward and colleagues (2019) replied in the same journal that it picks mammal examples, ignores the native animals killed by invasive predators and may weaken conservation. From a sentientist point of view, compassionate conservation is an advance, but a limited one: as Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) notes, it deals mainly with the harms caused by conservation actions themselves, not with the natural harms that most wild animals suffer. That is why he distinguishes it from welfare biology.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
welfare-based conservation
See also
Conservation biology, Conservation welfare, Welfare biology, Invasive alien species
Example
"Advocates of compassionate conservation propose controlling an invasive species by sterilization rather than culling, protecting the ecosystem without killing individuals."

Conscientious objection to animal experimentation

noun phrase · Reducing and Ending the Use of Animals

The right of students, teachers and professionals to refuse to take part in practices that use or kill animals, such as dissection in classes, without suffering academic or professional harm.

Italy has had a law recognizing this right since 1993. In many courses, refusals opened the way to replacement methods, such as models, computer simulations and the bodies of animals that died of natural causes, and comparative studies have found no loss of learning with these methods.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Conscientious refusal of animal dissection
See also
Replacement methods, 3Rs, Vivisection, Animal experimentation
Example
“The biology student filed a conscientious objection and was allowed to complete the course with digital simulators instead of dissecting animals.”

Conscious consumption

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

The practice of making purchasing decisions informed by ethical, social or environmental criteria.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
ethical consumption, responsible consumption, ethical consumerism
Antonyms
Consumerism
See also
Boycott and ethical consumption, Boycott, Cruelty-free
Example
"Practicing conscious consumption, she began reading labels and buying cosmetics not tested on animals, even if they cost a little more."

Consciousness

noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The state of having subjective experience; the philosophical and neuroscientific basis on which sentience is discussed.

Attributing consciousness to non-human species usually requires a stricter standard of proof than the one required to attribute it to other human beings, an asymmetry that sentientist currents identify as unjustified.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
subjective awareness, conscious experience, phenomenal consciousness
Antonyms
Unconsciousness
See also
Animal consciousness, Subjective experience, Sentience
Example
"Debates about consciousness ask whether there is something it is like to be an octopus, that is, whether there is subjective experience behind the behavior."

Consent

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The informed and voluntary agreement of an agent to a given action.

Its structural absence in relation to animals, who cannot consent to the use made of them, is identified by antispeciesists as one of the most evident ethical problems of animal exploitation, including in practices presented as 'humane'.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
assent, agreement, permission
Antonyms
Coercion
See also
Forced mating, Autonomy, Paternalism
Example
"In research with people, consent is mandatory and can be withdrawn at any time, something impossible when the participants are animals."

Consequentialism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A theory that judges actions by the consequences they produce, aiming to achieve the best possible outcomes and avoid bad outcomes for everyone affected by a decision.

Applied consistently, this principle does not morally distinguish between humans and animals when counting who is 'affected' by an action.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
consequence ethics, teleological ethics
Antonyms
Deontology
See also
Utilitarianism, Deontology, Utility maximisation
Example
"For consequentialism, an action is right if it produces the best outcomes, so it matters how much suffering each food choice causes or prevents."

Conservation biology

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The applied science that studies how to protect biological diversity, that is, species, populations and ecosystems, from threats of extinction and degradation.

The field was defined by Michael Soulé in the article "What Is Conservation Biology?" (1985), which also gave it value postulates, such as the claim that biological diversity has value in itself. In it, animals are studied mainly as members of species or parts of ecosystems, and the suffering of each one usually takes second place, which explains why killing animals of invasive species is common practice. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) distinguishes it from welfare biology, which studies what is good or bad for animals as sentient individuals, and from two intermediate fields, compassionate conservation and conservation welfare. These areas use similar knowledge, such as ecology and population dynamics, but have different ultimate goals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
conservation science
See also
Welfare biology, Compassionate conservation, Conservation welfare, Invasive alien species, Extinction
Example
"A conservation biologist proposed protecting the last stretch of forest in the region to keep an endangered species alive."

Conservation welfare

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A field that combines conservation biology with animal welfare science to assess and improve the welfare of wild animals affected by conservation actions.

The expression was proposed by the New Zealand scientist Ngaio Beausoleil and colleagues in 2018, and in the article "I Am a Compassionate Conservation Welfare Scientist" (2020) she explained why the field is not the same as compassionate conservation: it accepts the goals of conservation and seeks to reduce harms to animals step by step, working with conservationists, rather than starting from principles such as "first, do no harm". The field may also study how natural harms, or harms indirectly caused by humans, affect welfare, when these data serve conservation. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) notes that this knowledge may be useful to welfare biology, but the ultimate goal is different: here welfare matters within the limits of conservation, there it matters for its own sake. Organizations such as Wild Animal Initiative see the field as a bridge between conservationists and those concerned with wild animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Conservation biology, Compassionate conservation, Welfare biology, Animal welfare, Wild animal suffering
Example
"Before capturing the reserve's animals, the team adopted conservation welfare practices to reduce stress and injuries during handling."

Conservatism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

In this context, a stance that tends to resist changes in social norms regarding the use of animals, defending traditional practices.

From an antispeciesist standpoint, defending a practice merely because it is traditional is considered a fallacy (the appeal to tradition), unable to morally justify the suffering it may cause.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
traditionalism
Antonyms
Progressivism
See also
Progressivism, Reactionism, Status quo
Example
"Cultural conservatism often defends festivals and traditions involving animals as part of heritage, resisting changes in the laws that restrict them."

Consumption

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

The act of acquiring and using goods and services; in animal ethics, discussed in terms of its role in perpetuating (or reducing) animal exploitation.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
purchasing, acquisition, buying
See also
Conscious consumption, Boycott, Boycott and ethical consumption
Example
"For vegan advocates, each purchase is a vote, and consumption of animal products sustains the demand that keeps factory farms running."

Contextual universalism and particularism

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

Two positions on where standards of justice come from: particularism says they come from each community's shared understandings; contextual universalism accepts universal values but says each culture interprets and realises them in its own way.

Particularism is associated with Michael Walzer, in Spheres of Justice (1983), and contextual universalism with Bhikhu Parekh, in Rethinking Multiculturalism (2000). Particularism has a serious problem: if justice is whatever each community accepts, no locally accepted cruel practice could be criticised, whether against humans or animals. Contextual universalism seems more reasonable, but it has a limit: not every practice can pass as a local interpretation of a principle, and calling vaquejada or bullfighting a cultural form of respecting animals empties the principle. The useful distinction is between the way a value is applied, which can vary, and the exception that cancels it, which cannot.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Context-sensitive universalism
See also
Cultural relativism, Moral relativism, Moral universality, Communitarianism
Example
“Contextual universalism accepts that the principle of avoiding suffering is general, but that its application depends on each community’s context.”

Contractualism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A theory that grounds morality in agreements between rational agents capable of reciprocity.

Because it requires the capacity to make and keep agreements, this theory faces a structural difficulty in directly including animals as rights holders, and it is one of the ethical currents most criticized by antispeciesists.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
social contract theory, moral contractualism
See also
Moral person (Rawls), Original position and veil of ignorance, Reciprocity (as a criterion of inclusion)
Example
"For contractualism, only those who can make agreements and keep rules enter the contract, which leaves animals out, according to its critics."

Contradiction

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

A logical incompatibility between two statements or practices.

In the field of animal ethics, it is often pointed out between declared values, such as loving animals, and habitual behaviors, such as consuming products of their exploitation; a phenomenon also described as cognitive dissonance.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
inconsistency, incoherence
Antonyms
Logical consistency
See also
Logical consistency, Moral consistency, Moral schizophrenia
Example
"Claiming to love animals while eating meat every day was pointed out by colleagues as a contradiction that is hard to justify."

Coping

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

An animal's effort, through body and behavior, to deal with the challenges of their environment and keep their physical and mental balance.

The welfare scientist Donald Broom defined an individual's welfare as their state as regards their attempts to cope with the environment: the harder or more impossible it is to cope, the worse the welfare. An animal can be coping successfully and still be suffering, and failure to cope leads to disease, stereotypies and helplessness.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
coping strategies
See also
Stress, Animal welfare, Learned helplessness, Stereotypic behavior
Example
“When the environment offers no way out, some animals use passive coping and stay motionless, which may be a sign of suffering.”

Corn coffee

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

A drink made from roasted and ground corn, used as a substitute for regular coffee.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
cereal coffee
See also
Cereals (oats), Plant-based, Vegan diet
Example
"Wanting to cut back on caffeine at night, she started brewing a roasted and ground corn coffee, mild in flavor and free of animal products."

Cosmetics animal testing ban

noun phrase · Reducing and Ending the Use of Animals

Laws that prohibit testing cosmetics, toiletries and perfumes, or their ingredients, on animals, and in some cases selling products that were tested.

The European Union banned testing of finished products in 2004 and completed its ban on selling cosmetics with ingredients tested on animals in 2013. In Brazil, Law 15,183 of 2025 banned the use of live vertebrate animals in tests of cosmetics, personal hygiene products, perfumes and ingredients used only in these products. There are loopholes: ingredients that also have other uses may be tested when other rules, such as chemical safety rules, require it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Cosmetic animal testing prohibition, Ban on animal-tested cosmetics
See also
Cruelty-free, Replacement methods, Draize test, Animal experimentation
Example
“With the ban on cosmetics testing on animals, brands turned to cell cultures and computer simulations.”

Counterexample

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A case that shows a general claim, a definition or an argument form to be false, by meeting its conditions and contradicting its conclusion.

A single counterexample is enough to defeat a universal generalization, such as "only those with duties have rights" or "what is natural is good". The best known in philosophy is Edmund Gettier's, who in 1963, with two short cases, shook the definition of knowledge as justified true belief. In the debate about animals, babies and people with severe cognitive disabilities work as counterexamples to criteria that require reason or language for moral status, and this is the core of the argument from marginal cases. Counterexamples also show that an argument form is invalid: it is enough to find another argument with the same form, true premises and a false conclusion. To answer a counterexample, one must show that it does not meet the conditions or reformulate the principle, and a reformulation made only to exclude the awkward case, with no other reason, is ad hoc.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
counter-example
See also
Argument from marginal cases, Necessary condition, Validity, Edge cases
Example
“Babies are a counterexample to the claim that only those with duties have rights.”

Creophagy

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A technical term for the habit of eating meat.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
meat-eating, flesh-eating
Antonyms
Vegetarianism
See also
Creophilia, Carnivorism, Omnivorism
Example
"In a technical text, the author preferred the term creophagy to describe the habit of eating meat, without the emotional load of words like carnism."

Creophilia

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A preference for or liking of meat.

Liking meat describes a taste, and does not answer the ethical question of what happens to the animal.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
love of meat, preference for meat
See also
Creophagy, Carnivorism, Omnivorism
Example
"His creophilia was notorious: at any party he headed for the meat table and never tried the vegetable and grain dishes."

Critic

noun / adjective · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Someone who examines and evaluates something, pointing out strengths and flaws; as the adjective "critical", what involves that examination, as in critical thinking, or what is decisive, as in a critical moment.

Being critical isn't being contrarian: good criticism acknowledges what is right before pointing out what is wrong, which is why the guide shows, for each argument, what it gets right. Critics of veganism aren't enemies to defeat, and many of their objections raise real points. Likewise, animal advocates need to accept criticism, including from within the movement, to correct mistakes and improve their arguments.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
analytical, questioning, reflective
Antonyms
Uncritical
See also
Critical thinking, Anti-vegan, Skepticism
Example
"The teacher asked students to read the text with a critical eye, separating facts from opinions and checking the cited sources."

Critical anthropomorphism

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The conscious and controlled use of our own experience to form hypotheses about what an animal feels or thinks, which are then tested by observation and experiments; an approach associated with the ethologist Gordon Burghardt.

It sits between two errors: projecting human feelings onto everything an animal does, and denying any mental life on principle. Critical anthropomorphism takes into account the biology and typical behavior of the species. A dog wagging its tail isn't necessarily happy, but a pig that avoids a place where it felt pain offers a clue that can be tested.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Anthropomorphism, Morgan's canon, Ethology, Animal cognition, Animal emotions
Example
"The researcher used critical anthropomorphism: she imagined how she would feel in the cow's place, formed a hypothesis about fear and tested it by measuring physiological signs."

Critical thinking

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

The ability to evaluate claims and arguments carefully: identifying premises, weighing evidence, recognizing fallacies and biases, and reaching conclusions proportionate to the reasons.

It isn't the same as distrusting everything or disagreeing on principle; it includes knowing when to trust experts and changing one's mind in the face of good reasons. Its hardest test is applying it to one's own beliefs, not just to other people's. In the debate about animals, it helps spot appeals to tradition, nature and convenience, but it cuts both ways: a good argument for animals also has to withstand critical scrutiny.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Critical reasoning, Critical analysis
Antonyms
Dogmatism
See also
Free thought, Skepticism, Logic, Evidence
Example
“A good debate calls for critical thinking: examining each side's reasons instead of repeating slogans or accepting everything unquestioned.”

Cruelty-free

expression · Reducing and Ending the Use of Animals

A label or designation indicating that a product was not tested on animals.

For a long time the term had no legal definition, and each company used it as it pleased; independent certification labels also check ingredient suppliers. Cruelty-free is not the same as vegan: a product may not be tested on animals and still contain animal-derived ingredients, such as beeswax, lanolin or carmine. In Brazil, the 2025 law that banned cosmetics testing on animals also sets rules for this kind of label.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
not tested on animals, no animal testing, free of cruelty
See also
Cosmetics animal testing ban, Lanolin, Cochineal carmine
Example
"The Cruelty Free seal on the shampoo bottle means the maker does not test the product on animals, but says nothing about the ingredients used."

Cruelty-kindness view

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

Tom Regan's name for the position that all we owe animals is not to be cruel to them and, where possible, to be kind.

Regan discusses it in The Case for Animal Rights (1983) and in the essay of the same name (1985). His criticism is that cruelty and kindness describe motives and character, not what makes an act right or wrong. A kind person can do something wrong, and a great deal of harm is done with no cruelty at all, out of indifference, routine or profit. So "just don't be cruel" does not answer whether a use of animals is permissible: a slaughter carried out with no pleasure in the suffering is still a death. The criticism hits the versions of virtue ethics that only forbid cruelty, not authors such as Rosalind Hursthouse, for whom compassion and justice already condemn current practices. Nathan Nobis includes this view among the theories examined in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016).

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
cruelty-kindness view
See also
Virtue ethics, Animal cruelty, Compassion, Welfarism
Example
“The cruelty-kindness view speaks to the character of the one who acts, but it doesn't say whether slaughter without cruelty is permissible.”

Crunchy (natureba, Brazilian usage)

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A Brazilian colloquial term, close to the English "crunchy" or "granola", for someone who adopts a lifestyle centered on what they consider natural, such as natural or organic food, handmade products and alternative therapies, sometimes with elements of mysticism; naturebismo is the name for that lifestyle.

It is used fondly or ironically, and in the ironic sense it usually suggests naivety and a liking for practices without a scientific basis, such as homeopathy, for which a review by Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC, 2015) found no reliable evidence of effectiveness for any health condition. Veganism is not a natural lifestyle: it is about not exploiting animals, and a vegan can eat ultra-processed food, get vaccinated and trust medicine, just as a natureba can eat meat and honey. Pinning the label on those who defend animals is a way of dismissing the argument by attacking the person, as in the argument "Vegans are all hippies"; and defending veganism because it is natural falls into the appeal to nature, the same mistake as saying that eating meat is natural. There are vegans who adopt and spread pseudoscientific practices, which the guide criticizes in the argument "Vegans support pseudoscience", but that says nothing about the merits of the case for animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Crunchy, Granola, Tree hugger
See also
Pseudoscience, Naturalistic fallacy, Evidence-based (or rationalist) veganism, Anti-veganism, Vegan
Example
"When she turned down the barbecue, her uncle laughed and called her crunchy, as if caring about animals were just a lifestyle fad."

Crustacean-vegetarianism (crustovegetarianismo, Brazilian usage)

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A vegetarian diet that includes eating crustaceans, based on the (contested) argument that these animals would have lesser or no capacity to suffer.

The idea that crustaceans do not suffer is increasingly contested. A review of more than 300 studies, carried out by the London School of Economics for the British government in 2021, concluded that decapod crustaceans, such as crabs, lobsters and shrimp, should be treated as sentient, and British law has recognized them as such since 2022. Switzerland banned boiling lobsters alive in 2018. None of this proves that every crustacean feels, but the doubt weighs against killing them without need.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
vegetarianism with crustaceans
See also
Sentience, Seafood, Ostroveganism
Example
"He called himself vegetarian but ate shrimp, which his friends labeled crustovegetarianism, a target of scientific debate over crustacean sentience."

Culinary activism

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

The use of vegan cooking (tastings, food events) as a tool for awareness-raising and conversion to veganism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Activism, Vegan movement, Working-class veganism (veganismo popular, Brazilian usage), Proselytism, Vegan diet
Example
"The restaurant held a free vegan dinner as culinary activism, hoping that good food would make guests rethink their habits."

Cultivated meat

noun phrase · Reducing and Ending the Use of Animals

A food product derived from cellular agriculture, presented as an alternative to traditional animal farming.

It is also called lab-grown meat ("labmeat"), cell-cultured meat or cultured meat; the name "clean meat", adopted by the Good Food Institute in 2016, has fallen out of use. Production still uses animal cells, taken by biopsy from living animals or from established cell lines, and early culture media used fetal bovine serum, taken from the blood of fetuses of slaughtered cows; serum-free media now exist, such as the one approved in Singapore in 2023. Sale has been authorized in Singapore in 2020, the United States in 2023, Israel in 2024 and Australia in 2025, and banned in Italy in 2023, Hungary in 2025 and several US states, such as Florida, Alabama and Texas. For veganism, the product is not vegan by origin, but it could greatly reduce the breeding and slaughter of animals if it replaced part of livestock farming, which still depends on cost, scale and acceptance; the guide discusses this debate.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
lab-grown meat, cell-based meat, in vitro meat, cultured meat
See also
Cellular agriculture, Technological veganism
Example
"Singapore was one of the first countries to approve the sale of cultivated meat, made from animal cells multiplied in bioreactors."

Cultural relativism

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

In anthropology, the principle of understanding each practice within the culture where it exists; in ethics, the thesis that a practice is right if the culture that performs it accepts it.

The first sense, associated with the anthropologist Franz Boas, is a valuable method: it helps us understand a practice before judging it and avoids mistaking one's own custom for everyone's standard. The second is a form of moral relativism and inherits its problems, because it would make any accepted practice, however cruel, immune to criticism. In the debate about animals, both traps appear: using culture to shield rodeos, bullfighting or Brazil's vaquejada, and condemning other peoples' practices while accepting those of one's own culture, like someone outraged at dog eating in another country who eats pigs at home.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Anthropological relativism
Antonyms
Moral universality, Moral objectivism
See also
Moral relativism, Double standard, Instrumentalization, Moral universality
Example
“By saying bullfighting is a cultural tradition and therefore untouchable, he invoked cultural relativism to avoid discussing the bull's suffering.”

Dairy industry

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The economic sector devoted to the production and sale of milk and its derivatives, dependent on the repeated separation of mothers and their young.

To produce milk, a cow must give birth, so she is inseminated roughly once a year. The calf is usually separated within the first hours or days; females generally replace the herd, and males are killed young or raised for meat. The cow is slaughtered when production falls, usually at four to five years, in a species that can live 15 to 20 years.

Synonyms, example and related terms

Dairy sector, Dairy business
See also
Weaning, Veal, Dairy products
Example
"The dairy industry separates calves from their mothers soon after birth so that the milk can be sold."

Dairy products

noun · Animal-Derived Products

Products derived from animal milk (cheese, yogurt, butter).

Many people who stop eating meat keep dairy because they think it involves no death, but milk production depends on repeated pregnancies, separates calves from their mothers and ends with the slaughter of the cows and of many males.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Dairy, Milk products, Dairy foods
See also
Milk, Dairy industry, Veal, Plant milk
Example
"After cutting dairy, he started using plant butter and nut cheese in his recipes."

Decision

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

A deliberate choice between alternatives, morally assessed according to process and consequences.

Everyday consumption decisions, even if they seem trivial, have direct and often ignored consequences for the lives and suffering of sentient beings.

Synonyms and related uses
choice, deliberation, resolution
See also
Choice, Weakness of will, Dilemma
Example
