Declarative (or explicit) knowledge

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

Knowledge of facts and ideas that can be stated, written down and taught in words; "knowing that", such as knowing that fish have nociceptors.

The philosopher Gilbert Ryle, in 1949, distinguished "knowing that" from "knowing how". The terms declarative, used more in psychology, and explicit, used more in knowledge management, are close and often treated as synonyms. It is the kind of knowledge a book or this guide conveys: data, definitions, arguments. It is necessary, but not enough to hold a good conversation; that also takes procedural knowledge.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
knowing that, explicit knowledge, propositional knowledge
Antonyms
Tacit knowledge, Procedural knowledge
See also
Procedural knowledge, Tacit knowledge, Surface learning
Example
"Knowing that vitamin B12 does not come from plants is declarative knowledge: it can be written on a sheet and taught to anyone."

Deep ecology

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A current of environmental ethics and a movement started by the Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss, which ascribe value of their own to every form of life and to the diversity of nature, regardless of their usefulness to humans, and call for deep changes in society's relationship with the environment.

Næss introduced the distinction between shallow and deep ecology in a lecture in Bucharest in 1972, published in 1973 in the journal Inquiry as "The Shallow and the Deep, Long-Range Ecology Movement", where he defended "biospherical egalitarianism, in principle". In 1984, Næss and George Sessions summed up the movement in an eight-point platform, made public in the book Deep Ecology (1985) by Bill Devall and Sessions: among the points, that human and non-human life have value in themselves and that humans have no right to reduce the richness and diversity of life except to satisfy vital needs. From a sentientist point of view, the problem is that value falls on life in general, on species and on ecosystems, not on those who feel: a plant counts like an animal, and the good of the whole can justify killing individuals, as in hunting and in culls of invasive species, which many environmentalists of this line accept. Næss himself admitted that any realistic practice requires some killing and exploitation, and the platform does not say what vital needs are. Even so, deep ecology comes close to animal ethics in rejecting anthropocentrism, and some of its followers are vegetarian and criticize factory farming. The guide discusses this conflict in the "Environmentalism" objection.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Ecosophy
Antonyms
Shallow ecology
See also
Shallow ecology, Holism, Ecocentrism, Biocentrism, Environmentalism (moral)
Example
"Inspired by deep ecology, the group argued for protecting the forest for its own sake, not for the timber or tourism it might bring in."

Political or ethical objection →

Deep learning

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A way of studying aimed at understanding the meaning, the reasons and the links between ideas, and applying them to new situations.

In argumentation, it is the difference between memorizing that an argument is wrong and understanding why it fails, which premise is false or which principle would lead to conclusions the person themselves rejects. That understanding makes it possible to recognize the same error in new forms. That's why the guide offers layers: the short answer to use now and the full answer, with the best counter-reply, for those who want to understand. Not to be confused with deep learning in artificial intelligence, a machine learning technique; in education the term is also called a deep approach to learning.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
deep approach to learning
Antonyms
Surface learning
See also
Surface learning, Critical thinking, Procedural knowledge, Declarative (or explicit) knowledge, Reflective equilibrium
Example
"Instead of memorizing definitions, the student used deep learning: she linked each concept to an example and tried to apply it to a new situation."

Dehorning

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A procedure for removing the horns of cattle, generally without adequate anesthesia.

Done after the horn has attached to the skull, it is more invasive than disbudding: it uses saws, wire or cutters and can open the sinuses. In the United Kingdom, dehorning any cattle requires local anaesthesia given by a veterinarian, but many countries have no such requirement. There are naturally hornless (polled) breeds, and genetic selection for this trait is pointed to as an alternative.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
horn removal
See also
Disbudding, Anesthesia, Industrial livestock farming
Example
"On the farm, calves were dehorned in the first weeks, a method used to prevent accidents when the animals are kept in groups."

Demandingness objection

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The objection that a moral theory or proposal should be rejected if it demands too much of people, to the point of leaving no room for their own lives.

It is aimed mainly at consequentialism and gained force after Peter Singer's article "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" (1972), which argued for giving up to the point where giving more would cause a sacrifice comparable to the one prevented. In the case of wild animals, it is said that helping them would require dropping everything, given the scale of suffering in nature. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that the objection assumes that being demanding is a defect, which is exactly what is in question, and that the cost to those who help must be weighed impartially against the harm prevented; he also points out that rest and leisure can make someone more effective, not less. Authors such as Liam Murphy, in Moral Demands in Nonideal Theory (2000), propose limiting the duty to each person's fair share, which still leaves a real duty to help.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Overdemandingness objection, Over-demandingness objection
See also
Supererogatory, Ought implies can, Consequentialism, Effective altruism
Example
“Hearing that utilitarianism requires giving away almost all one's income, she raised the demandingness objection: no moral theory should ask for such extreme sacrifices.”

Denying the antecedent

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A formal fallacy that concludes "not B" from "if A, then B" and "not A".

It is invalid because B may be true for some other reason: "if it is a dog, it is a mammal; it is not a dog; therefore, it is not a mammal" fails in the face of a cat. Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), shows that many objections to animals take this form: if animals had rights, it would be wrong to make them suffer; they have no rights; therefore, it is not wrong, when making them suffer could be wrong for another reason, such as the suffering itself. "No duties, no rights" hides the same error when it starts from "whoever has duties has rights" and concludes, from "animals have no duties", that they have no rights. Its sister fallacy is affirming the consequent, which concludes "A" from "if A, then B" and "B". The nearby valid forms are modus ponens, which concludes "B" from "if A, then B" and "A", and modus tollens, which concludes "not A" from "if A, then B" and "not B".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
fallacy of the inverse, inverse error
Antonyms
modus tollens
See also
Validity, Necessary condition, Fallacies, Counterexample
Example
“‘If they had rights, it would be wrong to make them suffer; they have no rights; so it isn't wrong’ is a case of denying the antecedent.”

Fallacies →

Deontology

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A theory based on moral rules and duties, regardless of the consequences of actions.

Deontological formulations that ground duties exclusively in rationality or autonomy tend to exclude animals; formulations centered on basic rights, such as Tom Regan's, include them as subjects of direct duties.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
duty ethics, deontological ethics
Antonyms
Consequentialism
See also
Consequentialism, Duties, Perfect and imperfect duties
Example
"For deontology, certain acts, such as torturing an innocent, are wrong in themselves even if they produced a good result for many people."

Political or ethical objection →

Devocalization

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A surgical procedure that removes or damages an animal's vocal cords to prevent or reduce its vocalization.

The surgery is done mainly on dogs, so that they bark less. It is prohibited for non-therapeutic purposes by the Council of Europe's European Convention for the Protection of Pet Animals and by laws in several countries and some US states; in Brazil, the Federal Council of Veterinary Medicine has banned devocalization of dogs since 2008. The criticism is that the procedure treats barking as the guardian's problem rather than as the animal's way of communicating, when there are alternatives such as training and changes in routine.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
debarking, ventriculocordectomy
See also
Ear cropping, Tail docking, Physical integrity
Example
"To avoid neighbors' complaints, the owner resorted to devocalizing the dog, a surgery that stops him from barking normally."

Diet

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

The habitual eating pattern of a person or group, as in the Mediterranean diet or a vegan diet; in popular usage, also a regimen to lose weight or treat a health condition.

The word comes from the Greek díaita, "way of life". In nutrition, everyone has a diet, because the term describes what one eats, not a restriction. So "vegan diet" doesn't mean a regimen: it's simply eating without animal products.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
eating pattern, regimen, food regimen
See also
Healthy diet, Restrictive diet, Vegan diet
Example
"The diet of many Brazilian families revolves around rice, beans and vegetables, a base that adapts easily to vegan eating."

Dietary transition

noun phrase · Reducing and Ending the Use of Animals

A gradual process of changing eating habits, usually toward reducing or eliminating animal products.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Dietary change, Switching to a plant-based diet
See also
Reducetarianism, Flexitarianism, Veganism, Vegan diet
Example
“Instead of changing everything at once, she made her dietary transition gradually, swapping one meal a week and noting which recipes she liked.”

Digital activism

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

The use of social media and the internet for mobilization and awareness-raising.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
online activism, cyber-activism
See also
Activism, Street activism, Protest, Social movement, Guerrilla marketing
Example
"A petition shared on social media gathered thousands of signatures in a few days and led the city to review the use of horses on carts."

Dilemma

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

A situation in which an agent faces conflicting moral obligations, with no solution that satisfies all of them.

Dilemmas involving animals, such as choosing between a cultural tradition and animal welfare, tend to be resolved, from the standpoint of equal consideration, in favor of avoiding avoidable suffering.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
quandary, moral conflict, predicament
See also
Duties, Edge cases, Hypothetical scenarios
Example
"The doctor faced a dilemma: spare a laboratory animal or test a drug that might save sick children."

Diminishing marginal utility

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The economic principle that each additional unit of a good brings less benefit than the previous one, so that the same amount is worth more to someone who has little than to someone who has a lot.

The idea appears in Daniel Bernoulli (1738) and became established with the nineteenth-century marginalist economists. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), shows that it is why equal consideration of interests usually favors the worse off: a little more rice changes the day of someone who is starving and does almost nothing for someone who eats well. But he notes that this does not always happen, and that the principle can even widen an inequality when the larger benefit lies with someone better off. For animals, the reasoning weighs in their favor: the same resource, spent on improving the life of someone living in a cage, tends to yield more well-being than spent on the comfort of someone who already lives well, although comparing well-being across species is difficult and contested. Prioritarians such as Derek Parfit think the principle is not enough and that priority to the worse off should carry weight of its own.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Law of diminishing marginal utility
See also
Equal consideration, Prioritarianism, Egalitarianism, Maximin
Example
“By diminishing marginal utility, the same money makes more difference to someone who is starving than to someone who already has plenty.”

Direct action

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

Direct intervention against animal exploitation, sometimes outside the law (e.g. rescues, sabotage).

The best-known example is the Animal Liberation Front (ALF), which emerged in the United Kingdom in 1976, claims rescues and property damage and says it rejects harming any living being. In Brazil, the removal of about 180 beagles from the Instituto Royal in São Roque in 2013 reignited the debate. Governments often treat some of these actions as crime or terrorism, as in the US Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act of 2006, and there is disagreement within the movement about the legitimacy and effectiveness of acting outside the law.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
direct intervention
See also
Rescue, Ecoterrorism, Nonviolence, Institutional activism, Street activism
Example
"Instead of waiting for a new law, the group chose direct action and rescued animals from an illegal farm, which sparked debate about legality."

Direct argument

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

An argument that challenges the moral core: whether animals feel, whether the individual animal counts and whether using or killing it is wrong.

It is the ground on which the ethical question about animals is decided.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Antonyms
Indirect argument
See also
Indirect argument, Argument from relevance, Argument from marginal cases, Sentience, Argument
Example
"Instead of arguing about health, she made a direct argument: if the pig feels pain like the dog, there is no reason to kill one and spare the other."

Disbudding

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The removal or prevention of horn growth in cattle, usually by cauterization, in most cases without anesthesia.

It is usually done on calves a few weeks old, with a hot iron or caustic paste that burns the horn bud, and studies record signs of pain during and after the procedure. Veterinary bodies, such as the British BVA and BCVA, recommend local anaesthesia and an anti-inflammatory, but surveys of dairy farmers in the United States, Italy and France found that most use no pain relief at all. The reason is management: hornless animals take up less space and injure each other less in crowded groups. Breeding naturally hornless (polled) cattle is pointed to as an alternative.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
dehorning of calves, horn bud removal
See also
Dehorning, Anesthesia, Industrial livestock farming, Animal welfare, Pain
Example
"On the dairy farm, disbudding of calves was done with a hot iron in the first weeks of life, without anaesthesia, which led to complaints."

Disneyfication

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

An idealized, highly humanized portrayal of animals in films, cartoons and products, in which they talk, think and feel like people and have adventures without hunger, disease or death.

The term comes from the Disney studios' animated films, but it describes a wider phenomenon in popular culture. These stories can stir empathy for animals, but they also give a false picture of how animals live, both in the wild and on farms. There is also a contrast: many children grow up loving cartoon piglets and chickens while eating those same animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Disneyization, media humanization of animals
See also
Anthropomorphism, Critical anthropomorphism, Cognitive dissonance, Happy exploitation
Example
“After the cartoon with talking piglets, many children are shocked to learn what a slaughterhouse is: Disneyfication hiding reality.”

Divine command theory

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The theory that an act is right or wrong because God commands or forbids it.

The classic objection is the Euthyphro dilemma, from Plato's dialogue of that name: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? On the first answer, morality becomes arbitrary, since God could have commanded cruelty; on the second, what makes the act good are the reasons God would have, and those can be examined directly. James Rachels uses this dilemma against the theory, and Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), follows Rachels: if an authority says some use of animals is permissible, either there are reasons for it or there are not, and it is the reasons that decide. Many religious people do not accept the theory in its simple form: the natural law tradition of Thomas Aquinas grounds morality in reason, and modified versions, such as Robert M. Adams's, tie obligation to God's loving nature.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
theological voluntarism, divine command ethics
See also
Ethical theories, Religious speciesism, Moral principle, Deontology
Example
“On divine command theory, eating animals would be permissible only because God permitted it; the Euthyphro dilemma asks whether there would then be any reason for that permission.”

Domestic animal

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A species selected and bred over generations under human control, genetically adapted to living with humans or to production (as opposed to a wild animal).

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
domesticated animal
Antonyms
wild animal
See also
Domestication, Companion animal, Farmed animal, Artificial selection, Mixed community
Example
"Dogs, cats, cows and chickens are domestic animals: they were selected over generations to live with humans or to produce for them."

Domestication

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The process, over many generations, by which animal populations came to live under human control and were modified by artificial selection; the dog was first, more than 15,000 years ago, and cattle, sheep, goats and pigs were domesticated around 10,000 years ago.

Domestication changed bodies and behavior: hens that lay around 300 eggs a year, broiler chickens that grow so fast that many have leg problems, cows with enormous udders. A common argument says these animals exist thanks to us and so we may use them. But having brought someone into existence doesn't give the right to make them suffer. For veganism, ending exploitation doesn't mean releasing domesticated animals, but no longer breeding them for use and caring for those who already exist.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Artificial selection, Domestic animal, Sanctuary, Synanthropic animals
Example
“The domestication of the wolf over millennia produced the dog, but also breeds with health problems created by human selection.”

Dominionism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

The view that humans have the right to rule over and use other animals and nature, often based on the passage in Genesis in which God gives humans dominion over the animals.

There are different readings of this passage within the religions themselves. Many theologians, Jewish and Christian, understand dominion as stewardship, that is, a responsibility to care, and not as a license to exploit. The debate shows that faith does not necessarily lead to speciesism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
dominion theology, dominion over nature
Antonyms
stewardship
See also
Theocentrism, Religious speciesism, Anthropocentrism, Misothery
Example
“He cited the biblical passage about ‘ruling over’ animals as proof of human dominion, but other readers interpret it as care.”

Dorism (a rare coinage close to painism)

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A neologism sometimes used to designate an ethics centered on pain (from the English 'pain') as the central moral criterion, close to painism.

By making pain, and not species, the central moral criterion, this approach converges with the principles of sentientism and equal consideration of interests.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Painism, Pain, Suffering, Sentientism
Example
“The professor warned that ‘dorism’ is a rare coinage and that the term most used in the literature is painism.”

Double standard

expression · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Applying different criteria to similar cases, as suits whoever is judging. The Portuguese expression is "dois pesos e duas medidas" (two weights and two measures).

It is a form of inconsistency and the opposite of moral universality. In the treatment of animals, it is very common: the same act is a crime against a dog and routine against a pig, other peoples' hunting is barbaric and ours is tradition, the suffering of a cute animal moves us and that of a fish goes unnoticed. Pointing out a double standard doesn't show which of the two treatments is right, but it shows that at least one of them has to change. And the demand applies to animal advocates too: the same yardstick should be applied to one's own choices.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
one rule for you, another for me
Antonyms
consistency
See also
Moral consistency, Moral universality, Speciesism, Cultural relativism
Example
“Condemning cockfighting while defending the slaughter of chickens is, for many critics, a double standard.”

Downed animal

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An animal that cannot stand up or move because of illness, exhaustion or injury, usually during transport or confinement; a situation associated with serious welfare violations.

The industry term is "downer". Because they are hard to move, downed animals may be dragged, pushed or moved with electric shocks to slaughter. In the United States, a 2008 Humane Society video recorded at a California slaughterhouse showed workers using forklifts, water hoses and shocks to force downed cattle to stand, which led to the largest meat recall in the country up to then, about 143 million pounds. In 2009 the US Department of Agriculture banned the slaughter of downed cattle for food, but the rule does not cover pigs and other species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
downer, non-ambulatory animal
See also
Live animal transport, Slaughter, Industrial livestock farming, Live cargo
Example
"The inspector halted the lorry on finding a downed animal on the trailer, unable to stand after hours of travel under the sun."

Draize test

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A toxicological test that applies substances to the eyes or skin of animals (often rabbits) to measure irritation; today widely criticized and replaced by alternatives.

It was created in 1944 by John Draize and Jacob Spines, toxicologists at the US FDA. In the eye test, the substance is applied to the eye of albino rabbits and the lesions are assessed over days; animals with irreversible damage are killed. Today there are OECD-accepted methods that do not use live animals, such as tests on corneas of slaughtered cattle and on human tissue models, but they replace the test only in part, and the rabbit test remains in the guidelines.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Draize eye test, rabbit eye test
See also
Induced skin irritation, Animal experimentation, Replacement methods, Cosmetics animal testing ban
Example
“The brand abandoned the Draize test, which used restrained rabbits, and began validating its products on lab-grown tissue.”

Duties

noun · Animal Law and Legislation

Moral or legal obligations that an agent has toward others.

The discussion about the existence of direct duties toward animals, and not only indirect ones mediated by the interests of third-party humans, is central to recognizing their status as moral subjects, and not merely objects of protection.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
obligations, moral responsibilities
See also
Perfect and imperfect duties, Positive and negative duties, Deontology, Rights
Example
"Many philosophers argue that we have direct duties to animals, and not only duties to other humans concerning them."

E↑ A–Z

Ear cropping

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The surgical amputation of part of an animal's ears (common in some dog breeds) for aesthetic reasons.

The cut is made on puppies of breeds such as Dobermann, pit bull and Great Dane, so that the ears stand erect, and it requires weeks of bandaging and splints. It is banned for cosmetic purposes in much of Europe, the United Kingdom, Australia and, in Brazil, by the Federal Council of Veterinary Medicine since 2008, but it is still legal in much of the United States.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Ear docking, Cosmetic ear surgery
See also
Tail docking, Devocalization, Pedigree, Artificial selection
Example
“The breed standard required ear cropping, a painful surgery done purely for looks and banned in many countries.”

Eco-veganism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

Veganism motivated mainly by protecting the environment and ecosystems.

Because the definition of veganism concerns not exploiting animals, the environmental reason is indirect: someone who stops consuming animals only for the environment may eat a plant-based diet without being vegan in the strict sense.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
environmental veganism, green veganism
See also
Veganism, Sentientist environmentalism, Sustainable livestock farming, Antienvironmentalism
Example
“He became vegan out of eco-veganism: what convinced him was the deforestation caused by livestock farming, and only later did he think about the animals.”

Ecocentrism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A view that attributes moral value to ecosystems and natural processes, not only to individuals.

This difference of focus appears, for example, when conservation policies justify killing individuals of species considered invasive in the name of ecosystem balance, a practice open to question from an individual-centered sentientist standpoint.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
ecological holism
Antonyms
anthropocentrism
See also
Holistic environmentalism, Holism, Biocentrism, Anthropocentrism
Example
“Under ecocentrism, a forest matters in itself, and not merely because it offers timber or recreation to humans.”

Beyond veganism →

Ecofeminism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A current that connects domination over nature and animals with structures of gender oppression.

By placing animal exploitation within a broader critique of logics of domination, ecofeminism engages directly with intersectionality and antispeciesism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
ecological feminism
See also
Intersectionality, Oppression, Feminist veganism, Anthropocentrism
Example
“The ecofeminism talk linked the exploitation of dairy cows to that of women, pointing to similar structures of reproductive control.”

Political or ethical objection →

Ecological balance

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

The idea that nature, left to itself, tends towards a stable and harmonious state in which populations remain constant.

The notion comes from the ancient idea of the "balance of nature" and is still widely used to reject any help for wild animals. In ecology, however, it has no single definition: the ecologist Charles Elton was already writing in 1930 that this balance does not exist, and Volker Grimm and Christian Wissel (1997) gathered more than 160 definitions of stability, to the point of considering the term nearly useless. Ecosystems are now seen as dynamic, open and subject to disturbance. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) adds that, even where there is something like stability, it is maintained precisely because most offspring die, so that balance does not mean the well-being of individuals. This does not make ecological risk irrelevant: poorly planned interventions can make things worse, which is why those who defend helping wild animals call for research before action.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
balance of nature, ecological harmony
Antonyms
ecological imbalance
See also
Idyllic nature, Ecology, Holism, Wild animal suffering
Example
“Talking about ecological balance can hide the fact that nature fluctuates widely and that most offspring of many species die young.”

Ecology

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The science of the relationships between living beings and their environment.

Ecological approaches tend to prioritize the balance of populations and ecosystems, which can conflict with a sentientist ethics centered on the welfare of each individual, including wild animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Biology, Ethology, Ecology of fear, Ecological balance
Example
“Ecology studies how wolves, deer and plants influence each other, but by itself it does not decide what we ought to do morally.”

Ecology of fear

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

In ecology, the study of how predation risk changes the behaviour, physiology and distribution of prey, even when they are not killed.

The concept was proposed by Joel Brown, John Laundré and Mahesh Gurung in a 1999 article, and from it comes the idea of the "landscape of fear", the map of places prey avoid out of fear of predators. In conservation, the expression has also come to mean the reintroduction of predators, such as wolves in Yellowstone National Park, in the United States, from 1995, so that fear drives deer and other herbivores away from plants one wants to protect. The cascading effect attributed to the Yellowstone wolves is debated among ecologists, who disagree about how much of the vegetation's recovery is due to them. Oscar Horta (2010) and Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) criticize the practice: it uses the fear, hunger and death of sentient animals as tools for environmental goals, and shows that intervening in nature is already accepted when the aim is not the good of the animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Predation, Holism, Conservation biology, Wild animal suffering
Example
“With the return of wolves, elk changed pastures and schedules, a classic example of the ecology of fear.”

Ecoterrorism

noun · Activism and the Movement

A term used, above all by governments and opponents, for illegal actions, such as sabotage and arson, motivated by environmental or animal causes.

The term is disputed, because it associates damage to property with terrorism, which targets people. Under laws such as the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act (USA, 2006), animal activists have been treated this way. This guide does not recommend violent or illegal actions.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
environmental terrorism
See also
Extremism, Direct action, Nonviolence, Protest
Example
“Critics called the sabotage ecoterrorism, while the activists described it as civil disobedience against deforestation.”

Edge cases

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Extreme or rare situations at the boundary of a rule, such as the desert island with no other food or the choice between saving a dog and a child.

Used well, they test whether a principle holds in every case or needs adjusting, and show where a rule's limits lie. The argument from marginal cases, for example, uses humans with limited capacities to test whether rationality is really the criterion for moral consideration. Used badly, they turn the exception into the rule: from the fact that someone would eat an animal on a desert island it doesn't follow that they may buy one at the supermarket, where there is no necessity at all. The useful question about an edge case is: what does it show about the ordinary case?

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
borderline cases, hard cases, limit cases
See also
Hypothetical scenarios, Argument from marginal cases
Example
"When asked whether someone could eat meat to survive on a desert island, the professor noted that edge cases do not set the rule for everyday life."

Argument family →

Effective altruism

noun phrase · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

A movement that seeks to maximize the positive impact of actions and resources, including animal welfare as an important cause.

Its criteria of scale, neglectedness and tractability tend to favor the animal cause.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
EA
See also
Altruism, Expected impact, Longtermism, Utility maximisation, Utilitarianism
Example
"Following effective altruism, the couple split their annual donation among organizations chosen on evidence of how many animals each dollar can help."

Political or ethical objection →

Egalitarianism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A position that defends an equal distribution of moral consideration, or of well-being, among individuals, prioritizing the reduction of inequality between them.

Applied consistently with the principle of equal consideration, egalitarianism opposes letting an individual's species determine the weight given to their well-being in the distribution.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Equal-treatment view
Antonyms
Elitism, Hierarchy
See also
Equal consideration, Prioritarianism, Justice, Sufficientarianism
Example
"A defender of egalitarianism, she argued that no one should carry less moral weight for belonging to a particular group."

Political or ethical objection →

Egoism (egocentrism)

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

An attitude of putting one's own interests first, without considering, or barely considering, the interests of others.

In everyday use, egoism and egocentrism blur together, but they aren't the same: in psychology, egocentrism is difficulty seeing things from other people's point of view, common in young children, and not a moral choice. In philosophy, psychological egoism says people always act out of self-interest, and ethical egoism says they ought to; the guide discusses the latter on its page about egoism and Objectivism. The argument "I like it, so I eat it" puts one's own pleasure above another being's life.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
self-centeredness
Antonyms
altruism
See also
Altruism, Speciesism, Anthropocentrism, Partiality
Example
“Saying that only one’s own interests count, without looking at others’ suffering, is egoism, and antispeciesism asks that the circle be widened.”

Political or ethical objection →

Elitism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A criticism or characteristic sometimes attributed to sectors of the animal movement, associated with discourses or practices that favor socially or economically privileged groups.

Currents of popular and intersectional veganism arise, in part, as a response to this criticism, seeking to make the animal cause accessible regardless of social class.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
exclusivity
See also
Food classism, Food justice, Working-class veganism (veganismo popular, Brazilian usage), Intersectionality
Example
“Critics say very expensive vegan fairs reinforce elitism; that is why many groups began promoting affordable community meals.”

Empathy

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The capacity to understand and share the emotional states of another being.

Empathic biases tend to favor species that are physically similar to humans or have aesthetic appeal, such as mammals, which can lead to moral neglect of less 'charismatic' species, such as fish and invertebrates, a problem that sentientism seeks to correct by fixing sentience, and not similarity, as the criterion.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
affective understanding, putting oneself in another’s shoes
Antonyms
indifference, apathy
See also
Compassion, Apathy, Altruism, Ethics of care
Example
“Watching the rescue video, she felt empathy for the injured horse and decided to donate to the sanctuary that took him in.”

Empirical knowledge

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

Knowledge gained through experience and observation, which can be tested against evidence; in Brazilian schooling, also everyday practical knowledge without systematic method, as opposed to scientific knowledge.

In philosophy, it is contrasted with a priori knowledge, which doesn't depend on experience, like that of logic and mathematics. Many questions in the debate about animals are empirical: whether an animal feels pain, how much a diet pollutes, whether a vegan diet is adequate. They are settled by observation and research. Others are moral: whether an animal's suffering counts, and how much. Separating the two kinds of question avoids confusion, because no data alone decides what we should do, and no principle alone decides the facts.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
a posteriori knowledge, experiential knowledge, experimental knowledge
Antonyms
A priori knowledge
See also
Evidence, Epistemology, Tacit knowledge
Example
"Measuring the animals' body temperature before and after transport produces empirical knowledge about the stress the journey causes."

Environmental Crimes Law (animal abuse)

proper noun · Animal Law and Legislation

In Brazil, Law 9,605 of 1998, whose Article 32 makes it a crime to abuse, mistreat, injure or mutilate wild, domestic or domesticated animals, whether native or exotic.

The same article punishes anyone who carries out a painful or cruel experiment on a live animal, even for teaching or scientific purposes, when alternative resources exist. In 2020, Law 14,064, known as the Sansão Law, raised the penalty for abusing dogs and cats to two to five years in prison. The difference in penalty between dogs and cats and other animals is an example of institutional speciesism, and the practices of regulated livestock farming are generally not treated as abuse.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Law 9.605/1998, Brazilian Environmental Crimes Act
See also
Animal cruelty, Institutional speciesism, Animal law, Animal protection legislation
Example
"The guardian was reported under the Environmental Crimes Law after neighbours said the dog lived without water or shelter."

Environmental enhancement

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

Any modification of the conditions of the natural environment that has a net positive effect on the well-being of the sentient individuals living there.

The definition is by the Portuguese philosopher Catia Faria, in her thesis Animal Ethics Goes Wild (2016) and her book Animal Ethics in the Wild (Cambridge University Press, 2022). Faria argues that if we have a duty to meet the needs of wild animals, and if preserving natural environments means maintaining the suffering and death of most of them, then we have an obligation, not merely a permission, to change these environments for the better. The proposal reverses the common idea that our duty towards nature is to preserve it as it is. Critics, from environmentalists to some animal advocates such as Clare Palmer, point to the risk of unforeseen effects and to disrespect for the independent lives of wild animals, and Faria herself discusses, in a 2023 article, how to keep interventions from creating new vulnerabilities.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Environmental intervention, Habitat modification
See also
Natural harms, Welfare biology, Wild animal suffering, Idyllic nature
Example
"One of the proposed environmental enhancement projects was to install shelters so wild animals could better face the harsh winter."

Environmental enrichment

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

Changes to the environment of captive animals, such as objects, hiding places, material to root in, challenges to obtain food, or company, to encourage natural behaviors and reduce boredom and frustration.

Studies show that enrichment can reduce stereotypies and improve the health of animals in zoos, laboratories and farms. But it has limits: a toy in a cramped pen doesn't make up for lack of space, social life or freedom. It can also be used as a showcase to justify captivity.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
captive enrichment
Antonyms
environmental deprivation
See also
Stereotypic behavior, Zoo, Humane washing, Stereotypy
Example
“The zoo installed logs, hiding places and hidden food as environmental enrichment, but activists note that it does not replace freedom.”

Environmentalism (ecologismo)

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A synonym for environmentalism: a movement that advocates protecting the environment and the sustainable use of natural resources.

It can be anthropocentric, ecocentric or sentiocentric, depending on what it considers valuable in itself.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
green movement, green activism
Antonyms
anti-environmentalism
See also
Political environmentalism, Antienvironmentalism, Holistic environmentalism, Ecocentrism
Example
“The neighborhood environmental group organized a tree-planting day and then began pressing the city for a waste policy.”

Political or ethical objection →

Environmentalism (moral)

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A view that discusses moral obligations toward the environment, sometimes converging with and sometimes conflicting with animal ethics. Environmentalism can be a moral view or a political movement (see Political environmentalism).

It can diverge from a sentientist ethics when it prioritizes the balance of ecosystems or species over the welfare of specific sentient individuals, as in population management policies for wildlife.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
environmental ethics
Antonyms
Antienvironmentalism
See also
Political environmentalism, Anthropocentric environmentalism, Holistic environmentalism, Sentientist environmentalism, Ecocentrism
Example
"In the debate over managing a reserve, her moral environmentalism prioritized the endangered species, while his was concerned with each injured animal."

Political or ethical objection →

Epicurean view of death

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The view, attributed to Epicurus, that death is not a harm to the one who dies, because while the person exists death is not present, and when death comes the person no longer exists.

It is opposed to the view of death as a deprivation harm, defended by Thomas Nagel in the article "Death" (1970), according to which death is bad because it takes from the one who dies the good experiences still to come. The Epicurean view has contemporary defenders, such as David Suits, and is sometimes used to justify killing animals painlessly. Critics, among them Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022), answer that it would lead to conclusions almost no one accepts, such as that painlessly killing a happy human being does not harm them, and point out that, even on this view, the pain and fear that usually come before death remain bad. Most philosophers accept some form of the deprivation account and mainly debate the size of the harm.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Epicurean argument about death, Epicurus' view of death
Antonyms
Deprivation account
See also
Harm of death, Extrinsic harm, QALY (quality-adjusted life year), Interest
Example
"Under the Epicurean view of death, killing an animal painlessly does not harm it, since once dead it no longer exists to be harmed."

Epistemology

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The branch of philosophy that studies the nature, origin and limits of knowledge; relevant for discussing how we can know the mental states of other species.

Skepticism applied unevenly, demanding absolute certainty only about the animal mind and not the human one, is identified by sentientists as a subtle manifestation of speciesism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
theory of knowledge, gnoseology
See also
Philosophy of mind, Evidence, Empirical knowledge, Skepticism
Example
“A question of epistemology is how we can know whether a fish feels pain, since we cannot directly access its mind.”

Equal concern and respect (Dworkin)

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

Ronald Dworkin's principle that the state must treat each person with equal concern, for their interests and well-being, and equal respect, for their life choices.

Dworkin set it out in Taking Rights Seriously (1977), while interpreting John Rawls's theory, and developed it in Sovereign Virtue (2000). He restricted it to humans able to make plans and act justly, but the two halves have different sources: respect is tied to autonomy, while concern comes from our being beings who feel and have needs, which is also true of sentient animals. For this reason, authors such as Alasdair Cochrane argue that the concern half extends naturally to animals, even if the respect half applies to them differently. Not to be confused with Peter Singer's equal consideration of interests: Dworkin's is a principle about how the state treats its members; Singer's is a general moral principle about the weight of similar interests.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Equal consideration, Autonomy, Liberalism, Justice
Example
"The principle of equal concern and respect requires the state to treat every citizen as an equal, without favouring some people's way of life over others'."

Equal consideration

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The principle that similar interests, such as avoiding pain, should weigh equally, regardless of whose they are.

It is the central principle of sentientism and antispeciesism: applied consistently, it requires that the capacity to suffer, not species, determine whose interests are taken into account.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Equal consideration of interests, Equal interests principle
Antonyms
Speciesism, Partiality
See also
Interest, Impartiality, Speciesism, Sentience
Example
"By the principle of equal consideration, a pig's pain counts as much as a child's when the intensity of suffering is similar."

Equivalence thesis

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The thesis that the difference between causing a harm and allowing it to happen has no moral importance in itself.

It was defended by James Rachels, in the article "Active and Passive Euthanasia" (1975), and, with qualifications, by Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (1979; 2nd ed., 1993). Singer holds that there is no intrinsic difference between killing and letting die, but he grants differences that usually come with the distinction, such as motivation, the certainty of the outcome and causal responsibility; motivation and certainty, for him, carry moral weight, so failing to help those dying in poverty should not be condemned as killing, but is closer to a death caused by reckless driving. He also separates judging the act from the blame the person deserves. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) applies the thesis to wild animals: if it is true, letting an animal die of a disease we could treat is not, in itself, less serious than causing them the disease. Much of deontology rejects the thesis and defends the distinction between doing and allowing, as Philippa Foot, Warren Quinn and Frances Kamm do. Even those who reject the thesis usually accept some duty to help when the cost is low, which is already enough for part of the reasons to help wild animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Equivalence of doing and allowing
Antonyms
Act–omission asymmetry
See also
Omission, Positive and negative duties, Natural harms, Consequentialism
Example
“By the equivalence thesis, letting an animal die without helping would be morally the same as killing it, which many consider an exaggerated conclusion.”

Ethical theories

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

An umbrella term for the set of normative approaches (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, care ethics and others) used to justify moral positions, including on animals.

How each of these theories treats, or fails to treat, animals as moral subjects is one of the main axes of comparison among them within animal ethics.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Moral theories, Schools of ethics
See also
Utilitarianism, Deontology, Virtue ethics, Contractualism, Normative ethics
Example
“Each of the main ethical theories answers differently the question of who counts morally, and that changes the place of animals.”

Ethicist

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

An expert in ethics: a person who studies, teaches or researches ethics, or who advises institutions on moral questions.

Being an ethicist means knowing about ethics, not a guarantee of acting better. The philosophers Eric Schwitzgebel and Joshua Rust compared ethics professors with other professors in the United States and, in a study published in 2014, found that ethicists more often condemned eating the meat of mammals, but didn't report eating less meat than other philosophers. The result shows the gap between knowing and doing, which is why moral consistency is a challenge for everyone, animal advocates included.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
ethics specialist, ethics scholar
See also
Ethics, Animal ethics, Bioethicist, Moral consistency
Example
“The committee invited an ethicist to analyze whether the research protocol respected basic moral principles.”

Ethics

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The branch of philosophy devoted to the study of what is right, wrong, good or bad in conduct.

Historically formulated almost always from anthropocentric perspectives, ethics has been increasingly challenged to extend its principles to all beings capable of suffering.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
moral philosophy
See also
Moral philosophy, Normative ethics, Animal ethics, Practical ethics
Example
“Ethics asks what we ought to do and why, even when custom says something is right.”

Ethics of care

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A theory that values relationships, empathy and relational responsibility above abstract principles.

A frequent criticism is that this ethics may favor animals with whom one already has an emotional bond, such as companion animals, leaving the interests of anonymous, distant animals, such as those raised for consumption, in the background.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
relational ethics, feminist care ethics
Antonyms
principle-based ethics
See also
Empathy, Compassion, Virtue ethics, Human-animal bond
Example
“According to the ethics of care, our responsibility toward the dog we adopt grows out of the relationship we build with it.”

Political or ethical objection →

Ethology

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The science that studies animal behavior in its natural environment.

By revealing complex behaviors (play, grief, cooperation), ethology has eroded the idea that only humans have a rich emotional and social life.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal behavior science, behavioral biology
See also
Animal behavior, Animal cognition, Ecology, Animal psychology
Example
“Through ethology, watching crows solve puzzles in the wild helps us understand how much they plan.”

Euphemism

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A mild word or expression used in place of a more direct or unpleasant one.

Animal use is full of euphemisms: "slaughter" or "processing" instead of killing, "sacrifice" for the killing of animals at the end of experiments, "harvest" for hunting and fishing, "animal protein" instead of the flesh of an animal. They are not necessarily dishonest, but they reduce discomfort and draw attention away from the victim. Pointing this out calmly, without accusing the speaker, helps the conversation.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
softened wording, euphemistic language
Antonyms
dysphemism
See also
Objectification, Absent referent, Humane washing, Speciesist term
Example
“Calling slaughter ‘processing’ is a euphemism that distances the consumer from the reality of what happens.”

Fallacies →

Euthanasia

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The controlled induction of an animal's death, generally to spare it from suffering; distinct from slaughter, which aims at consumption or production.

It is truly euthanasia only when death is in the animal's own interest, as in untreatable suffering. Killing healthy animals for lack of space, at the end of an experiment or because they are no longer profitable is something else, even when the method is painless, and calling it euthanasia is a euphemism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
mercy killing, putting down
See also
No-kill shelter, Euphemism, Slaughter, Suffering
Example
“The veterinarian recommended euthanasia for the dog, ill and in pain, after treatment alternatives had been exhausted.”

Evidence

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Information obtained by observation, measurement, experiment or record that makes a claim more or less likely.

Not all evidence weighs the same. In general, personal accounts count less than observational studies, which count less than controlled experiments, and reviews that pool many studies count more than a single study; the consensus of scientific bodies shows where the evidence converges. Having little evidence is not the same as having evidence against. And the demand applies to both sides: animal advocates also need to back their claims about health, the environment and data with evidence.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
indications, empirical data
See also
Fact, Science, Pseudoscience, Evidence-based practice
Example
“There is robust evidence, obtained through experiments, that hens feel fear and anticipate events.”

Evidence-based (or rationalist) veganism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

An approach that chooses the foundations, arguments and strategies of veganism by reason and by the best available evidence on what most reduces suffering and exploitation, with a willingness to revise positions.

It applies to animal advocacy the same logic as evidence-based medicine, which calls for decisions grounded in the best research rather than tradition or the opinion of authorities. In practice, this means three things. Grounding veganism in sentience, which anyone can evaluate, rather than faith, affection or borrowed reasons such as health and the environment. Dropping false or exaggerated claims, even when they favour the cause, as the "Stop saying" section shows. And choosing tactics by what research shows works, with the help of organizations such as Faunalytics and Animal Charity Evaluators, admitting uncertainty when the evidence is weak. It isn't an established label: it works as a meta-strategy, which doesn't pick a side in advance, but a way of deciding. It is the approach of this guide, and also the title of the book from which part of its content comes.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Rationalist veganism, Science-based veganism
See also
Evidence, Evidence-based practice, Critical thinking, Effective altruism
Example
“She chose to donate to the campaigns that, according to studies, reduce the most suffering per dollar spent, a practice of evidence-based veganism.”
  • rvgn.org

Beyond veganism →

Evidence-based practice

noun phrase · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

A way of deciding that uses the best available evidence about what works, rather than relying only on intuition, tradition or preference.

The idea took hold in medicine in the 1990s, with evidence-based medicine, and spread to other fields such as education and public policy. In animal advocacy, research organizations study which campaigns, messages and strategies reduce suffering the most. It requires humility: evidence about strategies is limited and changes over time. And it doesn't replace ethics: evidence helps choose the means, but the reason to defend animals comes from sentience. See Evidence, Rationalist (or evidence-based) veganism and Effective altruism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Evidence-informed practice, Evidence-driven approach
See also
Evidence, Evidence-based (or rationalist) veganism, Effective altruism, Science
Example
“The NGO decided to adopt evidence-based practices and tested different leaflets to see which actually changed people's habits.”

Evolutionary continuity

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The idea, set out by Charles Darwin, that the mental differences between humans and other animals are differences of degree, not of kind, because all species descend from common ancestors.

If the human body and brain come from a long history shared with other animals, it would be odd for the capacity to feel to have appeared out of nowhere in our species alone. That is why evolutionary continuity is one of the pillars for attributing pain and emotion to other vertebrates, and increasingly to some invertebrates. It doesn't say that all animals feel the same, only that the question has to be answered with evidence, species by species, and not by a line drawn in advance.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Darwinian continuity, mental continuity
Antonyms
Human exceptionalism
See also
Sentience, Animal consciousness, Animal cognition
Example
"By evolutionary continuity, if humans feel pain and joy, it is reasonable to expect that other mammals, with similar brains, do too."

Expected impact

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The value of a possible outcome multiplied by the probability of it happening, used to compare decisions under uncertainty.

It is the practical application of expected value maximisation: between the certainty of a small harm and a reasonable chance of a very serious one, it may be wiser to accept the former. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) uses the idea on two points: to decide whether helping wild animals is worthwhile without waiting for certainty, and to answer the objection that, since an intervention may go wrong, nothing should be done, given that not acting also has consequences and probabilities. The same reasoning supports caution with beings of uncertain sentience, such as insects. The well-known criticism is the problem of fanaticism: tiny probabilities of enormous outcomes can dominate every decision, and many philosophers look for limits on this.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Expected value, Probability-weighted impact
See also
Expected value maximisation, S-risks, Effective altruism, Wild animal suffering
Example
"The organisation chose the campaign with the highest expected impact: even with a modest chance of success, it could improve the lives of millions of hens."

Expected value maximisation

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

A decision principle under uncertainty that weighs possible outcomes by their probability.

In contexts of uncertainty about the sentience of a given species, this principle can justify moral caution: even a moderate probability of sentience is enough to recommend avoiding harm to it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Expected-value rule
See also
Expected impact, S-risks, Effective altruism, Longtermism
Example
"Under expected value maximisation, an action with a low chance of success but enormous benefit may be preferable to one with a small, certain gain."

Extensive livestock farming

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Raising animals over large areas, at lower animal density.

Animals generally have more space and can express more natural behaviours, but they still go through castration, branding, transport and slaughter, and are more exposed to heat, cold and predators. Because it uses a lot of land, extensive cattle ranching is the main cause of deforestation in Brazil, especially in the Amazon, according to analyses compiled by Our World in Data.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Extensive grazing, Pasture-based farming
Antonyms
Intensive livestock farming, Industrial livestock farming
See also
Intensive livestock farming, Agribusiness, Extinction, Livestock farming
Example
“Extensive livestock farming lets cattle roam large pastures, but it needs so much land that it ends up advancing into native forests.”

Externality

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A cost or benefit that an activity causes to other people, or other beings, and that doesn't show up in the product's price.

In the production of meat, milk and eggs, the most cited externalities are water and air pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, deforestation, antibiotic resistance and the risk of new diseases from animals. Since these costs aren't in the price, society pays them, and the product seems cheaper than it is. The animal-centered critique adds a point usually left out even of this account: the suffering and death of the animals themselves, which aren't even treated as a cost, because the animals are seen as the product.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
external cost, spillover effect
See also
Subsidies, Tax incentive, Antimicrobial resistance, Industrial livestock farming
Example
“River pollution caused by a farm is an externality: the cost falls on the population, not on the price of the meat.”

Argument in the guide →

Extinction

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The complete disappearance of a species; a relevant topic in debates about conservation and human responsibility for biodiversity.

Conservation usually focuses on species and ecosystems, and sentientism on the individuals who can feel: the two views converge when habitat loss kills and displaces animals, and diverge when protecting one species involves killing individuals of another. In 2019 the intergovernmental platform IPBES estimated that about 1 million plant and animal species are threatened with extinction and named land-use change, mainly for agriculture and livestock, as the main direct cause.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
species loss, species disappearance
Antonyms
survival
See also
Invasive alien species, Sentientist environmentalism, Holistic environmentalism, Conservation biology
Example
“The extinction of the Tasmanian tiger is a reminder that a species can vanish entirely within a few decades through human action.”

Extremism

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A position at the far end of a spectrum; in political use, ideologies or actions that reject democratic rules, pluralism and the rights of others, often accepting intimidation or violence.

What counts as extreme depends on what a society considers normal, and that reference point shifts over time. In a society shaped by moral anthropocentrism, speciesism and carnism, someone who simply stops eating and using animals is called an extremist, while breeding and killing more than 80 billion land animals a year, most of them confined, seems moderate only because it is common. The label describes distance from custom, not the seriousness of what is advocated: refusing to take part in a harm is a more restrained position than inflicting it. Martin Luther King, in his Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963), answered the label by saying the question was not whether to be an extremist, but for what cause. Two cautions: there have indeed been violent actions in the name of animals, which this guide rejects, but they don't represent the vast majority of vegans; and turning the label around, calling meat eaters extremists, also shuts the conversation down.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
fanaticism
Antonyms
moderation
See also
Radicalism, Carnism, Moral anthropocentrism, Speciesism
Example
“Some label animal advocates extremists, but the term must be used carefully, distinguishing strong opinion from violence.”

Argument in the guide →

Extrinsic harm

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

Harm that is not bad in itself, but because of what it prevents or causes; the main case is deprivation, when something good someone would have had is taken away.

An extrinsic harm can happen without any pain: a quick death takes away all the good experiences to come, and comfortable confinement takes away freedom, exploration of the environment and companionship. That's why the question "what if the animal doesn't suffer?" doesn't settle the debate: even without intrinsic harm, there can be serious extrinsic harm. Also called harm by deprivation.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
deprivation harm, instrumental harm
Antonyms
Intrinsic harm
See also
Harm, Intrinsic harm, Harm of death
Example
"Losing one's sight is an extrinsic harm: it does not hurt in itself but deprives the person of experiences they would have and a life they could lead."

F↑ A–Z

Fact

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Something that happens or is the case, and that can be checked by observation or evidence.

Facts alone don't decide what we should do: from the fact that we have eaten meat for millennia it doesn't follow that we should keep doing so (see Hume's law on the fallacies page). But moral arguments depend on getting the facts right. "Fish don't feel pain" is a factual claim, and it can be checked. Telling apart fact, opinion and value helps you know what kind of answer each claim calls for.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
verifiable event, objective datum
Antonyms
opinion, myth
See also
Opinion, Truth, Evidence, Myth
Example
“It is a fact that chickens have a nervous system and respond to painful stimuli; the moral discussion comes afterward.”

Fallacies

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Errors of reasoning that make an argument seem convincing even though the conclusion doesn't follow from the premises; in the singular, fallacy.

Some fallacies are formal, errors in logical structure; others are informal, such as the appeal to tradition, the appeal to nature, the appeal to popularity and the straw man, which distorts the other person's position. Spotting a fallacy doesn't prove the conclusion is false, only that that argument doesn't support it. The guide has a page with the most common fallacies about animals.

It is used in laws and technical standards worldwide, including Brazil, and so appears even in texts on animal welfare. Some people prefer "animal raised for consumption" or "exploited animal", which make clear who benefits.

Fishing

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The capture of aquatic animals, with a growing debate about fish sentience.

In number of individuals, it is the largest form of vertebrate killing: estimates by Alison Mood and Phil Brooke indicate more than a trillion wild fish caught each year. Fish die by suffocation, crushing or decompression, usually without any stunning, and fishing also catches other animals unintentionally, such as turtles, dolphins and birds. There is growing evidence that fish feel pain.

Synonyms and related uses

See also
