Hypothetical scenarios

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Imagined situations used to test ideas and principles; when built for this purpose in philosophy, they are called thought experiments.

They are used on both sides of the debate, and can help or hinder. They help when they isolate what matters morally: vegans ask, for example, whether extraterrestrials more intelligent than us could breed and eat us, to test whether intelligence justifies exploiting those who are less intelligent; or whether an AI that felt pain would deserve consideration, to test whether the criterion is sentience rather than species or the material a being is made of. They hinder when the scenario is impossible or poorly described and hides premises, when an intuition about an artificial case is treated as proof, or when it serves to dodge the real decision, as in "what if they discover plants feel?" faced with a choice made today. This also applies to animal advocates: an analogy with extraterrestrials that ignores relevant differences is unconvincing.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
thought experiments, imagined scenarios, hypothetical cases
See also
Edge cases, Sentience in extraterrestrial life, Sentience in AI and digital systems, Logical consistency
Example
"In a debate, he used a hypothetical scenario: what if an alien civilization saw us the way we see other animals? Would that be fair?"

Argument family →

I↑ A–Z

Idyllic nature

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

The view that the lives of animals in nature are, in general, good and happy, in balance and free of significant suffering.

It is the popular and default view, supported by skewed images: large, charismatic animals appear far more often on covers and in documentaries than most wild animals, which are invertebrates and have many offspring, almost all dying early. Oscar Horta and Animal Ethics criticize this view. The opposite view, that suffering predominates in nature, is also disputed: Zach Groff and Yew-Kwang Ng (2019) found an error in Ng's 1995 model and concluded that the balance is uncertain, and Heather Browning and Walter Veit (2023) argue that wild lives may be considerably more positive than assumed. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that, even with a positive balance, there would still be reasons to help the animals who suffer, and points out that the idea of a balance of nature has no clear definition in ecology.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Idealised nature, Romantic view of nature
See also
Welfare biology, Ecological balance, Wild animal suffering
Example
"Whoever imagines the forest as a peaceful paradise ignores that most offspring of many species die young from hunger, disease and predators."

Impartial spectator and ideal observer

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

An imaginary figure used as a touchstone of moral judgment: someone impartial, well informed and able to put themselves in the place of everyone affected, whose verdict would indicate what is right.

The impartial spectator comes from eighteenth-century philosophers such as Francis Hutcheson, David Hume and Adam Smith, the latter in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759); the modern version, the ideal observer theory, was proposed by Roderick Firth in 1952. Peter Singer places it, alongside the golden rule, Kant and R. M. Hare's universalizability, among the ways of saying that ethics takes a universal point of view, in which it does not matter whether the beneficiary is me or someone else. An observer who knew what a pig's or a fish's pain is like would have no reason to discount it by species, which gives the idea antispeciesist force. But it is also criticized: John Rawls, in A Theory of Justice (1971), objected that a spectator who adds up everyone's experiences ignores the distinction between persons, and the sympathy Smith relied on tends to favor those who are near and resemble us.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Impartial spectator, Ideal observer
See also
Impartiality, Moral universality, Prescriptivity, Partiality
Example
“She asked what an impartial spectator would say if they knew the pig's pain as well as the dog's.”

Impartiality

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The principle of giving equal weight to similar interests, without favoring anyone for reasons that don't matter morally, such as who they are, where they are or what group they belong to.

It takes several forms in philosophy: in the dictum attributed to Bentham that each is to count for one and none for more than one, in Henry Sidgwick's "point of view of the universe" and in John Rawls's veil of ignorance, which asks us to choose rules without knowing what place we would occupy in society. Peter Singer extended the idea to animals with equal consideration of interests: species, like race or sex, doesn't change the weight of a pain. Impartiality doesn't forbid all special care for those close to us, and there is a long debate about how much partiality it allows.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Neutrality, Even-handedness
Antonyms
Partiality, Favouritism
See also
Partiality, Equal consideration, Temporal impartiality, Moral universality
Example
"The referee acted with impartiality, judging both sides by the same criteria without favouring the home team."

Incremental reforms

noun phrase · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

Gradual and partial changes in the conditions of animal exploitation, promoted by reformist currents as a step towards (or a substitute for) deeper change.

Examples are the European Union ban on battery cages for hens, in force since 2012, and the ban on veal crates. The debate is whether these changes pave the way to ending exploitation or make it more acceptable to the public; evidence on this effect is still limited.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Gradual changes, Stepwise improvements
Antonyms
Immediate abolition
See also
Welfarism, Reformism, Moral gradualism, Neo-welfarism
Example
“The law that enlarged cages was an incremental reform: it improved animals' lives slightly, without ending the practice.”

Indexical speciesism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A form of speciesism according to which each being should favour members of their own species, whatever it is.

The distinction comes from Mark Bernstein (2004) and Dale Jamieson (2008), who contrast it with absolute speciesism, which Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) prefers to call object-referent: the view that everyone should favour a certain species, like anthropocentrism, for which everyone should favour humans. The indexical version seems more modest, because it would allow humans to favour humans and wolves to favour wolves, and it is close to Bernard Williams's defence in "The Human Prejudice" (2006). The antispeciesist criticism is that it does not explain why species, rather than race, sex or nationality, should be the group that licenses favouring one's own: the same logic would justify an indexical racism. Its defenders compare favouring one's own species to favouring one's own family, which many consider legitimate.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
species partiality, in-group species bias
Antonyms
impartiality
See also
Speciesism, Anthropocentric speciesism, Anthropocentrism, Partiality
Example
“She said that each should look after their own species first, a position philosophers call indexical speciesism.”

Indirect argument

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

An argument that discusses health, the environment, the economy, practicality or who defends veganism, rather than whether animals deserve respect.

It helps correct facts but does not settle the moral question on its own, and the answer to it is indirect too. Often it supports, at most, vegetarianism, eating less or environmentalism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Antonyms
Direct argument
See also
Direct argument, Fallacies, Tu quoque, Critical thinking, Steelman
Example
"Saying that veganism is expensive or that vegans are annoying is an indirect argument, since it says nothing about whether animals deserve respect."

Individual

noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

A unique and distinct being within a species, with its own identity, experiences and interests; the central unit of analysis in animal ethics, as opposed to approaches that think in terms of species or populations.

This emphasis on the individual, rather than on the species or the population, is one of the pillars of sentientism: what matters morally are the interests of each particular sentient being, not the category to which it belongs.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Antonyms
Collective, Species
See also
Subjects-of-a-life, Sentient being, Personality, Sentience
Example
"The biologist insisted on treating each animal in the group as an individual with its own personality, not just another specimen of the species."

Individual cell (cela, confinement unit)

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An individual containment compartment, often used for animals in confinement.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
individual pen, confinement cubicle, stall
See also
Animal confinement, Gestation crate, Veal crate
Example
"Each cell in the shed held only one animal, with no room to turn around, which made it easier to control feeding and production."

Induced skin irritation

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A toxicological test that applies substances to animals' skin to measure irritant reactions, associated with methods such as the Draize test.

In the classic test, OECD guideline 404, the substance is applied to the shaved skin of rabbits and the reaction is observed for up to 14 days. Since 2010 the OECD has accepted tests with laboratory-reconstructed human skin, which can now replace the animal test in many cases. In the European Union, selling cosmetics tested on animals has been banned since 2013.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Skin irritation test, Dermal irritation test
See also
Draize test, Replacement methods, Cosmetics animal testing ban
Example
"The laboratory replaced the induced skin irritation test on rabbits with lab-grown skin models."

Industrial fishing

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Large-scale fishing, associated with overexploitation and mass suffering.

The FAO estimated that 37.7% of assessed fish stocks were overfished in 2021, compared with 10% in 1974. Trawl nets and longlines also catch non-target animals, such as turtles, dolphins, sharks and seabirds, many of them thrown back dead. The fish caught die by asphyxiation, crushing or decompression, without stunning.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Large-scale commercial fishing
Antonyms
Artisanal fishing
See also
Fishing, Aquaculture, Seafood, Stunning of animals
Example
“Trawl nets haul in tons of fish at once, and many die from suffocation or crushing on board.”

Industrial livestock farming

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An industrial-scale model, oriented towards maximum productivity and lowest cost.

It is the dominant model in global production of chicken, eggs and pork. Its low costs depend partly on externalities that do not appear in the price, such as water and air pollution from manure, heavy antibiotic use, the risk of new diseases and the animals' suffering.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Factory farming, Intensive animal agriculture
Antonyms
Extensive livestock farming, Family livestock farming
See also
Animal confinement, Externality, Antimicrobial resistance, Factory farm
Example
“In industrial livestock sheds, thousands of chickens grow in a few weeks, with no access to the outdoors or space to move.”

Inference to the best explanation

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A form of reasoning that accepts, among the hypotheses that would explain a set of facts, the one that explains them best, because it is simpler, more complete or more consistent with the rest of what we know.

It is also called abduction, an idea associated with Charles S. Peirce; the current name was proposed by Gilbert Harman in 1965. It is one of the forms of reasoning we use to attribute minds to other people, and Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), shows that it applies to animals too: the hypothesis that a dog who yelps, runs away and guards an injured paw feels pain explains the behavior better than the hypothesis that it is an automaton with no experience, especially given the similarities in nervous systems and evolutionary history. It differs from the argument by analogy, which starts from the similarities between two cases, although the two usually go together. Nobis uses the same form in ethics: start from firm judgments, such as that racism is wrong, ask which principle best explains them and see what that principle implies for animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
abduction, abductive reasoning
See also
Problem of other minds, Analogy, Sentience, Reflective equilibrium
Example
“That the octopus feels pain is the inference to the best explanation of how it guards and tends the injured part of its body.”

Infighting

noun phrase · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

Conflict within a single movement, between people or currents that defend the same cause, when the dispute comes to consume more energy than the struggle for the shared goal.

Disagreeing about strategy is normal and can be useful, because it forces each side to show evidence. The problem begins when disagreement turns into personal attacks, purity tests and exclusion, which push away people who might join and help no animal. The End Infighting project gathers guidance on reducing these conflicts in the animal movement.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
internal conflict, factionalism, movement squabbles
Antonyms
unity
See also
Abolitionism, Reformism, Institutional activism, Social movement, Activist burnout
Example
"The NGO nearly split over infighting: part of the group wanted campaigns for laws and part demanded direct actions, and the dispute filled the meetings."
  • infighting.org

Insectivory

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

In biology, a diet based mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, characteristic of animals such as anteaters, many bats, swallows and geckos; applied to humans, eating insects, also called entomophagy.

Eating insects is traditional in several cultures, and insect farming has been promoted as a source of sustainable protein, for human consumption and mainly for animal feed. Since there is evidence that some insects may be sentient, and they are farmed and killed by the billions, the practice raises the same ethical questions as other animal farming.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Sentience, Carnivorism, Omnivorism, Herbivory
Example
"The anteater is an example of strict insectivory: its diet is based almost only on ants and termites."

Argument in the guide →

Institutional activism

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

Work through public policy, lobbying and strategic litigation.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
policy advocacy, institutional advocacy
See also
Lobby, Lobbying, Direct action, Animal advocacy, Reformism
Example
"The organization chose institutional activism: it met councillors, presented a study and secured passage of a law banning animals in shows."

Institutional speciesism

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

When laws, public policies or institutions build species-based discrimination into their structure.

It shows up, for example, when animal protection laws allow broad exceptions for economic practices such as livestock farming, treating the suffering of farmed animals as morally less relevant than that of companion animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
structural speciesism, systemic speciesism
See also
Speciesism, Animals as property, Animal protection legislation, Commodification
Example
“When public subsidies favor livestock farming and the law permits cruel production practices, there is institutional speciesism.”

Instrumental value

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The value attributed to something because of its usefulness for another end, and not for its own sake.

Treating animals exclusively as bearers of instrumental value, as resources, is the core of the abolitionist and antispeciesist critique of their status as property.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Value as a means
Antonyms
Intrinsic value
See also
Intrinsic value, Instrumentalization, Animals as property, Moral status
Example
“When an animal has only instrumental value, it is worth what it produces, such as milk or wool, and ceases to be worth anything when it stops producing.”

Instrumentalization

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

Treating someone merely as a means to others' ends, ignoring their own interests; also using a cause or a person for ends foreign to it.

The idea comes from Immanuel Kant, for whom people must always be treated also as ends, and never merely as means. Using someone as a means isn't always wrong: when we buy bread, the baker serves us, but consents and is paid. The problem is using someone merely as a means, without consent and against their interests. Kant didn't extend this principle to animals, but philosophers such as Tom Regan argued that every subject-of-a-life has value of their own and can't be treated as a mere resource. That is what happens in animal farming, where the animal's whole life is organized around what they produce. In the political sense, people also speak of instrumentalizing a cause, for example when animal protection is used only to attack the practices of minority groups, while those of the majority are left out.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Treating as a means
See also
Instrumental value, Intrinsic value, Objectification, Subjects-of-a-life
Example
"By treating the hen as a mere egg machine, the company practises instrumentalisation, ignoring that she has interests of her own."

Intelligentism

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Discrimination that gives less weight to someone's interests because they have lower intelligence or fewer cognitive capacities.

The term is rarely used, but it describes a very common criterion: the idea that animals considered more intelligent, such as primates, dolphins or dogs, deserve more consideration than fish or insects, or that humans matter more because they are more intelligent. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) lists it alongside speciesism, racism, sexism, sizeism and ableism, as forms of discrimination that occur not only when someone's interests are ignored but whenever they are given less weight. The sentientist criticism is that intelligence does not change how much pain hurts: a small child or a person with an intellectual disability suffers as much as anyone else, and the same reasoning applies to animals, as the argument from marginal cases shows. Those who defend some hierarchy answer that cognitive capacities may increase what someone loses, for example through death, which is different from giving less weight to the same interest.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Intelligence-based discrimination
Antonyms
Equal consideration
See also
Sizeism, Speciesism, Argument from marginal cases, Equal consideration
Example
"Saying an animal's interest counts for less because it solves fewer logic problems would, to her, be a case of intelligentism."

Biases →

Intensive livestock farming

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Raising animals at high density with heavy use of inputs and technology.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Intensive farming, Industrial animal farming
Antonyms
Extensive livestock farming
See also
Industrial livestock farming, Extensive livestock farming, Animal confinement, Agribusiness
Example
“Intensive livestock farming raises output per hectare, but it usually subjects animals to confinement and accelerated growth.”

Interest

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

What matters to a being, because it affects their life and well-being for better or worse; having interests, such as avoiding pain and staying alive, is the minimum criterion for deserving moral consideration.

Philosophers distinguish "taking an interest in" something, which is wanting it, from something "being in someone's interest", which is being good for them: an animal may not want a vaccine, and it can still be in their interest. In the moral sense, only sentient beings have interests, because only to them can anything matter. A plant needs water, but there is no one for whom lacking it is bad. Under equal consideration, similar interests count equally, whatever the species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Stake
See also
Equal consideration, Sentience, Animal welfare, Interest-based rights (interest theory)
Example
"Every sentient animal has an interest in avoiding pain, and that interest exists even if it cannot express it in words."

Interest-based rights (interest theory)

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

The theory that to have a right is to have an interest strong enough to impose duties on others, without depending on the ability to make choices or enter agreements.

It stands opposed to the will (or choice) theory, associated with H. L. A. Hart, for which only those who can exercise or waive a right can hold it. Joel Feinberg, in "The Rights of Animals and Unborn Generations" (1974), argued that having interests is the condition for having rights, and Joseph Raz gave the best-known formulation in The Morality of Freedom (1986). Since sentient animals have interests, the theory grants them rights without requiring reason or reciprocity, and the same holds for babies and people with severe cognitive disabilities. Alasdair Cochrane uses it to argue that animals have a right not to suffer, but not always a right to liberty, a position abolitionists criticise for leaving room for using animals without suffering. Another open question is how to weigh conflicting interests, since not every interest generates a right.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
interest theory of rights
Antonyms
will theory (choice theory)
See also
Interest, Rights, Animal rights, Subjects-of-a-life
Example
“Under interest theory, a baby and a dog can both hold rights, since both have important interests even though neither makes legal choices.”

Political or ethical objection →

Intersectional veganism

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A strand of veganism that links the defense of animals to fighting other forms of oppression, such as racism, sexism, class inequality and ableism.

In practice, this means, for example, considering slaughterhouse workers, who are among the most exploited in the food chain; working so that plant-based food is affordable to people who are poor or live on the margins; fighting racism and sexism within the movement itself; and avoiding comparisons and campaigns that offend historically oppressed groups. There is a debate about the limits: part of the movement fears the animal cause will be diluted across many causes, and another part points out that excluding people drives allies away. This guide doesn't require every vegan to embrace every cause, but asks that no one use the animal cause to harm other groups, and that no one use other causes to dismiss the animals. See Intersectionality, Afro-veganism (or Black veganism), Working-class veganism (veganismo popular, Brazilian usage), Ecofeminism and Instrumentalization.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Vegan social justice, Intersectional vegan approach
See also
Intersectionality, Afro-veganism (or Black veganism), Ecofeminism, Instrumentalization, Working-class veganism (veganismo popular, Brazilian usage)
Example
“The collective adopted intersectional veganism and began linking the defense of animals to the fight against racism and inequality.”

Beyond veganism →

Intersectionality

noun · Intersectionality and Social Justice

A theoretical framework that analyzes how different forms of oppression, such as racism, sexism, class inequality and ableism, intersect and produce specific experiences of discrimination.

The term was coined by the legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989 to show that the discrimination faced by Black women isn't simply the sum of racism and sexism, and so went unnoticed in both anti-racist and feminist struggles. The idea has roots in Black feminism, as in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977. Crenshaw dealt with oppressions among humans. Including species is an extension proposed by authors in animal ethics, such as Carol J. Adams and Lori Gruen, who see a common logic of domination between speciesism and other oppressions; other authors, including Black feminists, debate whether this extension is appropriate or dilutes the original meaning.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Intersecting oppressions, Overlapping oppressions
See also
Intersectional veganism, Ecofeminism, Afro-veganism (or Black veganism), Animal slavery
Example
"Intersectionality helps explain why a meatpacking worker faces gender, class and race pressures at once."

Beyond veganism →

Intrinsic harm

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

Harm that is bad in itself for the one who suffers it, regardless of its consequences, such as pain, fear, distress and boredom.

It is the easiest kind of harm to recognize, because it is felt: an animal mutilated without anaesthesia or confined in a space where they can barely move suffers an intrinsic harm. Many animal welfare reforms try to reduce only this kind of harm, and leave aside extrinsic harm, such as death.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
direct harm, harm in itself
Antonyms
Extrinsic harm
See also
Harm, Extrinsic harm, Suffering
Example
"The pain of a burn is an intrinsic harm: bad for the one who feels it in itself, even if nothing else happens afterward."

Intrinsic value

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The value a being has in itself, regardless of its usefulness to others; also called value in itself or inherent value.

It is the central concept of animal rights theories, which hold that every subject-of-a-life has intrinsic value, incompatible with being treated as a mere resource.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Value in itself
Antonyms
Instrumental value
See also
Instrumental value, Moral status, Subjects-of-a-life, Animal rights
Example
“To say an animal has intrinsic value is to say its life matters in itself, not just because it serves some human end.”

Intuitive and critical levels

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

R. M. Hare's distinction between the intuitive level of moral thinking, that of the general rules we follow in everyday life without calculating each case, and the critical level, that of careful reflection on which rules to adopt and on exceptional cases.

Hare developed it in Moral Thinking (1981), and Peter Singer adopted it in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993): since we calculate badly when we are in a hurry, emotional or have interests at stake, firm rules such as not lying and not killing tend to have better consequences than redoing the sum at every decision. It is the main utilitarian answer to the charge that calculation never forbids anything. For animals it cuts two ways: Singer grants, at the critical level, that painlessly killing some animals who lack self-awareness might not be wrong in itself, but recommends, at the intuitive level, not killing them for food, because that leads us to treat them as objects. Bernard Williams criticized the idea as "Government House" utilitarianism, in which the theory is hidden from those who follow the rules, and animal advocates point out that many inherited intuitions are speciesist, which requires the critical level to revise them, not merely protect them.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Two-level moral thinking, Two-level utilitarianism
See also
Preference utilitarianism, Replaceability (replaceability argument), Reflective equilibrium, Consequentialism
Example
“On the intuitive and critical levels, even someone who admits exceptions in theory can follow, in everyday life, the rule of not killing animals for food.”

Invasive alien species

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A species taken by humans outside its native range that spreads and causes harm to ecosystems, other species or the economy, such as the European wild boar in Brazil.

These species are usually fought by large-scale killing, which creates a conflict between the conservationist view, which values species and ecosystems, and the sentientist view, which looks at each individual. The invasive animals themselves are not to blame for being there. Sentientists don't deny the ecological harm, but call for methods that cause less suffering and for attention also to the native animals affected. In Brazil, the boar hunting authorized for control has been criticized for also serving as a pretext for sport hunting. Not every alien species is invasive: an alien species is one living outside its native range, and an invasive species is an alien one that spreads and threatens goals such as biodiversity, so the criterion is environmental, not the suffering of animals. A case cited by Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) is that of the ruddy duck (Oxyura jamaicensis), brought to the United Kingdom in the 1940s, which escaped into the wild and reached Spain, where it interbred with the endangered white-headed duck (Oxyura leucocephala); to protect the native species from hybrids, Spain has killed ruddy ducks since the 1990s, and the UK culled thousands of them in an eradication programme begun in 2005.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
invasive species, alien invader
Antonyms
native species
See also
Holistic environmentalism, Sentientist environmentalism, Animal population control, Conservation biology
Example
“The wild boar, taken outside its native range, became an invasive alien species, and there is debate on how to control it without cruelty.”

Jurisdiction

noun · Animal Law and Legislation

The power of a state, court or authority to apply the law and settle disputes; also the territory or subject matter over which that power applies.

Animal protection varies greatly from one jurisdiction to another: a practice banned in one country may be allowed next door, and companies sometimes move abroad what is banned at home. That's why animal advocacy happens at several levels at once: municipal, state, national and international.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Competence, Authority
See also

Example

Justice

noun · Animal Law and Legislation

An ethical and legal principle of the fair distribution of benefits, burdens and moral consideration among the members of a community.

Its extension to animals is a central theme of animal law: if justice presupposes giving equal consideration to similar interests, excluding animals from that consideration merely because of their species would be, by definition, unjust.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Fairness, Equity, Rightness
Antonyms
Injustice
See also
Food justice, Egalitarianism, Law, Legality
Example
"To her, justice means giving each being what it is due, which includes not causing unnecessary suffering to animals."

Justification

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A reason given to show that an action or a belief is right.

In ethics, anyone who causes harm to someone needs a justification, and the guide examines precisely the justifications given for using animals. A good justification has to be factually true and morally relevant. It is also different from an explanation: explaining why someone does something, such as habit or culture, doesn't show that it is right to do it.

Synonyms, example and related terms

Reason, Grounds, Rationale
See also
Argument, Fallacies, Rationality, Logical consistency

Lacto-ovo vegetarianism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

Vegetarianism that includes eggs and dairy but excludes all meat, including fish and seafood.

It is the most common form of vegetarianism in the West. Eggs and milk don't require killing the animal at the time of consumption, but the industries that produce them do kill: in egg production, billions of male chicks are killed at birth, and hens and cows are slaughtered when production falls; in dairy, calves are separated from their mothers.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Lacto-ovo vegetarian diet, Ovo-lacto vegetarianism
See also
Ovo-vegetarianism, Lacto-vegetarianism, Vegetarianism, Veganism
Example
“Many vegetarians are lacto-ovo vegetarians: they do not eat meat, but still consume milk, cheese and eggs.”

Lacto-vegetarianism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

Vegetarianism that includes milk and dairy products but excludes eggs and all meat.

It is the traditional form of vegetarianism in India, linked to Hinduism and Jainism. In commercial production, the cow must give birth to give milk, calves are separated from their mothers, and males usually go to slaughter.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Lacto-vegetarian diet, Vegetarianism with dairy
See also
Lacto-ovo vegetarianism, Vegetarianism, Veganism, Dairy products
Example
"As a lacto-vegetarian, she skipped eggs and meat but still had cheese and yoghurt in her meals."

Land ethic

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

The American forester and ecologist Aldo Leopold's proposal to extend the moral community to soil, water, plants and animals, taken together as "the land".

It appears in the essay "The Land Ethic", in A Sand County Almanac (1949), published a year after the author's death, and is summed up in the maxim that a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community, and wrong when it tends otherwise. It is one of the sources of ecocentrism and deep ecology; J. Baird Callicott, its leading interpreter, showed in "Animal Liberation: A Triangular Affair" (1980) how far it stands from animal liberation. Leopold was a hunter, and the land ethic accepts hunting and the culling of individuals when they serve the balance of the ecosystem; this is why Tom Regan, in The Case for Animal Rights (1983), called it environmental fascism, for sacrificing the individual to the good of the whole. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), asks what it would be for an ecosystem to have an interest frustrated, and concludes that the line of sentience is a firmer basis for moral consideration. From a sentientist point of view, the value of the environment is real, but it comes from the beings who live and feel in it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Leopold's land ethic
Antonyms
Sentientist environmentalism
See also
Ecocentrism, Holism, Deep ecology, Hunting, Environmentalism (moral)
Example
"In the name of the land ethic, the park authorized culling deer to protect the vegetation."

Language

noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

A system of symbolic communication used to represent and convey meaning.

Its historical use as a criterion for the moral exclusion of nonhuman animals is criticised by sentientist currents, for which the absence of complex verbal language is irrelevant given the proven capacity to suffer.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Symbolic communication
See also
Animal language, Speciesist term, Euphemism, Animal cognition
Example
"Language shapes thought: calling an animal 'raw material' or 'a head of cattle' changes how we see it."

Lanolin

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A fatty substance extracted from sheep's wool, used in cosmetics.

It is extracted from wool after shearing, without killing the animal, but it is a by-product of the wool industry and therefore is not considered vegan. Lanolin is also the main raw material for the vitamin D3 in supplements; vegan versions of D3 are made from lichens.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Wool grease, Wool wax
See also
Wool, Cruelty-free, Fur and leather
Example
"Lanolin appeared on the moisturiser's ingredient list, and she realised the product was not vegan."

Law

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The body of rules that governs life in society and is enforced by the state; also, in another sense, what someone can claim, as in "having a right".

Legal scholars call the first sense objective law, the rules, and the second subjective right, someone's entitlement. Historically, most legal systems treated animals as things, objects of law, not as subjects. It's worth remembering that what is legal isn't automatically just: law changes when society recognizes injustices it once accepted.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
legal system, jurisprudence, legislation
See also
Statute, Animal law, Rights, Animal rights
Example
"In Brazilian law, animals are still treated partly as things, but recent rulings have recognized their status as sentient beings."

LD50 (lethal dose 50%)

acronym · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A toxicological measure indicating the dose of a substance capable of killing 50% of a population of tested animals; a classic and controversial method of toxicity testing.

The measure was proposed in 1927 by the British pharmacologist J. W. Trevan, to standardize the potency of substances such as digitalis and insulin, and became a regulatory requirement for drugs, pesticides, additives and cosmetics. In the classic test, groups of animals, usually rats or mice, receive doses of a substance until the dose that kills half of them is found, often with intense suffering before death. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), cites the test as applied to food colorings and preservatives as an example of experimentation that serves no vital medical purpose. The OECD adopted three alternative methods, the fixed dose procedure (1992), the acute toxic class method (1996) and the up-and-down procedure (1998), and, when it revised them in December 2001, decided to delete the classic test, Test Guideline 401, from its guidelines, effective December 2002; the new methods use fewer animals, and the fixed dose procedure replaces death with signs of toxicity as the endpoint, but all of them still use animals and still involve deaths. Critics also question how well the number predicts effects in humans.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
median lethal dose
See also
Animal experimentation, 3Rs, Replacement methods, Draize test
Example
“The toxicity report cited the LD50 in mice, and today agencies increasingly accept alternative methods that make this kind of test unnecessary.”

Learned helplessness

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

A state in which a person stops trying to change a situation because they have come to believe that nothing they do will make a difference.

The concept comes from experiments by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier in the 1960s with dogs given electric shocks, an example of the very animal suffering the guide discusses. In 2016, the same authors revised the theory: passivity in the face of pain would be the default response, and what is learned is the perception of control. In activism, it shows up as the feeling that exploitation is too big to change. Seeing concrete results, even small ones, helps get out of it. See Activist burnout and the argument "One person doesn't make a difference".

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Activist burnout, Activist fatigue
Example
"After so many campaigns with no results, the group fell into learned helplessness and stopped believing any action could change the situation."

Legality

noun · Animal Law and Legislation

The conformity of an action or rule with the legal system in force, distinct from its moral legitimacy.

Many forms of animal exploitation are fully legal, which shows the difference between what the law permits and what is morally justifiable, a distinction central to any antispeciesist critique of the legal status quo.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Lawfulness
Antonyms
Illegality, Unlawfulness
See also
Statute, Law, Justice, Animal protection legislation
Example
"The legality of a practice does not settle whether it is morally right: slavery was once legal in many countries."

Leghold trap

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A metal trap with two jaws that snap shut on an animal's leg and hold it until the trapper arrives; used mainly to catch animals for their fur.

The animal may stay trapped for hours or days, with fractures, dehydration and fear, and some chew off their own leg to escape. Non-target animals, including dogs and protected species, are also caught. The European Union approved a ban on these traps in 1991, effective from 1995, but they remain legal in other countries.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
foothold trap, steel-jaw trap, gin trap
See also
Hunting, Fur and leather, Suffering, Animal cruelty, Fishing
Example
"The animal stayed caught for hours in the leghold trap, its paw injured, until the hunter arrived, a practice banned in several countries."

Liberal neutrality

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The principle that the state should stay neutral among citizens' different conceptions of the good life, limiting itself to securing rights and freedoms, summed up as the priority of the right over the good.

It is a central idea of John Rawls, above all in Political Liberalism (1993), and of Ronald Dworkin. The risk for animals is that how we treat them gets classed as a matter of taste or private belief, like religion or lifestyle, on which the state should take no side; veganism then becomes just one worldview among others. Rawls himself granted that cruelty to animals is wrong, but placed it outside justice. Authors such as Robert Garner, Alasdair Cochrane, Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka reply that neutrality applies to choices that affect oneself, not to harm done to others: if animals' interests count, protecting them is a matter of justice, like banning violence against humans, not the imposition of an ideal of life.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
State neutrality, Liberal state neutrality
Antonyms
Perfectionism
See also
Liberalism, Personal choice, Liberal veganism, Original position and veil of ignorance
Example
"Under liberal neutrality, the government would promote no religion or way of life, but it is debated whether it should protect animals."

Political or ethical objection →

Liberal veganism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A current that argues for ending animal exploitation within liberal democracy and the market economy, through rights, laws, consumer choices and innovation.

It is not an established label. Authors such as Alasdair Cochrane, Martha Nussbaum, Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka defend animals from liberal theory.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Liberal animal rights approach
See also
Liberalism, Animal rights, Liberal neutrality, Mixed community
Example
“Liberal veganism argues that the same principles of liberty and equality before the law should be extended to animals.”

Liberalism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A political and philosophical current whose principles are individual liberty, equality before the law, civil rights and limits on the power of the state.

Under John Stuart Mill's harm principle, restricting liberty is legitimate to prevent harm to others: if animals can be harmed, using them falls within what liberalism examines.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Liberal doctrine
Antonyms
Authoritarianism, Totalitarianism
See also
Liberal neutrality, Freedom, Autonomy, Liberal veganism
Example
"Liberalism holds that everyone has a right to their own choices, but it is debated whether this includes choices that harm animals."

Liminal animals and animal sovereignty

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

Categories from Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka's political theory: liminal animals are non-domesticated animals who live among humans, such as pigeons and rats, and animal sovereignty is the right of communities of wild animals to govern themselves in their own territory.

In Zoopolis (2011), the authors propose that our obligations to animals depend on the political relationship: domesticated animals would be citizens, liminal animals denizens with rights of their own, and wild animals sovereign communities, like foreign nations. From this they conclude that we should respect the autonomy of wild animals and intervene only in limited cases, although they accept that intervening is sometimes permissible and even obligatory. Oscar Horta (2013) and Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answer that the analogy with nations does not fit well: animals who are born by the hundreds and almost all die within a few days do not form communities capable of self-government, and the border between human and wild territory does not change what each animal feels. Defenders of the approach reply that it avoids paternalism and takes seriously the lives wild animals lead without us.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Zoopolis theory
See also
Synanthropic animals, Mixed community, Paternalism, Wild animal suffering, Animal rights
Example
"Discussing the square's pigeons as liminal animals, the professor asked what rights they would have as city residents, being neither domestic nor wild."

Liquid smoke

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

A condiment that gives foods a smoky flavor without the use of real smoke, useful for reproducing flavors associated with smoked meats in vegan recipes.

smoke flavoring, smoke essence
See also
Vegan churrasco (Brazilian barbecue), Bacon, Plant-based meat, Plant-based
Example
“A dash of liquid smoke gave the marinated tofu a smoky flavor, as in vegan bacon.”

Live animal transport

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A stage of the production chain associated with stress, injuries and mortality.

Animals can spend hours or days without food, water or rest, in extreme heat or cold, and many are injured or die on the way. The export of live cattle by ship, on voyages lasting weeks, is especially criticized, and Brazil is one of the major exporters. New Zealand banned the export of farm animals by sea in 2023, and the United Kingdom banned live exports for slaughter and fattening in 2024.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal transport
See also
Live cargo, Downed animal, Slaughter, Slaughterhouse
Example
“Live animal transport on ships lasting many days exposes cattle and sheep to heat, hunger and disease, according to animal protection organizations.”

Live cargo

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A term from the transport sector that designates live animals carried as merchandise.

The term treats animals as merchandise, in a category close to other perishable cargo. For sea voyages, some countries, such as Australia, set a mortality rate above which the voyage must be investigated, which shows that a certain number of deaths is treated as normal.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
live freight, live animal shipment
See also
Live animal transport, Commodification, Euphemism
Example
"At the port, the ship carrying thousands of cattle appeared in the paperwork only as live cargo, with no mention of the animals as individuals."

Livestock (gado)

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A generic term for farmed animals, especially cattle.

In English, "cattle" comes from the Anglo-Norman "catel", meaning goods or property, and shares its origin with "capital" and "chattel", which shows how animals were long counted as wealth. In Portuguese, "gado" is also used for people seen as an obedient mass, a usage that reinforces the idea of these animals as a group without individuals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
herd
See also
Animals as property, Commodification, Speciesist term, Livestock farming
Example
“By calling cows just ‘livestock’, the farmer treats them as units of production, and critics point to the word as a speciesist term.”

Livestock farming

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The breeding and use of animals for economic purposes, mainly food.

It is one part of agriculture and livestock farming (agropecuária), along with crop farming. Veganism opposes livestock farming, not crop farming.

Synonyms and related uses
Animal husbandry
See also
Agropecuária (agriculture and livestock), Agriculture, Industrial livestock farming, Extensive livestock farming, Livestock industry

Livestock industry

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The set of economic activities linked to raising animals for the production of food and other products.

According to FAO data, more than 80 billion land animals are slaughtered each year worldwide, not counting fish and male chicks killed at hatching. A 2018 study by Joseph Poore and Thomas Nemecek estimated that meat, dairy, eggs and farmed fish occupy 83% of farmland and provide 18% of calories consumed. The FAO estimated that livestock supply chains account for about 12% of human greenhouse gas emissions, in a 2023 revision, or 14.5%, in a 2013 estimate. Brazil is among the largest producers and exporters of beef and chicken.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Livestock sector, Animal agriculture industry
See also
Agribusiness, Industrial livestock farming, Meat industry
Example
"The livestock industry carries significant weight in the country's exports and great political influence over decisions on land use."

Living being

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

Any organism that exhibits biological processes such as metabolism, growth and reproduction; a broader category than "sentient being", since it also includes plants and microorganisms. Not every living being is sentient.

This distinction is central to sentientism, which grants direct moral consideration only to beings capable of feeling, which sets it apart from biocentric currents that extend moral value to every form of life.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Organism, Living thing
Antonyms
Inanimate thing
See also
Biocentrism, Sentient being, Ecocentrism, Sentience
Example
“A tree is a living being, but for sentientism that is not enough to say it has experiences or interests of its own.”

Lobby

noun · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

The activity of organized groups that seek to influence laws, public policies and government decisions in favor of their interests; also the group that exerts this pressure.

The word comes from the lobbies where legislators were approached. Lobbying is legal and common in democracies, but each group's power is very unequal. In Brazil, the farming sector has one of the largest parliamentary caucuses in Congress, and it tends to weigh in on issues such as environmental licensing and animal welfare rules. Animal protection organizations also lobby, for example for bans on cosmetics testing on animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Pressure group, Political pressure
See also
Lobbying, Agribusiness, Representation
Example
"The livestock sector's lobby worked in Congress to block a bill that raised welfare requirements on farms."

Lobbying

noun · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

The practice or system of lobbies and lobbyists acting on those who decide public policy.

Whether the activity should have its own transparency rules, such as registering lobbyists and disclosing meetings, has been debated for years, to reduce the risk of undue influence.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Lobby, Agribusiness, Representation
Example
"Regulated lobbying requires lobbyists to register and disclose whom they met, which brings transparency to the process."

Logic

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The branch of philosophy that studies correct reasoning: when a conclusion follows from the premises.

An argument is valid when, if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true too; and it is sound when, besides being valid, its premises are actually true. Every chapter of the guide runs this test: it reconstructs the strongest version of the objection and shows whether it fails on validity or on a premise. Logic alone doesn't settle facts or values: it shows what follows from what one accepts, so it needs premises supported by evidence.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Formal reasoning
Antonyms
Illogic
See also
Argument, Fallacies, Logical consistency, Evidence
Example
"By logic, if all sentient beings deserve consideration and pigs are sentient, then pigs deserve consideration."

Logical consistency

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The absence of contradiction between the statements of an argument or of a set of beliefs.

Consistency guarantees internal logic, but not external truth: a set of beliefs can be perfectly consistent and still false, if it starts from a false premise. So, besides consistency, a good argument needs true premises, supported by evidence. In debate, pointing out an inconsistency shows that some belief has to change, but doesn't by itself say which. It differs from moral consistency, which asks us to apply the same principles to similar cases.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
non-contradiction, consistency
Antonyms
Contradiction, Inconsistency
See also
Logic, Moral consistency, Evidence
Example
"The argument failed for lack of logical consistency: it said suffering matters, yet defended practices that cause it needlessly."

Longtermism

noun · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

The philosophical position that positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority of our time, because the future may last a very long time and hold an immense number of beings.

Formulated within effective altruism by philosophers such as William MacAskill, Toby Ord and Nick Bostrom, in practice it focuses mostly on humanity's future, especially on reducing the risks of extinction. Animal advocates argue that the same logic requires including all the sentient beings of the future, most of whom will probably not be human, and draw attention to s-risks.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Long-term view
Antonyms
Presentism, Short-termism
See also
Effective altruism, S-risks, X-risks, Temporal impartiality, Future nonhuman populations
Example
"By longtermism, reducing today a risk that threatens billions of beings in the future would be more urgent than improving small things in the present."

Macrobiotics

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A dietary system of Japanese origin, based on the idea of balance between yin and yang, that prioritizes whole grains, legumes and vegetables; someone who follows it is called macrobiotic.

It was popularized in the West in the 20th century by George Ohsawa and Michio Kushi. Many versions are almost plant-based but include fish, so macrobiotics isn't the same as veganism. Very restrictive versions, especially in children, have been linked to nutritional deficiencies, such as of vitamin B12 and vitamin D.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Macrobiotic diet
See also
Diet, Healthy eating, Rice, Seaweed (kombu, nori)
Example
"On the macrobiotic diet, he started eating brown rice, cooked vegetables and seaweed, avoiding ultra-processed foods."

Maleficence

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The evil or harm done to someone; the opposite of benefit.

In bioethics, the principle of non-maleficence, "first, do no harm", is one of the oldest in medical ethics. Applied consistently, it asks us not to cause unnecessary harm to any being who can suffer it, which includes animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Harm, Detriment
Antonyms
Benefit
See also
Harm, Benefit, Bioethics, Suffering
Example
"The committee assessed whether the possible harm to the patient would outweigh the expected benefit of the new treatment."

Manipulation

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Influencing someone's beliefs or choices by means that bypass or exploit their capacity to evaluate, such as deceiving, hiding information, exploiting biases and emotions or applying pressure, instead of offering good reasons.

The difference from persuasion lies in the means, not the goal: those who persuade present reasons and evidence the other person can examine and reject; those who manipulate count on them not noticing what is happening. Appealing to emotions isn't, in itself, manipulation: showing how animals live on a factory farm is true and relevant, and the emotion it arouses is part of understanding the problem. It becomes manipulation when the image is fake or out of context, when the numbers are exaggerated, or when guilt and shame are used to stop the person from thinking. The line isn't always sharp, and philosophers debate how to draw it. Both sides of the debate can manipulate: the industry, with euphemisms and adverts of happy animals, and animal advocates, with inflated statistics. For a cause that asks for consistency, persuading honestly is also a matter of respect.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Undue influence
Antonyms
Rational persuasion
See also
Mass manipulation, Euphemism, Post-truth, Autonomy
Example
"The advertisement used images of cows in green meadows to manipulate consumers' perception of how the animals actually live."

Margarine

noun · Animal-Derived Products

A spread made mainly from vegetable oils; many are vegan, but several contain whey, milk powder or vitamin D3 from lanolin, so it is worth reading the label.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Plant spread, Vegetable spread
See also
Butter, Vegetable fat, Plant-based cream, Dairy products
Example
"She checks the margarine label, because some versions contain milk or whey."

Marking

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The identification of animals by hot-iron branding, ear tags or other means, usually without anaesthesia.

Hot-iron branding burns the skin until it scars and causes intense pain; freeze branding, with an iron chilled in liquid nitrogen, also hurts, though generally less. Other methods include ear notching, as in piglets, ear tags and tattoos. Ear tags and microchips cause less pain and replace branding in many places; in Brazil, the 2020 pig welfare rule bans ear notching from 2030. See Tabuleta (livestock tag, Brazilian usage), Anesthesia and Physical integrity.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal identification
See also
Anesthesia, Physical integrity, Tabuleta (livestock tag, Brazilian usage)
Example
"Hot-iron branding of cattle is done without anaesthesia and leaves a permanent scar on the animal's skin."

Martin's Act

proper noun · Animal Law and Legislation

A British law of 1822, proposed by the Irish MP Richard Martin, which prohibited the mistreatment of cattle, horses, sheep and other farm and working animals; it is considered one of the first national animal protection laws.

The law did not protect dogs and cats, and animals remained property, but it paved the way for the first animal protection society, in 1824, which later became the RSPCA. It shows that legal protection of animals began with the idea of cruelty, not of rights.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Cruel Treatment of Cattle Act 1822, Ill-Treatment of Cattle Act
See also
Animal cruelty, Animals as property, Welfarism, Animal protection legislation
Example
"Martin's Act is remembered as one of the first modern laws to punish cruelty to animals, although it was limited to cattle."

Mass manipulation

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Manipulation aimed at large audiences, through the press, advertising, political propaganda, social media and other means of communication.

One of the pioneers of public relations, Edward Bernays, argued in his book Propaganda (1928) that public opinion could be deliberately shaped, and by his own account helped popularize the bacon-and-eggs breakfast in the United States, in a campaign for a bacon producer backed by doctors' opinions. Twentieth-century totalitarian regimes used propaganda on a large scale, and today social media allow messages tailored to each profile, as the Cambridge Analytica case showed in 2018. In food, industry campaigns helped associate meat and milk with strength, health and tradition, while showing little of how animals live and die. Two cautions apply: not all mass communication is manipulation, and saying that those who disagree "have been manipulated" doesn't answer their arguments; it can also be a way of dodging the debate.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Mass propaganda, Media manipulation
See also
Manipulation, Post-truth, Meat industry, Carnism
Example
"Repeated television campaigns linking meat consumption to parties and family are examples of mass manipulation, according to critics."

Maximin

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A decision principle that prescribes choosing the course of action in which the well-being of the worst-off is as high as possible, regardless of the total or average sum of well-being.

In contexts of animal exploitation, this principle would favour prioritising the reduction of suffering of the worst-off individuals (often animals in extreme confinement), even when this does not maximise aggregate well-being.

Antonyms
Maximax
See also
Original position and veil of ignorance, Prioritarianism, Justice, Utility maximisation
Example
"Under the maximin criterion, the chosen policy would be the one giving the best possible outcome to society's worst-off."

Meat

noun · Animal-Derived Products

The muscle tissue and other organs of animals used as food.

Everyday language tends to separate meat from the animal: people speak of fillet, rump or breast, not of the dead steer or hen; in English, pork and beef do the same. In Brazil, many people do not count fish and seafood as meat, although they are also animal tissue. People also speak of "producing" meat, as if it were any other commodity, when every piece comes from an animal who was raised and slaughtered, usually very young.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal flesh, animal meat
See also
Absent referent, Euphemism, Slaughter
Example
"On the supermarket tray, the word meat appears with no hint that the piece came from a steer that lived, felt and was slaughtered."

Meat animal

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An animal raised specifically for slaughter and meat consumption.

The expression defines the animal by its function for humans, as if being eaten were one of its traits. Meat strains were selected to grow fast: a broiler chicken reaches slaughter weight in about six weeks, and rapid growth is associated with leg and heart problems.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
livestock for meat
See also
Farmed animal, Speciesist term, Artificial selection, Fattening, Livestock farming
Example

Meat industry

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The set of companies and activities that breed, slaughter, process and sell animals as meat, from genetics and feed to meatpacking plants, distribution and advertising.

It is one of the largest industries in the world: according to FAO data, more than 80 billion land animals are slaughtered each year for consumption, not counting fish, which are measured in tonnes. The sector is concentrated in a few companies, and one of them, Brazil's JBS, is the largest meat processor in the world; Brazil is also the largest exporter of beef and chicken. To protect its prices and image, the industry relies on lobbying, subsidies and advertising with happy animals, fights in court over the use of names like "burger" for plant-based products and, in the United States, backed laws that punish those who secretly film farms, several of which courts have struck down. The costs it doesn't pay fall on others: cattle ranching is the main driver of deforestation in the Amazon, and meatpacking workers face high rates of injury and psychological distress. Criticizing the industry isn't accusing each worker or small producer, who often have few alternatives.

Synonyms, example and related terms

Meat sector, Meatpacking industry
See also
Livestock industry, Industrial livestock farming, Lobby, Subsidies, Externality
Example
"The meat industry funded campaigns to convince consumers that its product was essential to a balanced diet."

Milk

noun · Animal-Derived Products

A mammary secretion produced by female mammals to feed their young, commercially extracted from cows, goats and other species.

To produce milk, a cow must have a calf, and in dairy farming she is usually artificially inseminated every year. Calves are generally separated from their mothers shortly after birth so the milk can be sold; females join the herd and many males go to veal or slaughter. When production drops, after a few years, the cows are slaughtered, long before the end of their natural lives.

Synonyms, example and related terms

Dairy milk
See also

Example

Minimalism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A lifestyle that seeks to own and consume less, keeping what is useful or meaningful and letting go of excess.

The name comes from the minimalist art of the 1960s, and the lifestyle became popular in the 2010s, through books, blogs and documentaries such as those by the duo The Minimalists. It has points in common with veganism: buying less, choosing second-hand and repairing instead of replacing reduce environmental impact, and many minimalists question the idea that consuming more brings happiness. But the two aren't the same. Minimalism asks how much is consumed; veganism asks what is consumed and who pays for it. A minimalist can own few things and still eat meat or wear leather, and a vegan can consume a lot. Some also criticize minimalism when it becomes just an aesthetic, with expensive products sold as simplicity.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Voluntary simplicity, Downshifting
Antonyms
Consumerism
See also
Conscious consumption, Consumption, Veganism
Example
"Embracing minimalism, he got rid of clothes and objects he did not use and began buying only what he needed."

Minority

noun · Activism and the Movement

A group that, for numerical or power-related reasons, has less social influence; a concept used by analogy to discuss the political position of animals as a group without its own representation.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Minority group
Antonyms
Majority
See also
Oppression, Affirmative action, Representation, Egalitarianism
Example

Mirror test

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

A self-recognition test in which a mark is placed on an animal's body, at a spot it can only see in a mirror, to observe whether it uses the reflection to examine or touch the mark.

It was created by the American psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr., who applied it to chimpanzees in a 1970 paper in Science. Besides the great apes, positive results have been reported in bottlenose dolphins (2001), an Asian elephant (2006), Eurasian magpies (2008) and the cleaner wrasse fish (2019), the last still disputed, including by Gallup. The test depends on vision and on the animal's interest in the mark, and may underestimate species that rely on smell: in 2017, Alexandra Horowitz proposed a scent-based version for dogs. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), uses reports of great apes in front of mirrors as evidence of self-consciousness, a criterion that for him makes death more serious. From a sentientist point of view, failing the test does not show that an animal does not feel, nor that it has no interest in going on living: what gives moral status is sentience, not visual self-recognition.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Mark test, Rouge test, Mirror self-recognition test
See also
Self-conscious and merely conscious beings, Animal consciousness, Animal cognition, Animals as persons
Example
"The dog failed the mirror test, but it recognizes its own scent and feels pain like any of us."

Misanthropy

noun · Activism and the Movement

Aversion to, distrust of or contempt for humanity in general.

It can appear in people who live with the injustice done to animals and conclude that humans are the problem. But misanthropy pushes away exactly the people who would need to change, and forgets that only humans have moral agency: only they can recognize the suffering of other beings and act to reduce it. The guide covers this in "Stop saying", under "If humans disappeared, the planet and the animals would be better off".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Dislike of humanity
Antonyms
Philanthropy, Humanitarianism
See also
Activist burnout, Humanitarianism, Apathy, Ecoterrorism
Example
"After years of witnessing cruelty, the activist feared that exhaustion would turn into misanthropy and distance him even from close friends."

Misothery

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

Contempt for or aversion to animals and nature, seen as inferior, dirty or cruel; a term coined by the writer Jim Mason in the book An Unnatural Order (1993), by analogy with misogyny.

It shows up in everyday expressions, such as calling a cruel person an animal or a beast, and in the idea that nature is nothing but violence. Mason argues that this attitude grew with agriculture and animal husbandry, and that it makes exploitation easier: it is easier to use those we despise.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Contempt for animals, Aversion to nature
See also
Dominionism, Anthropocentrism, Ecofeminism, Speciesism
Example
"The author analysed how misothery appears in ancient texts that present animals and nature as inferior and made to serve."

Mixed community

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The philosopher Mary Midgley's term for the community formed by humans and animals who live together and form bonds, above all domesticated ones, to whom we would have duties based on closeness.

Midgley introduced it in Animals and Why They Matter (1983) to show that human societies have always included animals and that partiality towards those close to us can extend to them too. J. Baird Callicott took up the idea in 1988, separating duties to domesticated animals, in the mixed community, from duties to wild ones, in the biotic community, where only the integrity of the ecosystem would count, which would permit culling wild animals to control populations. Proposals such as Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka's in Zoopolis (2011), which argue for citizenship for domesticated animals, follow the same intuition. The antispeciesist critique is twofold: if closeness justifies putting humans first, it would also justify putting whites or men first; and a wild animal's suffering weighs no less because the animal is far from us.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
human-animal community
See also
Partiality, Communitarianism, Domestic animal, Wild animal suffering
Example
"For some philosophers, anyone who lives with a dog belongs to a mixed community, in which the bond created generates duties we do not have toward distant animals."

Moral agent

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

A being capable of acting morally and of being held responsible for its choices (usually adult humans).

Restricting moral agency to humans does not imply that only humans deserve moral consideration: agency and moral patient status are distinct categories. Animals do not need to be agents for their interests to be taken into account.

moral actor

Moral patient
