Moral patient, Moral consideration, Subjects-of-a-life, Duties, Moral status
Example
"A baby is not a moral agent, since it is not answerable for its acts, but it remains a moral patient, whose interests must be taken into account."

Moral anthropocentrism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

The view that only human interests have moral value of their own, and that everything else matters insofar as it serves humans or affects them.

It underpins arguments such as "they're just animals." Sentientism rejects it for treating species, and not the capacity to feel, as the criterion.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
ethical anthropocentrism
Antonyms
Sentiocentrism, Biocentrism
See also
Anthropocentrism, Speciesism, Moral status, Moral consideration, Sentiocentrism
Example
"On moral anthropocentrism, dogs should be spared suffering only because it affects the people who love them, and not because they themselves matter."

Moral circle

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

An imaginary boundary that marks out who is included in the community of morally considered beings; historically expanded to groups previously excluded, such as enslaved people and women.

For antispeciesism, the logic of this historical expansion points to the full inclusion of animals as its next coherent step.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
moral community, circle of moral concern
See also
Moral consideration, Moral extensionism, Moral progress
Example
"Throughout history the moral circle has widened to include people once excluded, and many argue the next step is to include animals."

Moral consideration

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The act of including a being's interests in ethical weighing.

Under the principle of equal consideration, denying this recognition to a being solely because of its species constitutes speciesism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
moral concern, ethical consideration
Antonyms
Moral indifference
See also
Moral status, Equal consideration, Moral circle
Example
"Giving moral consideration to a fish means taking into account what is good or bad for it when deciding how to act, not just its value to us."

Moral consistency

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The logical requirement that ethical principles be applied consistently across similar cases, without arbitrary exceptions; the basis of the argument from marginal cases.

By this requirement, defending unequal treatment of humans and animals in morally equivalent situations is one of the main sources of criticism of speciesism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
treating like cases alike
Antonyms
Double standard, Hypocrisy
See also
Logical consistency, Double standard, Moral schizophrenia
Example
"For moral consistency, someone who condemns violence against dogs must explain why they accept the same pain in pigs, which also feel pain."

Moral extensionism

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The historical and philosophical process of expanding the moral circle to new groups previously excluded, such as women, colonized peoples and animals; a guiding thread running through much of the history of the animal advocacy movement.

For antispeciesism, this process remains incomplete as long as most sentient animals remain excluded from full moral consideration.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
expanding circle, moral expansion
See also
Moral circle, Moral inclusion, Moral progress, Antispeciesism
Example
“The abolition of slavery is often cited as an example of moral extensionism, and some now ask that it reach animals.”

Moral gradualism

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The position that moral status can vary in degree according to a being's cognitive complexity, rather than being all-or-nothing.

Critics point out that degrees of moral status, if used to justify differences in treatment unrelated to the capacity to suffer, can reintroduce by another route the arbitrariness that the principle of equal consideration seeks to eliminate.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
graded moral status, degrees of moral status
Antonyms
moral egalitarianism, equal consideration
See also
Moral status, Equal consideration, Intelligentism, Sentience
Example
“Under moral gradualism, a chimpanzee would carry more moral weight than a fish, which defenders of equal consideration dispute.”

Moral inclusion

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The act of recognizing a being as deserving of consideration within the moral community.

Extending moral inclusion to animals is, for antispeciesism, a necessary correction of a historical error analogous to the moral exclusion of other groups in the past.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Moral expansion, Moral recognition
Antonyms
Moral exclusion
See also
Moral circle, Moral consideration, Moral extensionism, Moral status
Example
"The moral inclusion of animals in the community of beings who deserve consideration was the centre of that ethics seminar's debate."

Moral objectivism

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The position that there are moral truths that are valid independently of opinion or culture.

If objective moral truths exist, and if the capacity to suffer is morally relevant, it follows that excluding animals from moral consideration would be objectively unjustified, and not a mere matter of cultural preference.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Moral realism
Antonyms
Moral relativism, Moral subjectivism
See also
Moral relativism, Cultural relativism, Moral universality, Moral philosophy
Example
“For those who defend moral objectivism, torturing an animal for fun is wrong regardless of what the local culture or the aggressor thinks about it.”

Moral patient

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

A being that can be morally affected, benefited or harmed, even without being a moral agent.

Nonhuman animals fall into this category: even though they cannot be held responsible for their actions, they have interests whose violation or promotion is morally relevant.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Being deserving of moral consideration
Antonyms
Moral agent
See also
Moral agent, Moral consideration, Moral status, Sentience
Example
“A baby cannot fulfill moral duties, but is a moral patient, as is a dog: both have interests that must be taken into account.”

Moral person (Rawls)

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

For John Rawls, a being with the capacity to form a conception of their own good and a sense of justice, a sufficient condition for being owed justice.

Rawls defined the term in A Theory of Justice (1971), in the section on the basis of equality, and concluded that animals, not being moral persons, fall outside justice, although cruelty to them is wrong. He treated this capacity as a sufficient condition, without saying whether it was necessary, and included children because they have the capacity potentially, but left vague the position of humans who will never have it. This is where the argument from marginal cases comes in: if justice applies to all humans, including those who lack these capacities, the real boundary is species, not moral personality. The notion is close to that of moral agent, but the question is different: Rawls is not asking who can be held responsible, but to whom justice is owed.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Rawlsian moral person
See also
Moral agent, Moral patient, Original position and veil of ignorance, Argument from marginal cases, Contractualism, Reciprocity (as a criterion of inclusion)
Example
“If only those with a sense of justice count as moral persons, small children and animals are left in an awkward position within this theory of justice.”

Moral philosophy

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The branch of philosophy that studies what is right and wrong, good and bad, and how we should act; in practice, another name for ethics.

It is usually divided into three parts: metaethics, which asks what moral judgments are and whether they can be true; normative ethics, which proposes criteria for what we should do, such as utilitarianism, deontology and virtue ethics; and applied ethics, which discusses concrete cases, such as abortion, the death penalty and the use of animals. Animal ethics is part of applied ethics, but depends on the other two.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
philosophical ethics, theoretical ethics
See also
Ethics, Normative ethics, Animal ethics, Ethical theories
Example
“In moral philosophy class, the teacher posed the dilemma of saving a dog or a stranger and asked students to justify the choice.”

Moral pluralism

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The position that several ethical theories capture partial truths, with none of them being sufficient on its own.

A pluralist can recognise, for example, both the relevance of the total sum of well-being and the importance of prioritising the worst-off, without committing exclusively to a single theory.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Ethical pluralism, Value pluralism
Antonyms
Moral monism
See also
Reflective equilibrium, Ethical theories, Moral philosophy, Prioritarianism
Example
“A moral pluralist, she combines respect for rights with concern for consequences, without committing to a single theory.”

Moral principle

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A general rule that says what kind of act is right, wrong or permissible, such as "it is wrong to cause unnecessary suffering".

It differs from a moral theory, which is a system that organizes and justifies several principles, such as utilitarianism or rights theory: two people can accept the same principle on the basis of different theories. Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), insists that a fact alone leads to no moral conclusion: "testing benefits humans" justifies something only together with a principle saying that this benefit makes the test permissible. So reconstructing an argument often requires writing out the hidden principle and testing it with counterexamples, in human and animal cases. The guide does this in the "Extrapolations" block of each chapter, which shows where the principle used to justify using animals would lead.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
moral rule, moral norm
See also
Ethical theories, Hidden premise, Counterexample, Reflective equilibrium
Example
“The fact that the test helps someone becomes an argument only together with a moral principle saying that helping justifies the harm.”

Moral progress

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The idea that humanity can expand and refine its ethical judgements over time, as in the historical widening of the moral circle.

For antispeciesism, overcoming speciesism represents the next frontier of this progress, historically comparable to the abolition of slavery and the winning of civil rights.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Moral advancement
Antonyms
Moral regress
See also
Moral extensionism, Moral circle, Moral relativism, Social progress
Example
“Abolishing slavery was seen as moral progress, and some think recognizing basic rights for animals would be the next step.”

Moral relativism

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The position that right and wrong are not universal, but depend on the culture, era or person judging.

Two theses need separating. The first is descriptive and true: cultures and people disagree about what is right. The second is relativism proper: there would be no standard for saying some of these views are better than others. It faces well-known objections, such as those of the philosopher James Rachels: if it were true, we couldn't condemn slavery where it was accepted, nor speak of moral progress, and reformers would always be wrong. Some also invoke relativism selectively, only for the practices they want to protect. Some philosophers, such as Gilbert Harman and David Wong, defend more sophisticated versions, and the debate continues. Even in those versions, an animal's suffering isn't a matter of opinion: they feel pain whatever the culture of the observer.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Ethical relativism
Antonyms
Moral objectivism, Moral universality
See also
Cultural relativism, Moral progress, Moral universality, Double standard
Example
“If everything is relative, it would make no sense to condemn past slavery: that is why moral relativism is often criticized.”

Argument in the guide →

Moral rights and legal rights

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

The distinction between a right someone has for moral reasons, independently of any law, and a right that a law or a court recognizes and enforces.

Legal rights are created by people and vary with time and place; to find out what they are, one only needs to check the law. Moral rights, if they exist, do not depend on recognition: enslaved people already had a right to liberty before the law recognized it, which is why we do not say abolition "gave" them that right. Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), draws two consequences from this. Asking whether we should "give" animals rights rests on a mistaken assumption, because moral rights are recognized, not granted; what is created are legal rights. And what the law allows is not, for that reason alone, morally permissible, just as what it requires is not always just. The distinction also helps against the objection that rights are a human invention: the law is a human invention, but that does not settle which moral rights exist, and whether animals have them is exactly what is in dispute.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
moral and juridical rights
See also
Rights, Animal rights, Legality, Law
Example
“The question isn't whether we should give animals rights: moral rights are recognized, and what the law creates are legal rights.”

Moral schizophrenia

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

An expression used by the legal scholar Gary Francione, in Introduction to Animal Rights (2000), to describe the contradiction of saying that animals matter while treating them as things: loving the dog and eating the pig, condemning cruelty and paying for it.

The contradiction the term points to is real, and psychology studies it under other names, such as the meat paradox and cognitive dissonance. The name, however, is criticized, and rightly so. Schizophrenia is a serious mental disorder, involving symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations, not a "split personality" nor mere inconsistency. Using the word as a metaphor for contradiction reinforces a mistaken idea of the illness and associates people who live with it with something negative, which feeds the stigma they already face. That's why mental health organizations advise against using diagnoses as metaphors. For a cause that criticizes discrimination, it's worth choosing words that don't demean another group: moral inconsistency, moral dissonance or the meat paradox describe the same problem without that cost.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
moral dissociation
Antonyms
moral consistency
See also
Cognitive dissonance, Moral consistency, Speciesist term, Carnism
Example
“Kissing the dog and eating the pig without a second thought is, for some abolitionists, a typical case of moral schizophrenia.”

Moral status

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The degree to which a being is taken into account for its own sake in the ethical decisions of others.

For sentientism, a being's moral status derives solely from its capacity to feel, not from its species, intelligence or usefulness to others.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Moral standing, Moral considerability
See also
Moral consideration, Moral patient, Moral circle, Sentience, Intrinsic value
Example
“To say an animal has moral status is to claim that what happens to it matters in itself, and not only for its usefulness to us.”

Moral universality

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The principle that valid moral judgments must apply equally to all relevantly similar cases, regardless of who carries them out.

It is the logical basis of the argument from marginal cases and of much of the antispeciesist critique: if a moral criterion holds for humans in a given situation, it must hold equally for animals in a relevantly similar situation.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Universalizability
Antonyms
Moral relativism
See also
Moral consistency, Impartiality, Equal consideration, Moral relativism
Example
“By moral universality, if a reason justifies protecting a dog, it must also hold for a pig in a similar situation.”

Morgan's canon

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

A rule of method proposed by the British psychologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan in 1894: an animal's behavior should not be explained by a higher mental capacity if it can be explained by a simpler one.

For much of the 20th century, the canon was used to deny emotions and thought to animals. Today many scientists point out that the simplest explanation is not always the one that denies a mind: if a dog and a human react to injury in the same way and have similar brain structures, it may be simpler to assume that both feel pain. Morgan himself didn't mean to forbid mental explanations when there is evidence for them.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Morgan's rule, principle of parsimony in behavior
See also
Anthropomorphism, Evolutionary continuity, Critical anthropomorphism
Example
"To explain how the dog opened the gate, the researcher applied Morgan's canon and first tested a simpler account based on trial and error."

Motivation

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

An internal factor, psychological, ethical or biological, that drives an agent to act in a certain way.

In the case of adopting veganism, the literature on behaviour change suggests that ethical motivations, centred on the interests of animals, tend to be more stable over time than motivations centred exclusively on health or appearance.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Drive, Reason for acting
Antonyms
Apathy
See also
Decision, Empathy, Compassion, Egoism (egocentrism)
Example
"Her motivation for going vegan came from watching a video about industrial pig farming."

Mulesing

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The surgical removal of skin around the tail of sheep (usually without anaesthesia) to prevent infestation by fly larvae, a common practice in wool production.

It is done mainly in Australia, on merino lambs, with shears, and for a long time without any pain relief. New Zealand banned the practice in 2018, and the Australian state of Victoria now requires pain relief; retailers and fashion brands in several countries refuse wool from mulesed sheep. The alternative advocated by veterinarians and animal protection organizations is to breed sheep with fewer skin folds, which are less susceptible to flystrike.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Mules operation, Sheep breech skin removal
See also
Wool, Anesthesia, Artificial selection, Physical integrity
Example
"Mulesing is done to prevent fly infestations, but campaigns against the practice say it causes intense pain to sheep."

Multiculturalism and cultural exemptions

noun phrase · Intersectionality and Social Justice

The policy of recognising a country's cultural and religious diversity, which sometimes includes exempting certain communities from general rules, such as animal protection laws.

Examples include religious slaughter without prior stunning, allowed for Jews and Muslims in countries such as the United Kingdom, and, in Brazil, the 2019 Supreme Federal Court ruling in RE 494601, which upheld a Rio Grande do Sul law allowing animal sacrifice in Afro-Brazilian religious rites. Advocates such as Will Kymlicka (Multicultural Citizenship, 1995) and Bhikhu Parekh see these exemptions as a way of treating minorities with equal respect. Paula Casal, in the article "Is Multiculturalism Bad for Animals?" (2003), argues that an exemption protects the practice, not the animals, and that the inconsistency of tolerating the cruelty of factory farming is a reason to fight both, not to create new exceptions. There is also the opposite risk: law and outrage tend to target minority practices and spare those of the majority, which is a double standard and can feed racism, as Claire Jean Kim (Dangerous Crossings, 2015), Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka discuss. A consistent yardstick applies the same criterion to the religious shrine, the slaughterhouse and the rodeo.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Cultural pluralism
Antonyms
Assimilationism
See also
Selective outrage, Cultural relativism, Double standard, Vaquejada
Example
"The debate over cultural exemptions asks whether a tradition that causes animals to suffer should be protected just because it is old."

Muzzle

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A device that wraps an animal's snout to restrict its ability to bite or open its mouth.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Halter, Harness, Nose ring, Restraint chute (tronco de contenção)
Example
"The horse was led to the pen with a muzzle strapped to its snout, which kept it from opening its mouth or biting the handler."

Myth

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A widely held belief that isn't supported by the facts; in anthropology, also a traditional narrative that gives meaning to a culture, without necessarily being false.

In the debate about animals, a myth is a widespread false belief, such as "plant protein is incomplete" or "fish don't feel pain". But calling something a myth requires showing the evidence: a belief doesn't become a myth just because we disagree with it, and vegans repeat myths too, such as some exaggerations about health (see "Stop saying").

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Unfounded belief, Misconception
Antonyms
Fact, Truth
See also
Fact, Truth, Pseudoscience, Post-truth
Example
"It is a myth that vitamin B12 exists only in animal products, as it is produced by bacteria and can be obtained through supplements."

N↑ A–Z

Natural harms

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

Harms that sentient beings suffer from causes that do not come from human practices, such as disease, parasites, hunger, cold, predation and disasters.

Luciano Carlos Cunha uses the expression in Razões para ajudar (2022, in Portuguese) as a synonym for non-anthropogenic harms and acknowledges that the label is debatable, because it seems to place humans outside nature. For anyone who looks at the suffering animal, the origin of the harm does not change what they feel: a fracture caused by a fall hurts as much as one caused by a trap, and for this reason Cunha and Oscar Horta deny that natural harms are value-neutral. A frequent confusion, pointed out by Horta, is to call anthropocentric what is merely anthropogenic: help decided on and carried out by humans is anthropogenic, but it would only be anthropocentric if it aimed at the good of humans and ignored that of the animals. Those who defend letting nature take its course usually accept the duty not to cause harm and reject the duty to prevent natural harms, and this asymmetry is at the heart of the debate about wild animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
natural evils, natural suffering, natural harm
Antonyms
Human-caused harm
See also
Suffering from natural causes, Wild animal suffering, Anthropocentrism, Equivalence thesis
Example
"Disease, parasites and drought are natural harms that strike wild animals, and many philosophers discuss whether we have a duty to reduce them."

Natural law theory (jusnaturalism)

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

A legal and philosophical doctrine holding that there is a law prior and superior to the laws made by the state, grounded in nature or in reason, which serves as the standard for judging whether laws are just.

It is opposed to legal positivism, for which law is only the set of rules laid down by the state. It has roots in Antiquity and in Roman law, passed through the natural law of Thomas Aquinas, its ethical and theological version, and took modern form with Hugo Grotius, in On the Law of War and Peace (1625), and John Locke, inspiring the declarations of human rights. In the dominant line, the criterion is reason, and animals, lacking it, are left out of the community of rights; the guide discusses this view in the "Natural law and Thomism" objection. But the tradition is not unanimous: the Roman jurist Ulpian defined natural law as what nature has taught all animals, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, in the preface to the Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755), wrote that animals, being sentient, partake in natural right, and that humans have a duty not to mistreat them needlessly. The natural-law idea that some rights are not created by law, only recognized by it, also underlies theories of animals' moral rights, such as Tom Regan's in The Case for Animal Rights (1983): on this view, the lack of legal protection does not prove that animals have no rights.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Natural law, Natural law theory, Natural right
Antonyms
Legal positivism
See also
Law, Rights, Animal rights, Moral anthropocentrism, Rationality
Example
"In the philosophy of law class, the professor set natural law theory against legal positivism, asking whether an unjust law is still law."

Political or ethical objection →

Naturalistic fallacy

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The error of inferring that something is morally right merely because it is "natural."

Widely used to justify meat consumption, this fallacy ignores that many practices considered "natural," such as violence between humans, are not for that reason considered morally acceptable.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
appeal to nature
See also
Fallacies, Argument, Idyllic nature, Bias
Example
“‘Lions eat meat, so eating meat is morally right’ commits the naturalistic fallacy, concluding what we ought to do from what happens in nature.”

Naturocentrism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

The view that gives direct moral value to what is natural because of its origin, that is, because it was not produced or altered by humans.

Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) uses the term to distinguish this position from holism: for naturocentrism, it is not enough for something to have certain characteristics; it must have arisen from natural processes. An example is Robert Elliot's article "Faking Nature" (1982), according to which an area restored by humans is worth less than the original, even if identical, just as a forgery is worth less than the authentic work; Eric Katz defended a similar idea in 1992. The sentientist criticism is that the origin of a harm does not change what it does to the one who suffers it: hunger caused by a drought hurts no less than hunger caused by humans. Critics also point out that the position assumes humans stand outside nature, a separation many philosophers and ecologists reject.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Valuing the natural
Antonyms
Anthropocentrism
See also
Holism, Natural harms, Naturalistic fallacy, Biocentrism
Example
"Naturocentrism leads to valuing an untouched forest above the comfort of animals suffering within it."

Necessary condition

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A condition without which something does not occur or hold: A is a necessary condition of B when there can be no B without A.

In conditional form, it is written "only if A, B", or "if B, then A". In the debate about moral status, those who deny consideration to animals tend to propose demanding necessary conditions: only those who are rational, have language, are persons or have duties deserve consideration, as in the chapters "Animals aren't rational" and "No duties, no rights". Nathan Nobis notes, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), that these proposals run into the argument from marginal cases: many humans, such as babies and people with severe cognitive disabilities, do not meet the condition and still deserve consideration, which shows it is not necessary. Animal advocates tend instead to point to sentience as a sufficient condition. Confusing the two kinds of condition is a common source of error, as in denying the antecedent.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
requirement, prerequisite
See also
Sufficient condition, Counterexample, Argument from marginal cases, Moral status
Example
“If rationality were a necessary condition for moral status, babies would be left out, which almost no one accepts.”

Necessity

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

What a being needs to live well; in ethics, the criterion that separates unavoidable harm from avoidable harm.

In biology, an animal's needs include food, shelter, movement, companionship and the expression of natural behaviors, and being deprived of them causes suffering. In ethics, almost everyone and many laws accept that causing unnecessary suffering is wrong; the debate is about what counts as necessary. For most people with access to varied food, eating animals isn't necessary for health, according to nutrition bodies such as the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. See the argument "Eating animals is necessary to survive".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Need, Vital requirement
Antonyms
Luxury, Whim
See also
Needs principle, Subsistence, Food security, Fundamental rights
Example
"Food, shelter and medical care are basic needs that everyone should have guaranteed."

Argument in the guide →

Needs principle

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A principle of distributive justice summed up in the formula "from each according to their abilities, to each according to their needs".

The formula circulated among French socialists such as Louis Blanc and became famous through Karl Marx in the Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875), as the motto of an advanced phase of communism. Since animals also have needs, authors such as David Sztybel and Ted Benton have argued that limiting the principle to humans is speciesism, and Benton argues that people find it easier to recognise needs in animals than rights. There are objections: Marx had a society of abundance in mind, not conflicts under scarcity; not every need weighs the same; and without a criterion such as sentience, the idea of need would also cover plants and microorganisms. Even so, the formula leaves a direct lesson: an animal's basic need should outweigh a trivial human preference, such as taste.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Necessity, Socialism, Historical materialism and species-being, Interest
Example
“The needs principle holds that goods should be distributed according to what each person needs, not what they can pay.”

Negative axiology

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A theory of value according to which there is what is bad in itself, such as suffering, but nothing that is good in itself.

On this view, benefiting someone always means reducing or preventing something bad, never adding something good; negative utilitarianism is its best-known version in normative ethics, with roots in a note by Karl Popper in The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945). The classic criticism is R. N. Smart's (1958): if only suffering counts, it would be good to destroy the world painlessly, since all suffering would then end. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) notes that the sentience criterion is compatible both with negative axiologies and with those that recognize positive values, and that the reasons to help wild animals hold under both, because both take suffering to be bad. Moderate versions merely give greater weight to suffering, without denying the value of happiness.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Negative utilitarianism, Trump and greater weight, S-risks, Negative experiences, Suffering
Example
"On negative axiology, only suffering has value, and that value is negative, so a life of pleasure is no better than a life merely free of suffering."

Negative experiences

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

A broad category of aversive subjective states (pain, fear, frustration, boredom) used to assess suffering.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
aversive states, aversive experiences
Antonyms
positive experiences
See also
Positive experiences, Pain, Suffering, Stress
Example
“Cage rearing imposes continuous negative experiences, such as frustration, fear and pain, which welfare assessment must include.”

Negative liberty

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

Liberty as the absence of interference: to be free is not to be prevented or coerced by others.

The distinction between negative and positive liberty became well known through the philosopher Isaiah Berlin, in the 1958 essay Two Concepts of Liberty. For animals, negative liberty is the most obvious: not being locked in cages, crates or tanks, not being tied up, not being forced to work or perform. But it isn't enough: an animal released in a place where they can't survive suffers no interference and can still suffer greatly.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Freedom from interference
Antonyms
Positive liberty
See also
Freedom, Positive liberty, Five Freedoms, Autonomy
Example
"Her negative liberty was guaranteed: no one stopped her from travelling, although she had no money for the ticket."

Negative utilitarianism

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A variant of utilitarianism whose goal is to minimize the total aggregate of suffering, holding that no amount of positive well-being can compensate for it. This variant tends to give stronger moral priority to eliminating animal suffering than to promoting positive experiences, which brings it closer to more urgent positions within the animal liberation movement.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Suffering-focused utilitarianism
Antonyms
Classical utilitarianism
See also
Utilitarianism, Classical utilitarianism, Negative axiology, S-risks
Example
“By negative utilitarianism, the central duty is to reduce suffering, and no pleasure, however great, makes up for the torment of a single being.”

Neo-welfarism

noun phrase · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

A term coined by the jurist Gary Francione for organisations that claim animal rights as their goal but advocate welfare reforms as a step.

It is used critically by abolitionists. Pragmatists reject the label and say the reforms are steps towards ending exploitation.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
New welfarism
Antonyms
Abolitionism
See also
Welfarism, Abolitionism, Incremental reforms, Reformism
Example
"Critics of neo-welfarism say campaigns for larger cages accept exploitation instead of demanding its end."

Beyond veganism →

Nervous system

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

A network of specialized cells (neurons) that allows an organism to process stimuli and coordinate responses; the proposed physiological basis for the capacity to feel.

The absence of a nervous system of the known kind in certain species should not, by itself, be taken as proof of the absence of sentience, given how limited scientific knowledge on the subject still is.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Neural system
See also
Central nervous system, Nociception, Sentience, Pain
Example
“Scientists compare the nervous systems of different species to estimate which ones have structures capable of supporting the experience of pain.”

No-kill shelter

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An animal shelter that does not kill healthy or treatable animals for lack of space or adopters, keeping euthanasia for cases of untreatable suffering.

In Brazil, Law 14,228 of 2021 prohibited zoonosis control agencies, public kennels and official establishments from killing dogs and cats, except by euthanasia in cases of serious or incurable infectious diseases. No-kill shelters depend on neutering, adoption and intake management, and can become overcrowded when these policies are lacking.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
no-kill animal shelter
See also
Euthanasia, Adoption, Animal population control, Rescue, Castration
Example
"The city expanded neutering and adoption fairs to keep its no-kill shelter from overcrowding, since no animal is killed for lack of space."

Nociception

noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

An automatic physiological response to harmful stimuli, distinct from conscious pain; a point of debate in species such as fish and invertebrates.

Sentientist currents hold that, where there is uncertainty about whether nociception is accompanied by conscious experience in a given species, the benefit of the doubt should favour the animal rather than the practice that exploits it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Detection of noxious stimuli
See also
Pain, Sentience, Nervous system, Subjective experience
Example
"Pulling your hand back from fire is nociception, which starts even before you feel the pain."

Argument in the guide →

Non-vegan

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A person who isn't vegan; also the adjective for products and practices that involve exploitation or ingredients of animal origin.

It is a neutral term, which describes without judging: most people are non-vegan, including vegetarians, reducetarians and those who have never thought about it. Non-vegan isn't a synonym for anti-vegan: it describes what a person consumes, not what they think of veganism. As an adjective, it appears on labels and menus to warn that a product contains milk, eggs, honey, gelatin or other ingredients of animal origin.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal product consumer
Antonyms
Vegan
See also
Vegan, Anti-vegan, Carnist, Veganism
Example
"The bakery marks in the window which breads are vegan and which are not, because some contain milk or eggs."

Nonhuman animal

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

Any animal that is not of the human species, such as mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates.

The expression reminds us that human beings are animals too and avoids the opposition "humans and animals", which suggests a greater separation than biology shows and usually comes with the moral exclusion of other animals. It is also written "non-human animal". In everyday writing, "animals" or "other animals" also work, as long as it is clear who is meant.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
nonhuman, non-human animal, other animals
Antonyms
Human being
See also
Animal, Speciesism, Anthropocentrism, Sentient being, Speciesist term
Example
"In the article, the author uses nonhuman animal to remind readers that people are also animals, and that the difference is one of species and not of nature."

Nonviolence

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

An ethical and political principle of rejecting violence as a means of action, historically associated with traditions such as Jainism and Hinduism (ahimsa) and with pacifist social movements, including strands of animal activism.

Extending this principle to animals implies recognising that causing them avoidable harm, and not only humans, is morally equivalent to an act of violence.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Ahimsa, Peaceful resistance
Antonyms
Violence
See also
Direct action, Protest, Self-defense, Extremism
Example
"Following nonviolence, the group held a silent vigil instead of confronting the slaughterhouse workers."

Normative and strategic regulationism

noun phrase · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

Terms proposed by Luciano Carlos Cunha to separate two positions usually called welfarism: the one that considers animal exploitation fair as long as it is regulated (normative) and the one that considers it unjust but defends regulating it as a strategy to end it (strategic).

Cunha introduces the distinction in Razões para ajudar (2022, in Portuguese) to clear up a confusion: since both positions are called welfarism, many people conclude that any concern for animal welfare is reformist, and that defending help for wild animals would be a form of welfarism. It is not: one can reject all exploitation and still care about the well-being of animals, including those who suffer from natural causes. Strategic regulationism corresponds largely to what Gary Francione called new welfarism, in Rain Without Thunder (1996). The debate between abolitionists and reformists over whether reforms bring the end of exploitation closer or postpone it remains open.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Regulationism, Regulatory approach
Antonyms
Abolitionism
See also
Welfarism, Neo-welfarism, Abolitionism, Incremental reforms
Example
“As strategic regulationists, the group backed laws that reduce suffering, seeing them as stepping stones toward ending exploitation.”

Normative ethics

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The branch of philosophy that defines criteria for what is right or wrong to do.

It is within normative ethics that the debate takes place over whether criteria such as species, intelligence or the capacity to suffer should determine who deserves moral consideration.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
normative theory, prescriptive ethics
See also
Ethics, Practical ethics, Ethical theories, Utilitarianism
Example
“Normative ethics compares theories such as utilitarianism and deontology to decide what is right to do.”

Nose ring

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A metal device inserted into the nose of some animals (such as cattle) to make them easier to restrain and lead.

The nasal septum is a sensitive area, and the ring works because pulling it causes pain, which makes the animal comply. In bulls it is used to lead large animals; in sows kept outdoors, rings and cuts to the snout are used to stop them from rooting, a natural behaviour of the species. In Brazil, the 2020 pig welfare rule only tolerates snout cutting for this purpose in outdoor sows and with anaesthesia.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
bull ring, nasal ring
See also
Halter, Muzzle, Physical integrity, Restraint chute (tronco de contenção), Livestock farming
Example
"The breeding bull wore a nose ring, and a tug on the rope was enough for the handler to lead it to the pen."

Nutrition

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The science that studies the processes by which organisms obtain and use food; central to discussions about the viability of plant-based diets.

Nutrition bodies have progressively recognised that well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets can be nutritionally adequate at all stages of life, which weakens the nutritional argument traditionally used against veganism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Nourishment
Antonyms
Malnutrition
See also
Animal nutrition, Nutrology, Vegan diet, Vitamin B12
Example
"Adequate nutrition on a vegan diet depends on planning, with special attention to vitamin B12 and iron."

Nutritional yeast

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

A deactivated fungus, rich in B-complex vitamins, used to give a "buttery" or cheese-like flavor to vegan dishes.

Only fortified yeast is a source of vitamin B12; unfortified yeast has no reliable amounts of the vitamin, so it is worth reading the label.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Nooch, Deactivated yeast, Nutritional yeast flakes
See also
Vitamin B12, Vegan cheese, Vegan diet, Nutrition
Example
"He sprinkled nutritional yeast over the pasta for a cheese-like flavour without using dairy."

Nutrology

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A medical specialty (recognised in Brazil) dedicated to the diagnosis and treatment of nutritional issues in humans, relevant to debates about health on vegan diets.

(see the note under Nutrition)

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Nutritional medicine
See also
Nutrition, Vegan diet, Vitamin B12, Healthy eating
Example
“Anyone adopting a vegan diet can be followed by a nutrition physician, who orders blood tests and advises on supplements when needed.”

O↑ A–Z

Objectification

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Treating a sentient being as a thing, resource or product, erasing their status as an individual with interests of their own.

Language plays a part: calling animals "units", "head" or "stock", or using "it" instead of "he" or "she", helps us forget that someone is there. That is why part of the movement proposes language that treats animals as subjects.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Reification, Thingification
See also
Commodification, Absent referent, Euphemism, Subjectivity
Example
“Calling a cow a ‘breeding unit’ and a chick an ‘input’ is a form of objectification that erases the fact that they are individuals.”

Obligatory

adjective · Normative Ethical Theories

Describes an act that one has a duty to do, so that failing to do it is morally wrong.

It is the same as morally required, and its counterpart is the forbidden, which is what one has a duty not to do. Between the obligatory and the merely permissible lies, for many authors, the supererogatory: the good and praiseworthy act that goes beyond duty. Much of the debate about veganism is about which of these categories it falls into: some accept that sparing animals is admirable but optional, and others argue that ceasing to exploit them is obligatory, like refraining from harming humans. If veganism is merely supererogatory, the arguments concluding that it is obligatory are unsound; if it is obligatory, treating it as optional is a mistake, which is why it pays to say clearly which thesis is at stake. An act can only be obligatory for someone able to perform it, a principle known as ought implies can.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
morally required, mandatory
Antonyms
Supererogatory, optional
See also
Permissible, Forbidden, Supererogatory, Ought implies can
Example
“She doesn't see veganism as a heroic gesture but as obligatory: ceasing to cause avoidable suffering is a duty, not a favor.”

Omission

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

Failing to act when action would be possible; discussed in terms of moral responsibility for harms not prevented.

In the case of wild animals, more radical sentientist currents argue that omission in the face of avoidable suffering in nature may also be morally questionable, one of the most controversial topics in contemporary animal ethics. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022), drawing on the equivalence thesis, defended by James Rachels and, with qualifications, by Peter Singer, argues that allowing a harm we could prevent is not, in itself, less serious than causing it, while much of deontology, with Philippa Foot and Warren Quinn, holds that doing is worse than allowing. This is the subject of the argument "We didn't cause it, so we have no duty to help".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Inaction, Abstention
Antonyms
Action
See also
Equivalence thesis, Positive and negative duties, Natural harms, Wild animal suffering, Action
Example
“He argued that failing to help an injured animal by the roadside is also a morally relevant omission, not just a neutral act.”

Omnivorism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A diet that includes both plant and animal foods; in biology, a trait of animals such as humans, pigs, bears and rats.

Being biologically omnivorous means being able to digest both kinds of food, not needing to eat animals: a well-planned plant-based diet meets human needs. Concluding that we should eat animals because we can is the naturalistic fallacy.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Omnivorous diet, Omnivory
Antonyms
Herbivory, Veganism
See also
Herbivory, Carnivorism, Vegan diet, Naturalistic fallacy
Example
“Saying humans are omnivores describes what the body can digest, but it does not by itself settle what is morally acceptable to eat.”

Argument in the guide →

One Health

noun phrase · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

An approach that treats human health, animal health and environmental health as interconnected, and proposes that they be cared for together across different fields and governments.

It is adopted jointly by the World Health Organization, the FAO, the World Organisation for Animal Health and the UN Environment Programme, which since 2022 have worked as a four-organization alliance on the subject. Its main focuses are preventing zoonoses and pandemics, antimicrobial resistance and food safety. In the debate about animals, it gives scientific grounding to a true point: reducing intensive farming, antibiotic use in healthy animals, the wildlife trade and deforestation is a public health prevention measure. It's worth noting that, in One Health, animal health is usually treated mainly as a means to protect humans, not for the sake of the animals themselves.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Unified health
See also
Zoonosis, Pandemic, Antimicrobial resistance, Superbug
Example
“The One Health approach brings together doctors, veterinarians and ecologists to understand how diseases move among people, animals and the environment.”

Stop saying →

Opinion

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A personal judgment about something, which may or may not be supported by reasons and evidence.

"That's my opinion" doesn't end the conversation. Opinions about facts can be checked, and moral opinions can be assessed by the reasons behind them and by their consistency with what the person already accepts. Everyone has the right to hold opinions, but not every opinion is equally well grounded. See Fact and the argument "Veganism is opinion, not science".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Viewpoint, Point of view
Antonyms
Fact
See also
Fact, Evidence, Skepticism, Critical thinking
Example
“When someone says fish sentience is just an opinion, it is worth remembering that there are studies that support or refute that claim.”

Argument in the guide →

Oppression

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The systematic exercise of power that subordinates and harms a group.

Its application, by analogy, to the treatment of animals within social and economic structures is central to the currents that describe speciesism as a form of structural oppression, comparable, with due differences taken into account, to other forms of domination.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Domination, Subjugation
Antonyms
Freedom
See also
Speciesism, Intersectionality, Animal liberation, Animal exploitation, Animal slavery
Example
“Antispeciesist movements claim that farming animals for consumption is a form of oppression, comparable, with differences, to other forms of domination.”

Organic meat

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Meat from production systems with organic certification (no pesticides or synthetic hormones), which does not necessarily mean better animal welfare conditions.

Welfare requirements vary by country: in the European Union, for example, organic rules require outdoor access and more space, and restrict some mutilations. The label, however, deals mainly with inputs, such as pesticides in feed, hormones and antibiotics, and is not a guarantee of welfare. In every case, the animal is still raised to be killed.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
certified organic meat
Antonyms
Conventional meat
See also
Happy meat, Humane washing, Free range
Example
"Even with the organic meat label, the farm followed production rules that do not eliminate slaughter or the transport of the animals."

Original position and veil of ignorance

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

John Rawls's thought experiment in which people choose principles of justice without knowing what place they would occupy in society, such as their class, race, sex or talents.

It was set out in A Theory of Justice (1971): behind the veil, no one can shape the rules in their own favour, so the rules chosen would be fair. Rawls left species out: those choosing know they are human and have a sense of justice, and animals fall outside the scope of justice. Donald VanDeVeer, in 1979, and Mark Rowlands, in a 1997 article and in the book Animals Like Us (2002), proposed hiding species, or rationality, behind the veil too: someone who might be born a pig on a factory farm would hardly approve of that system. Robert Garner objects that the outcome depends on the convictions about fairness built into the starting point, and Rawls himself acknowledged that our relations with animals lie outside what his theory sets out to cover.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Contractualism, Impartiality, Reflective equilibrium, Moral person (Rawls)
Example
“Imagine choosing society's rules without knowing whether you would be born human or animal: that is the spirit of the veil of ignorance.”

Political or ethical objection →

Ostroveganism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A vegan diet that includes bivalve molluscs, such as oysters, mussels and clams.

Its defenders argue that bivalves are probably not sentient, because they have no centralized brain, and that farming them causes little environmental harm. Science doesn't yet have a firm answer: scallops, for example, have dozens of eyes and swim to escape predators. So many vegans apply the precautionary principle and don't eat bivalves. The Vegan Society's definition of veganism excludes all animals, including bivalves.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Bivalveganism
See also
Sentience, Veganism, Vegan diet, Seafood
Example
“She follows an ostrovegan diet: she eats no animal products except oysters and mussels, because she considers it unlikely that bivalves feel pain.”

Ought implies can

expression · Normative Ethical Theories

The principle that one can only have a duty to do what it is possible to do.

It is traditionally attributed to Immanuel Kant and accepted by most moral theories. In the debate about wild animals, it appears as an objection: since it is impossible to help all the animals in nature, there would be no duty to help them. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that the principle only removes the duty to do the impossible, not the duty to do what is within reach, such as vaccinating, rescuing or researching, and that what is impossible today may cease to be so with more knowledge. The principle itself is debated: a study by Vladimir Chituc and colleagues (2016) found that people often judge that someone ought to do what they cannot, when they are to blame for their own inability.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Demandingness objection, Positive and negative duties, Wild animal suffering
Example
"Since ought implies can, nobody is obliged to save every animal in the world, because nobody can; the duty applies only to what is within reach."

Ovo-vegetarianism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

Vegetarianism that includes eggs but excludes dairy and all meat.

It is sometimes adopted because of lactose intolerance or objection to the dairy industry. Commercial egg production, however, also involves killing male chicks and slaughtering hens when laying declines.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Egg vegetarianism
See also
Lacto-ovo vegetarianism, Lacto-vegetarianism, Vegetarianism, Veganism
Example
“Because he cannot tolerate lactose, he became an ovo-vegetarian: he excludes meat and dairy but keeps eggs on the menu.”

Oxymoron

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A figure of speech that combines contradictory terms.

Expressions such as "humane slaughter" or "happy meat" are described this way by antispeciesists, who consider it incompatible to cause the death of a being that wants to live with any notion of genuine humaneness or happiness for that being.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Contradiction in terms
See also
Contradiction, Euphemism, Happy meat, Happy exploitation
Example
“‘Humane slaughter’ sounds like an oxymoron to those who believe killing a healthy animal that wants to live cannot be an act of humanity.”

P↑ A–Z

Pain

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage. This is the definition adopted in 2020 by the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP).

Pain is an experience, not just a reflex: that is what distinguishes it from nociception. There is strong evidence of pain in mammals and birds, and growing evidence in fish, octopuses and squid, crabs and lobsters; on the basis of a review of that evidence, the United Kingdom included octopuses, squid, crabs and lobsters in its 2022 animal sentience law.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
physical suffering
Antonyms
pleasure
See also
Nociception, Suffering, Sentience, Anesthesia
Example
“Without anaesthesia, castrating piglets causes intense pain, visible in the animals' screams and posture during and after the procedure.”

Argument in the guide →

Painism

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

A perspective proposed by the British psychologist Richard Ryder according to which pain is what matters morally, and whoever suffers most should have priority, whether human or not.

Ryder also coined the term 'speciesism' in 1970.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Pain, Suffering, Sentience, Dorism (a rare coinage close to painism)
Example
“Under painism, what matters most is the intensity of suffering, so the individual who suffers most should have moral priority.”

Pandemic

noun · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

An epidemic that spreads across several countries or continents and affects a large number of people, such as the 1918 flu, the HIV pandemic and COVID-19.

Most recent pandemics began with viruses from animals. According to the UN biodiversity panel (IPBES), in 2020, the main risk factors for new pandemics are land-use change, the expansion and intensification of agriculture and livestock farming, and the trade and consumption of wild animals. Animal farming plays a real part in this, as shown by the 2009 flu pandemic, which originated in pigs. But most zoonoses come from wild animals, and the origin of COVID-19 is still debated. That's why the guide recommends not saying that "going vegan prevents pandemics", but that eating fewer animals reduces one of the risk factors.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Global outbreak, Worldwide epidemic
See also
One Health, Zoonosis, Antimicrobial resistance, Industrial livestock farming
Example
“Experts warn that overcrowded farms facilitate viral mutation and increase the risk of a new pandemic of animal origin.”

Stop saying →

Paradigm shift

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

A profound transformation in how a society or field of knowledge understands a given subject, such as the growing acceptance of animal sentience.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Conceptual revolution, Paradigmatic turn
See also
Moral progress, Status quo, Social progress, Social conditioning
Example
"The shift from geocentrism to heliocentrism is a classic example of a paradigm shift in how we understand the world."

Parasitism

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

An ecological relationship in which one organism, the parasite, lives in or on another, the host, and feeds on it, harming it, usually without killing it right away.

It is one of the most common ways of life in nature and a huge cause of suffering: worms, ticks and parasitoid wasp larvae, which eat the host alive from the inside, affect most wild animals. Recognizing this suffering is not defending parasitism or proposing to eradicate it now; it is asking how to help where it is already possible, as in treating injured or sick animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Parasitic relationship
Antonyms
Mutualism
See also
Predation, Wild animal suffering, Natural harms, Ecology
Example
“Tick parasitism in deer shows that nature also involves suffering, which raises debates about intervention in wildlife.”

Argument in the guide →

Partiality

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

Giving special weight to the interests of some, such as family, friends, compatriots or one's own companion animals, because of the relationship we have with them.

Some partiality is accepted by almost everyone: caring for one's own children before strangers' children doesn't seem wrong. Philosophers such as Bernard Williams criticized theories that demand total impartiality, and the ethics of care values close relationships. Brian Barry, in Justice as Impartiality (1995), distinguished two levels: first-order partiality, in everyday choices, can be legitimate, but second-order rules and public policies must be impartial, because the state cannot hand out protection according to the affections of those who govern. The limit lies elsewhere: partiality can justify helping those close to us more, but not harming those far away. Loving one's own dog is legitimate partiality; paying for pigs to suffer isn't a way of caring for anyone. Partiality also becomes injustice when the criterion is arbitrary, such as skin colour or species, rather than a real relationship.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Favoritism
Antonyms
Impartiality
See also
Impartiality, Ethics of care, Mixed community, Double standard, Speciesism
Example
“Defending the lives of dogs and cats while ignoring those of pigs is a partiality that critics find hard to justify.”

Paternalism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

Interfering with someone's freedom or choices against their will, with the aim of benefiting them.

The name recalls the authority of parents over their children, and the classic philosophical discussion is Gerald Dworkin's article "Paternalism" (1972), which distinguishes justifiable cases, such as stopping a child from driving, from cases that disrespect the autonomy of adults. Tom Regan, in the preface to the 2004 edition of The Case for Animal Rights, accused the proposal to help wild animals who are victims of natural harms of being paternalistic. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that, for there to be paternalism, help would have to go against what the animal prefers, and no animal prefers to die of hunger or infection; providing food or vaccinating with baits goes against no one's will. The objection has more force against coercive interventions, such as capturing an animal to sterilize them, but even there paternalism is usually accepted with children and domestic animals when the harm prevented is great.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Overprotectiveness
Antonyms
Autonomy
See also
Autonomy, Consent, Liminal animals and animal sovereignty, Wild animal suffering
Example
“Critics say intervening in all of wildlife would be paternalism: treating animals as unable to run their own lives.”

Pea

noun · Plant-Derived Products

A legume used both as direct food and as a source of isolated protein in vegan products.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Plant protein, Soy protein, Beans, Plant milk
Example
“The plant-based burger uses pea protein as its base, which makes it an option for people with a soy allergy.”

Pedigree

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A genealogical record that documents an animal's lineage, used for selective breeding.

Pedigree breeding selects animals for the appearance set out in breed standards, which has concentrated hereditary diseases in many breeds, such as breathing problems in short-nosed dogs like bulldogs and pugs. The BBC documentary Pedigree Dogs Exposed (2008) led to revisions of breed standards in the United Kingdom and to the BBC dropping its coverage of the Crufts show. From a sentientist point of view, the criticism goes beyond health: commercial breeding of purebred animals continues while shelters are full.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Registered lineage, Breed certificate
Antonyms
Mutt, Mixed breed
See also
Artificial selection, Pet shop, Adoption, Breeding facility (criadouro)
Example
“He paid a lot for a pedigreed puppy, unaware that breed trait selection favors respiratory problems.”

I33 · Buying a pedigree dog or cat doesn't hurt anyone →

Perfect and imperfect duties

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A distinction of Kantian origin between duties that hold always and towards everyone, without exception (perfect), and duties that leave room for choice about when, how and towards whom to fulfil them (imperfect).

Immanuel Kant used it in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785) and The Metaphysics of Morals (1797): not lying would be a perfect duty, and helping those in need an imperfect one. Negative duties, not to cause harm, are usually associated with perfect duties, and positive duties, to help, with imperfect and weaker ones. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) disputes this association: since agriculture, transport and nearly everything we do kill animals, no one can fulfil negative duties towards all sentient beings, and they only seem perfect in a context that leaves animals out. For him, given the world as it is, both kinds of duty are imperfect, and being imperfect does not necessarily make a duty weaker; this is an original thesis, still little discussed in the literature.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
strict and wide duties, duties of justice and virtue
See also
Positive and negative duties, Duties, Deontology, Omission
Example
"In duty-based ethics, not lying is often seen as a perfect duty that always applies, and helping others as an imperfect duty that leaves latitude on how and when."

Permissible

adjective · Normative Ethical Theories

Describes an act that it is not morally wrong to do, that is, one that is not forbidden; it may also be obligatory, but need not be.

Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), suggests replacing the ambiguous question "is it right to use animals?" with a more precise one: is each use permissible, obligatory or forbidden, and why? The three categories are defined in terms of one another: the permissible is what is not forbidden, and the obligatory is that whose omission is forbidden; deontic logic, proposed by Georg Henrik von Wright in 1951, formalizes these relations. When people say eating meat is a personal choice, what they claim is that it is permissible, and that is what must be defended with reasons, not merely presumed. What the law allows is not, for that reason alone, morally permissible: legal and moral permission are distinct questions.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
morally permitted, allowed
Antonyms
Forbidden, impermissible
See also
Obligatory, Forbidden, Supererogatory, Personal choice
Example
“The question isn't whether using animals is ‘right’, but whether each use is permissible, and why.”

Perpetual vegan

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A vegan who, after learning about the speciesist attitudes they still hold and the broader questions of animal ethics, rejects those questions or takes a very long time to change, as if veganism were the finish line.

It is the same idea as the perpetual vegetarian, applied one step further. Veganism rejects animal exploitation, but the reason behind it, taking seriously the interests of those who feel, goes beyond exploitation: it calls for attention to all sentient beings, including fish and invertebrates, to wild animals suffering from natural causes and to minds that may arise in the future. For coherence, someone who is vegan for the animals needs to strive to be antispeciesist, and the road doesn't end at veganism. As with the vegetarian, the criticism is not meant to belittle someone who has already changed a lot, but to recall that the same principle still applies.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
stalled vegan
See also
Speciesist vegan, Antispeciesism, Sentientism, Perpetual vegetarian
Example
“She has been vegan for many years but never asked herself why she still uses animal-tested products: a perpetual vegan, as her friends put it.”

Perpetual vegetarian

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A person who became vegetarian and stays that way for a long time, even while recognizing the reasons for veganism and knowing that consuming milk, eggs and other animal products still causes suffering and death.

The expression is informal and critical, but it need not be an insult: it points to a stop halfway along the road. Someone who stops eating meat for the animals already recognizes that they matter, and milk and egg production also involves exploitation and death, such as the calves separated from their mothers and the male chicks culled at hatching. What usually sustains the stop is the feeling of already doing something important, a case of moral licensing: one step taken becomes a reason not to take the next. Fair criticism doesn't treat the vegetarian as an enemy, since they already reduce harm, but it recalls that the same reason that led to the first change calls for the next.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
stalled vegetarian
See also
Vegetarian, Vegan, Perpetual vegan, Vegetarianism
Example
“Vegetarian for twenty years, he keeps consuming eggs and milk without revisiting the decision: a perpetual vegetarian.”

Personal choice

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The argument that a choice that concerns only the person making it should not be criticized or banned.

Veganism answers that eating animals affects a third party, the animal, so it stops being only a personal choice. The guide addresses the argument in chapter E1.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
individual choice, private decision
See also
Choice, Autonomy, Negative liberty, Consent
Example
“‘Eating meat is a personal choice,’ he said, and the reply was that this choice affects other beings, not only the person making it.”

Argument in the guide →

Personality

noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

In animal ethics and law, the set of psychological characteristics (temperament, preferences, behaviour) that distinguish one individual from another; also used in the legal debate on personhood and legal personality.

Recognising legal personality for nonhuman animals is defended by antispeciesist jurists as a way of breaking with the status of mere property to which they are reduced in most legal systems.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Individuality, Individual temperament
See also
Animal legal personhood, Individual, Animal cognition, Animal emotions
Example
“Anyone who lives with pigs notices each has a personality of their own: some are curious, others shy, others playful.”

Pescatarianism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A diet that excludes the meat of land animals but includes fish and seafood.

It isn't a form of vegetarianism, though it is sometimes called one. Fish are sentient, and fishing kills more animals than any other human activity: fishcount estimates put the number of wild fish caught each year at over a trillion.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Pescetarianism, Pesco-vegetarianism
See also
Vegetarianism, Fishing, Seafood, Sentience
Example
“She stopped eating beef, pork and chicken but still eats fish twice a week: she has adopted pescatarianism.”

Pests

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A social and legal category that lowers the moral status of certain animals (rats, pigeons, insects) because of conflict with human interests.

The same animal can be a pest, food, a pet or a protected species, depending on the place and on who is looking: rats are fought in the New York subway, revered at a temple in India and kept as companions in many homes. The science journalist Bethany Brookshire defends this thesis in the book Pests: How Humans Create Animal Villains (2022): "pest" is a human label, applied to animals we fear, that thrive in niches we create or that threaten our control over space. The anthropologist Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger: An Analysis of Concepts of Pollution and Taboo (1966), described dirt as "matter out of place", something that disturbs an order of classification; the idea helps explain why animals seen as out of place, such as a rat in the kitchen or a pigeon in the square, come to be treated as contamination. From an antispeciesist point of view, the label does not change the animal's capacity to feel, and real conflicts can be handled with prevention, sealing entry points, waste management and non-lethal methods, leaving killing, when unavoidable, to the methods that cause the least suffering.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Vermin, Nuisance animals
See also
Synanthropic animals, Animal population control, Invasive alien species, Speciesist term
Example
“The city classified pigeons as an urban pest, but advocates note the label ignores that they are sentient individuals.”

Pet

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The same as a companion domestic animal, such as dogs and cats.

In Brazil the English word is widely used, including in shops and services. Some people prefer "companion animal" and "guardian" to "pet" and "owner", to mark that the animal is an individual and not property.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Companion animal, Pet animal
See also
Pet shop, Companion animal, Guardian or caregiver, Adoption
Example
“Many people say ‘pet’, but advocates prefer ‘companion animal’, which avoids the idea of ownership.”

Pet shop

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A commercial establishment that sells companion animals and related products.

Selling puppies and kittens in shops is criticized for encouraging large-scale commercial breeding, sometimes in poor conditions, while shelters have animals waiting for adoption. Since 2019 California has only allowed shops to offer dogs, cats and rabbits from shelters or rescues, and in 2020 England banned third-party sales of puppies and kittens. Shops also sell birds, fish and reptiles, some captured from the wild.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Pet store
See also
Breeding facility (criadouro), Adoption, Animal trafficking, Pedigree
Example
“The pet shop window displayed purebred puppies for sale, while a few blocks away a crowded shelter was looking for homes.”

Philosophy

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The discipline that investigates fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, values and reason, serving as the theoretical basis for animal ethics.

Historically centered on the human being as the measure of all things, Western philosophy has only recently begun to question this anthropocentrism systematically.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Moral philosophy, Political philosophy, Philosophy of mind, Ethics
Example
“Philosophy helps examine premises we use without noticing, such as the idea that some lives are worth less than others.”

Philosophy of mind

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The branch of philosophy that studies the nature of the mind and consciousness, and the relationship between the mind and the body, or the brain.

Some of its central questions lie at the heart of the debate about animals: how we know other beings have minds, the so-called problem of other minds; what it is to have an experience, Thomas Nagel's question of "what it is like to be a bat" (1974); and why physical processes give rise to experiences, the "hard problem of consciousness", as David Chalmers called it (1995). The same questions come back in the discussion of whether AIs and robots could come to feel.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Consciousness, Subjective experience, Epistemology, Sentience in AI and digital systems
Example
“In the philosophy of mind, the debate about what it is to have a mind extends from humans to octopuses and even AI systems.”

Physical integrity

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

The state of a body free from injury, mutilation or undue violation; a welfare principle that opposes practices such as tail docking or dehorning without necessity.

In livestock farming, many mutilations are routine and legal in much of the world, such as castration, tail docking, teeth clipping, beak trimming and dehorning, often without anesthesia. They exist to adapt the animal to the farming system, for example to stop stressed pigs from biting each other's tails, not for the animal's own good.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Bodily integrity, Physical wholeness
See also
Tail docking, Beak trimming, Castration, Dehorning
Example
"The ban on beak trimming was defended as protecting the birds' physical integrity, since they feel pain when the beak is cut."

Piling

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The crowding of birds in confinement, usually out of fear or stress, which can cause the animals at the bottom of the pile to suffocate.

Synonyms and related uses
smothering
See also
Animal confinement, Stress, Poultry farming, Stereotypy
Example
“Startled by a noise, the birds rushed into one corner of the shed, and the piling killed several by suffocation.”

Plant milk

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

A plant-based drink (soy, oat, almond, etc.) used as a substitute for animal milk.

In 2017, in the TofuTown case, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that names such as milk, butter and cheese are reserved, in trade, for animal products; that is why many European labels say "soy drink" or "oat drink". In everyday use, however, "coconut milk" and "soy milk" have existed for a long time.

Plant-based drink, Non-dairy milk, Vegan milk

Milk, Dairy products, Plant-based meat, Plant-based

Plant protein

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

Protein derived from plant sources (legumes, cereals, seeds), a nutritional alternative to animal protein.

Plant-based protein, Vegetable protein
Antonyms

See also
Animal protein, Soy, Pea, Nutrition
