Plant-based

adjective · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A term for a diet of plant origin, distinct from veganism in that it does not necessarily cover ethics or other uses of animals.

The term is attributed to the American biochemist T. Colin Campbell, in the 1980s, as a way to talk about diet without getting into ethics. On a label, "plant-based" does not guarantee that a product is vegan, and companies that sell animal products use the term to attract another audience.

Plant-derived
Antonyms
Animal-derived
See also

Plant-based cream

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

A plant-based substitute for butter or cream, usually made from vegetable oils.

plant-based butter, margarine, vegan cream
See also
Margarine, Butter, Vegetable fat
Example

Plant-based meat

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

A plant-based food product formulated to imitate the taste, texture or appearance of animal meat.

The name is contested. In 2017, the Court of Justice of the European Union reserved dairy names for animal products, and in 2026 the European Union adopted rules reserving about 30 meat-related names, such as "steak" and "bacon", while still allowing "burger" and "sausage" for plant products. Critics say these rules protect livestock farming more than consumers, who usually know what they are buying. These products are often called ultra-processed, but their nutritional profile varies greatly between brands.

meat analogue, meat alternative, fake meat
See also
Plant milk, Plant-based

Pleasure

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

A pleasant subjective experience; the counterpart of pain in hedonic assessments of well-being.

Enjoyment, Gratification
Antonyms
Pain, Suffering
See also
Pain, Happiness, Positive experiences, Suffering
Example

Political environmentalism

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

A social and political movement that defends the protection of the environment, through laws, campaigns, parties and organizations.

It can have an anthropocentric, holistic or sentientist basis, depending on what it considers valuable in itself.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
environmental movement, green movement
Antonyms
Antienvironmentalism
See also
Environmentalism (moral), Environmentalism (ecologismo), Social movement, Institutional activism, Antienvironmentalism
Example

Political pawns

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

People used for others' ends, without realizing it or without control over it, for example as support in mobilizations, as votes or as a base for pressure.

In English the idea appears in several forms: "pawns", "useful idiots", a harsher term that implies naive supporters, and "astroturfing", the practice of faking grassroots support, for example when an industry funds groups that appear to be spontaneous citizens' movements. Brazilian Portuguese says "massa de manobra". All of these are pejorative, and calling someone a pawn is often a way of dismissing them without answering what they say. Still, the phenomenon exists: economic sectors can mobilize small farmers and workers against rules whose costs and benefits fall unequally, and movements on any side can use supporters without explaining their goals. In the debate about animals, the same caution as with manipulation applies: discuss the arguments of those who mobilize, rather than assuming they disagree only because they were used.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Political tool, Pawns
See also
Co-optation, Mass manipulation, Manipulation, Instrumentalization
Example
"Misinformed voters became political pawns of a campaign that exploited their fears without offering concrete proposals."

Political philosophy

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The branch of philosophy that studies the organization of power, justice and rights; relevant for discussing the representation and citizenship of animals (e.g., sentiocracy).

Proposals such as sentiocracy challenge the traditional assumption that only humans can be political subjects, arguing for the inclusion of the interests of all sentient beings in the public sphere.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
political theory, political thought
See also
Justice, Liberalism, Contractualism, Animal rights
Example
“Political philosophy discusses whether animals should be regarded as citizens, residents or merely protected by the state.”

Pond argument

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

Peter Singer's argument that, if we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it, like someone who wades into a shallow pond to save a drowning child even though it ruins their clothes.

It appeared in "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" (1972) and in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), where Singer applies it to absolute poverty: distance, and the fact that others could also help, do not change the duty. He notes that non-consequentialists can accept the central premise, because the duty lapses when fulfilling it would require violating rights or sacrificing something comparable, and that the "drop in the ocean" objection does not touch it, since preventing part of the harm is enough. The argument is at the origin of effective altruism and carries over to animals with even more force, because no longer buying animal products costs little and is not helping but ceasing to fund the harm; Singer himself, however, framed it for human poverty. It is contested by the demandingness objection, by those who hold that proximity matters morally, such as Frances Kamm, and by critics of the effectiveness of aid, such as Leif Wenar in "Poverty Is No Pond" (2011).

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Drowning child argument, Shallow pond argument
See also
Absolute poverty, Demandingness objection, Equivalence thesis, Effective altruism
Example
“By the pond argument, if swapping cow's milk for a plant milk costs so little, the question is why not do it.”

Population dynamics

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The branch of ecology that studies how the size of populations changes over time, according to rates of birth, death and migration.

One of its most important data points for ethics is age-specific mortality, that is, the proportion of animals of a species that die at each stage of life, summarized in life tables and survivorship curves. In most species, which lay hundreds or thousands of eggs, almost all offspring die shortly after birth, a pattern ecologists call a type III survivorship curve. Authors such as Oscar Horta, Catia Faria and Luciano Carlos Cunha use these data to argue that, if these young animals can already feel, an early death, often from hunger or predation, is the typical experience of a wild animal. The most debated empirical point is when sentience begins in these early stages, which is still uncertain in many groups, such as fish and insect larvae.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
population ecology, animal demography
See also
Carrying capacity, r and K reproductive strategies, Altricial and precocial animals, Wild animal suffering
Example
"According to population dynamics, a species that produces thousands of offspring usually sees most die early, before reaching adulthood."

Positive and negative duties

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

Negative duties are duties not to do something, such as not to cause harm, and positive duties are duties to do something, such as to help those in need.

Many theories, especially deontological and libertarian ones, give negative duties more force than positive ones, and some deny that positive duties exist. On this basis, some animal rights advocates, such as Tom Regan and Gary Francione, argue that we should simply leave wild animals alone. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) argues that the reason for guaranteeing negative rights, protecting vital interests, also justifies positive duties, since these interests can be threatened by hunger, disease or predation, not only by agents. Defenders of the asymmetry answer that causing harm is worse than failing to prevent it, a position associated with Philippa Foot and Warren Quinn.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
duties to act and to refrain, positive and negative obligations
See also
Duties, Perfect and imperfect duties, Equivalence thesis, Omission
Example
"The negative duty not to hurt a dog is stronger, for many, than the positive duty to rescue every abandoned dog."

Positive education

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

An approach to raising and teaching, children and also animals, based on respect, encouragement and reinforcing the desired behaviour, rather than punishment, fear and pain.

With children, the name often refers to positive discipline, proposed by the psychologist Jane Nelsen in the 1980s based on the ideas of Alfred Adler, which aims to be firm and kind at the same time; it is also used for Martin Seligman's positive education, which brings well-being into schools. Research links physical punishment to worse outcomes for children, and in Brazil the 2014 Menino Bernardo Law bans physical punishment and cruel treatment in child rearing. With animals, the equivalent idea is positive reinforcement training, which rewards the desired behaviour; studies find more signs of stress in dogs trained with aversive methods, such as shock collars and leash jerks.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
positive training, reward-based training
Antonyms
punitive training, aversive training
See also
Animal training, Humane education, Respect, Compassion
Example
“Instead of yelling at the puppy, the owner used positive training, rewarding him with treats whenever he sat calmly.”

Positive experiences

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

A broad category of pleasant subjective states (pleasure, comfort, satisfaction), increasingly taken into account in welfare assessments beyond the mere absence of suffering.

pleasant states, positive welfare
Antonyms

See also
Negative experiences, Pleasure, Happiness, Environmental enrichment
Example

Positive liberty

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

Liberty as the capacity to act: to be free is to have real conditions to make choices and run one's own life.

For Isaiah Berlin, positive liberty was above all self-determination, being one's own master; today the term also covers having the means to act, such as health, resources and a suitable environment. For animals, it helps explain why opening the cages isn't enough: rescued animals need care and a place where they can live well, and wild animals free from human interference can still go hungry, fall ill and suffer. It is one of the reasons part of the movement argues for helping animals in the wild when this is possible without causing more harm.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Freedom as capacity
Antonyms
Negative liberty
See also
Freedom, Negative liberty, Wild animal suffering, Capabilities approach
Example
"For those who defend positive liberty, a person without access to education or health care is not fully free, even if no one stops them."

Post-truth

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A situation in which objective facts are less influential in shaping public opinion than appeals to emotion and personal belief.

The term was chosen as word of the year for 2016 by Oxford Dictionaries, the year of the Brexit referendum and the US presidential election. It isn't the same as fake news: fake news is the content, and post-truth is the climate in which it circulates and convinces, because it confirms what people already want to believe. In the debate about animals, it appears on both sides: in advertisements of happy cows that don't show the reality of farms, in nutrition myths that spread on social media, and also in exaggerations by animal advocates. The antidote is the same for everyone: verifiable sources, attention to what scientific bodies say, including where they disagree, and willingness to admit uncertainty.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Truth, Evidence, Cognitive dissonance, Pseudoscience
Example
“In post-truth times, a rumor repeated on social media can convince more people than a published study.”

Posthumanism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A philosophical current that questions anthropocentrism and the centrality of the human as the measure of all things, opening space to reconsider the moral status of animals and other entities.

By destabilising the privileged position of the human in the hierarchy of value, it creates relevant philosophical bridges with antispeciesism, although not every posthumanist strand treats animal ethics as a central priority.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Humanism, Anthropocentrism, Transhumanism, Philosophy
Example

Poultry farming

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The raising of birds (mainly chickens) for meat and egg production.

Birds are by far the land animals most killed for food: according to FAO data, more than 70 billion chickens a year, out of a total of more than 80 billion land animals. Broiler chickens are slaughtered at about six weeks; laying hens at around a year and a half, when laying declines; and male chicks of laying strains are killed at hatching. Brazil is one of the largest producers and the largest exporter of chicken meat in the world.

The application of normative ethical theories to concrete, specific questions of real life, such as how animals ought to be treated.

The relationship between humans and animals is one of the fields where practical ethics most clearly shows the divergences between normative theories when faced with real, everyday situations such as food.

Predation

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

An ecological relationship in which one animal, the predator, kills and eats another, the prey.

It is one of the main causes of suffering and death of animals in the wild. Recognizing this does not mean advocating killing predators, which would make prey populations grow and increase hunger and disease; the discussion about reducing the suffering caused by predation is about the distant future and calls for research before any intervention.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Predator-prey relationship
See also
Wild animal suffering, Parasitism, Natural harms, Ecology
Example
“A video of a lion hunting a zebra rekindled the discussion about whether predation in nature is something we should try to change.”

Argument in the guide →

Preference autonomy

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The capacity to have preferences and to act to satisfy them, without needing to reflect on moral principles; a criterion proposed by Tom Regan as an alternative to Kantian autonomy.

In The Case for Animal Rights (1983), Regan distinguished Kantian autonomy, which requires acting on rules one could will to be universal and which only adult humans would have, from preference autonomy, which many animals have: a dog choosing where to lie down or a pig searching for food acts on its own behalf. It is one of the traits that make someone a subject-of-a-life and, for Regan, grounds a right to respectful treatment, that is, never to be used merely as a means. Steven Wise and Evelyn Pluhar followed the same line in extending basic rights to animals on the basis of their capacity to act. The sentientist objection is that the criterion still leaves out sentient animals with simpler mental lives; the opposite objection, from Kantians and contractualists, is that preference is not autonomy in the moral sense.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Autonomy, Subjects-of-a-life, Moral agent, Moral patient, Interest
Example
"A hen has preference autonomy when she chooses where to scratch and where to sleep, even without reflecting on moral principles."

Preference utilitarianism

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The version of utilitarianism that judges acts by how far they satisfy or frustrate the preferences of all those affected, rather than by the sum of pleasure and pain.

It was defended by R. M. Hare and adopted by Peter Singer in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), who sees it as what results from universalizing one's own interests, understood as what each person prefers after reflecting on the facts. On this view, killing someone who prefers to go on living is wrong even though the victim is not around to regret it, so killing a being with future-directed desires generally weighs more than killing one who only feels pleasure and pain. For animals, the effect cuts both ways: everyone who has preferences counts, starting with the preference not to suffer, but those who are not self-conscious are more exposed to the replaceability argument. Critics ask how to measure and compare the preferences of such different beings, whether preferences shaped by custom or oppression should count as they stand, and why life should be worth more to those who make plans; Tom Regan replies that an individual's value does not depend on how many preferences they have.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Preference-satisfaction utilitarianism
Antonyms
Hedonistic utilitarianism
See also
Utilitarianism, Classical utilitarianism, Replaceability (replaceability argument), Self-conscious and merely conscious beings, Consequentialism
Example
"In preference utilitarianism, confining a sow in a crate is wrong because it frustrates what she prefers, such as walking, rooting and nest-building."

Premature slaughter

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The killing of an animal before it reaches maturity or full productive age, common in some production chains (e.g. male calves in the dairy industry).

The name suggests there is a normal age of slaughter, but in livestock farming almost all animals are already killed very young compared with how long they could live: broiler chickens at about six weeks, pigs at five to six months and dairy cows at four to five years, in a species that can live 15 to 20 years. The cases called premature are those in which the animal never even acquires commercial value, such as male calves of dairy breeds, killed at days or weeks of age, and male chicks of laying strains, killed on their first day.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
early slaughter
See also
Veal, Dairy industry, Hatchery, Slaughter, Farmed animal
Example
"On laying farms, male chicks have no commercial value and are killed on their first day, a typical case of premature slaughter."

Prescriptivity

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The property of moral judgements of not only describing but also guiding and requiring a certain action from those who accept them.

Recognising animal suffering as morally relevant implies, under this property of moral judgements, a duty to act, and not only an intellectual acknowledgement.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Action-guiding character
Antonyms
Descriptiveness
See also
Normative ethics, Moral philosophy, Naturalistic fallacy, Duties
Example
“Prescriptivity distinguishes ‘animals feel pain’ from ‘we should avoid causing pain’: the second sentence indicates a duty, not just a fact.”

Prima facie

adjective and adverb (Latin phrase) · Normative Ethical Theories

Describes a duty or reason that holds at first sight, that is, one that should be followed unless there is a stronger reason to the contrary.

The expression is Latin and was established in ethics by W. D. Ross, in The Right and the Good (1930), who listed prima facie duties, such as not causing harm, keeping promises and helping, which can conflict; in that case, one gives way to the other without ceasing to exist. Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), uses the idea to separate what is wrong to kill unless there is a very good reason, such as humans, from what is not wrong to kill even in that sense, such as plants and bacteria. Many animal advocates state their conclusions this way: killing or causing suffering to a sentient animal is prima facie wrong, which leaves room for cases such as self-defense or survival with no alternative. This does not weaken the argument in the ordinary case, because whoever invokes the exception must show the strong reason, and taste, habit or lower cost are hardly reasons of that kind.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
at first sight, defeasible
Antonyms
absolute
See also
Duties, Deontology, Forbidden, Necessity
Example
“Killing a sentient animal is prima facie wrong: anyone who wants to make an exception must show a very strong reason.”

Prioritarianism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A variant that attributes greater value to improvements in the well-being of the worst-off, without requiring strict equality between individuals.

By giving extra weight to the suffering of those who are worse off, prioritarianism tends to prioritise interventions that relieve the most intense forms of animal exploitation, even when they do not produce the greatest possible aggregate gain.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Priority to the worst off
See also
Maximin, Utilitarianism, Egalitarianism, Sufficientarianism
Example
“Under prioritarianism, relieving the suffering of an animal trapped in a tiny cage weighs more than adding comfort for those already well off.”

Problem of other minds

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The philosophical problem of justifying the belief that other beings have minds and experiences, since each of us has direct access only to our own.

No one feels another person's pain: we attribute it from behavior, from what the person says and from their similarity to us. The argument by analogy, formulated by John Stuart Mill in the nineteenth century, and inference to the best explanation are the best-known answers, and neither is accepted by all philosophers. Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), notes that we use the same kind of reasoning about animal minds: behavior in the face of pain, shared anatomy and shared evolutionary history point in the same direction. A skepticism that denied minds to animals merely for lack of direct access would also have to deny them to other humans, including those who do not speak, such as babies.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
epistemological problem of other minds
See also
Inference to the best explanation, Philosophy of mind, Consciousness, Anthropomorphism
Example
“If the problem of other minds were enough to deny pain to animals, it would also be enough to deny it to your neighbor.”

Procedural knowledge

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

Knowledge of how to do something, acquired and refined through practice; "knowing how", such as cooking, riding a bike or handling a difficult conversation.

Knowing all the arguments doesn't guarantee knowing how to use them: listening carefully, noticing what the person really means, staying calm and choosing the right answer at the right moment are skills learned through practice. That's why the guide has the simulated debate and the flashcard practice, which train responding, not just reading.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
knowing how, know-how, practical knowledge
Antonyms
Declarative knowledge
See also
Declarative (or explicit) knowledge, Tacit knowledge, Deep learning
Example
"Cooking a good pot of beans without a recipe is procedural knowledge, acquired by repeating the process until you get the right texture."

Progressivism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A political and social stance in favour of change and reform, associated with greater openness to expanding rights and moral consideration to new groups.

The inclusion of animals in the progressive agenda is, however, still less consensual than that of other historically marginalised groups, which reflects the persistence of speciesism even in politically progressive sectors.

Propolis

noun · Animal-Derived Products

A resinous substance produced by bees, used for medicinal and cosmetic purposes.

Like honey and wax, propolis comes from the hive, so it falls under the same debate about the exploitation of bees; it appears in syrups, sprays and cosmetics sold as natural.

Proselytism

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

The act of actively trying to convince other people to adopt a belief or practice, such as veganism; a term sometimes used pejoratively to criticise approaches seen as aggressive.

Activists argue that seeking to persuade others is a natural and legitimate consequence of recognising an ongoing injustice, as happened in other historical social movements.

Preaching, Evangelizing

A collective public demonstration of disagreement, used as a tool of animal activism to press for change.

Example

Proto-vegetarianism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A term used for primitive or partial forms of vegetarianism, generally motivated by practical or cultural reasons more than ethical ones.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Vegetarianism, Veganism, Religious veganism, Pescatarianism
Example
“Historians speak of proto-vegetarianism when describing ancient communities that avoided meat out of scarcity or custom, long before the word vegetarian existed.”

Pseudo-veganism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A current, practice or discourse that presents itself as veganism but does not start from respect for animals or from the refusal to exploit them, the premises of the term's original definition.

On this view, avoiding animal products only for health, for fear of divine punishment, for the environment or as a business strategy, with no link to animal ethics, is strict vegetarianism or a plant-based diet, not veganism. The position rests on the history of the word: in 1949, Leslie Cross, of the Vegan Society, proposed defining veganism as the principle of the emancipation of animals from exploitation by humans, and the definition the society has used since 1988, with small changes in wording, speaks of excluding, as far as is possible and practicable, all forms of exploitation of, and cruelty to, animals. But the usage is disputed: in everyday language, in commerce and in many studies, vegan names the diet or the product, whatever the motive, and many people start for health or the environment and later come to the ethical reason. So the term works better for separating diet from the ethical position than for disqualifying people, and it should not be confused with the speciesist vegan, who refuses animal exploitation but still discriminates by species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Antonyms
Veganism
See also
Speciesist vegan, Plant-based, Strict vegetarianism, Eco-veganism, Vegan washing
Example
"To the activist, calling a diet adopted only to lose weight vegan was pseudo-veganism: it lacked the reason the movement is named for, the animals."

Pseudoscience

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A set of claims presented as scientific without following the scientific method.

Both unfounded claims against the nutritional viability of veganism and exaggerated claims about its benefits can qualify as pseudoscience when not backed by robust evidence.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Fake science, Junk science
Antonyms
Science
See also
Science, Quackery, Evidence, Critical thinking
Example
“Promises to cure diseases with crystals, with no studies to support the claim, are a classic example of pseudoscience.”

Psychological integrity

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

The preservation of an individual's mental and emotional health, including the absence of chronic stress, fear or prolonged behavioral frustration.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Mental integrity
See also
Stress, Stereotypic behavior, Learned helplessness, Physical integrity
Example
"Keeping animals isolated in small spaces undermines their psychological integrity and can lead to repetitive behaviours."

Q↑ A–Z

QALY (quality-adjusted life year)

acronym · Criteria and Moral Status

A measure that multiplies length of life by the quality of that time, used in public health to compare treatments and, in ethics, to assess the harm of death.

The term appeared in print in 1976, in an article by Richard Zeckhauser and Donald Shepard, and the measure now guides decisions in health systems. Oscar Horta (2010) and Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) apply it to the harm of death and add a parameter: besides the good years death takes away, it also matters how many good years someone has already had, so that dying early, having enjoyed almost nothing of life, is especially bad. This worsens the picture for wild animals, most of whom die shortly after birth, and also for animals raised for food, who are killed very young. The measure is criticized for possibly discriminating against people with disabilities or chronic illnesses, whose quality of life is scored lower, a criticism made by John Harris (1987), and for depending on welfare comparisons that are hard to make across species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
quality-adjusted life years
See also
Harm of death, Epicurean view of death, Welfare range, A life worth living
Example
"The ministry compared two treatments using QALYs and chose the one that gave more years of good-quality life per unit of money spent."

Quackery

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The practice of deceiving people with promises that have no scientific basis in order to gain an advantage.

It occurs on all sides of the debate about food, from miracle cures to diets that promise to solve any disease, including among advocates of vegan or carnivore diets.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
snake oil, humbug
See also
Pseudoscience, Skepticism, Evidence-based practice
Example
"The clinic sold a miracle powder said to cure every disease, and regulators labeled the offer quackery for lack of any proof."

R↑ A–Z

r and K reproductive strategies

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The distinction between species that have many offspring and invest little in each (r-strategists) and species that have few offspring and care for them (K-strategists).

The letters come from the logistic equation: r is the population's growth rate and K the carrying capacity. The theory of r/K selection was formulated by Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson in 1967 and extended by Eric Pianka in 1970, who attached to it a series of predictions about other traits of animals. Today it is considered outdated in ecology and has given way to life-history theory, which speaks of a continuum between fast and slow life histories, as David Reznick and colleagues show in a 2002 review; the basic distinction between having many or few offspring, however, remains valid, as Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) notes. "Strategy" is a metaphor, because animals do not plan how they reproduce. The ethical point is that most animals are born into species of the first kind, in which almost all offspring die soon, although Heather Browning and Walter Veit (2023) dispute that this implies as much suffering as is usually assumed.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
r/K selection, r/K strategies
See also
Population dynamics, Carrying capacity, Wild animal suffering, Predation
Example
“Frogs, which lay thousands of eggs, follow the r strategy; elephants, with few well-cared-for young, follow the K strategy.”

Radicalism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A stance that seeks deep changes, going to the root of a problem, rather than superficial adjustments.

The word comes from the Latin radix, "root". That's why radical doesn't mean violent or extremist, though the words are often used as synonyms: radical concerns the depth of the change advocated, while extremism generally concerns methods and the rejection of pluralism and of others' rights. Many ideas considered radical in their time became consensus, such as the end of slavery and women's suffrage. In the animal movement, radicalism is associated above all with abolitionism, which advocates ending the use of animals as property, not just reforms. A position can be radical in its aim and moderate in tone and means.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Radical stance
Antonyms
Moderation
See also
Extremism, Abolitionism, Reformism, Activism (militancy)
Example
“In the movement, radicalism means going to the root of the problem, which does not imply violence.”

Rape rack

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The name activists give to the restraint structure used to immobilize females during forced mating or artificial insemination.

The livestock industry and veterinarians call structures of this kind a restraint chute (tronco de contenção) or brete (see those entries).

Synonyms and related uses
Insemination stock, Breeding rack
See also
Restraint chute (tronco de contenção), Brete (handling chute), Artificial insemination, Forced mating
Example
“Activists use the term ‘rape rack’ to denounce the structure in which cows are immobilized to be forcibly inseminated.”

Rationality

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The capacity to reason logically.

Its historical use as a criterion for the moral exclusion of animals is challenged by the argument from marginal cases: humans without full rational capacity, such as babies or people with certain disabilities, are still recognised as deserving moral consideration, which shows that rationality is not in fact the criterion actually applied.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Reason
Antonyms
Irrationality
See also
Logic, Logical consistency, Critical thinking, Cognitive dissonance
Example
“Saying animals do not deserve consideration because they are not rational leaves out babies and people with intellectual disabilities, which weakens the criterion.”

Raw foodism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A diet based on eating raw foods (often of plant origin), associated by some adherents with health benefits; it is not a synonym for veganism, but may overlap with it.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
raw food diet, raw eating
See also
Restrictive diet, Fruitarianism, Healthy diet
Example
"A follower of raw foodism, he began eating only raw fruit, leaves and nuts, but a nutritionist warned him about possible nutrient deficiencies."

Reactionism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A stance of opposition to social change, seeking a return to earlier norms or practices.

Applied to the animal question, it often relies on appeals to tradition and naturalness, both considered fallacies when used alone as a moral justification.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Reactionary stance
Antonyms
Progressivism
See also
Conservatism, Status quo, Progressivism, Naturalistic fallacy
Example
“Arguing that ‘it has always been this way’ is a reactionary stance that tries to stop change without offering moral reasons.”

Reciprocity (as a criterion of inclusion)

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The idea that only those who can give something in return, cooperate or keep agreements with others are owed justice or certain rights.

It underlies contractualism, from Thomas Hobbes to David Gauthier (Morals by Agreement, 1986), and appears in John Rawls, for whom society is a system of cooperation for mutual advantage. Peter Carruthers, in The Animals Issue (1992), used it to deny that we have direct duties to animals. The problem is that the criterion also excludes babies, people with severe cognitive disabilities and future generations, who cannot reciprocate; those who try to include them usually fall back on another criterion, which shows that reciprocity was not the real criterion. It also confuses who can be party to an agreement with who can be harmed by it: animals don't negotiate, but they bear the consequences.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Moral reciprocity
See also
Contractualism, Argument from marginal cases, Moral agent, Moral patient
Example
“If only those who can reciprocate duties deserve protection, babies and people in comas would be excluded, which shows a limit of reciprocity as a criterion.”

Reducetarianism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A commitment to reduce, without necessarily eliminating, the consumption of meat, dairy, eggs and other animal products.

The term was coined by Brian Kateman, founder of the Reducetarian Foundation in the United States. The idea is that many people reducing has a large effect, and that reducing is easier to start than eliminating. From the animals' point of view, every reduction counts; ethically, reducing is a path, not a destination.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Meat reduction, Reducing animal products
See also
Flexitarianism, Veganism, Dietary transition, Vegetarianism
Example
“He is not vegan, but he adopted reducetarianism and cut meat from three out of every four meals.”

Reflective equilibrium

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A method of justifying moral principles by adjusting them, back and forth, to our considered judgements about particular cases until principles and judgements form a coherent whole.

The name comes from John Rawls in A Theory of Justice (1971), who drew in part on how Nelson Goodman justified the rules of induction (Fact, Fiction, and Forecast, 1955); Norman Daniels later developed the wide version, which also brings in background theories. For animal ethics, the sensitive point is that considered judgements can carry prejudice: if it seems intuitive that only humans count, the method tends to confirm speciesism. Peter Singer, in 1974, criticised the weight given to intuitions, noting that many of them are leftovers of custom and self-interest. Robert Garner observed that in Rawls the exclusion of animals comes from these starting convictions, not from the contract. Defenders of the method reply that it also allows intuitions to be revised when they clash with well-grounded principles, and the argument from marginal cases works exactly that way.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Original position and veil of ignorance, Argument from marginal cases, Moral universality, Moral consistency
Example
“Noticing that her principle led to an unacceptable conclusion, she revised the principle, seeking reflective equilibrium with her firmest judgments.”

Reformism

noun · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

A current that accepts gradual improvements in the conditions of exploitation as a valid (or necessary) path to abolition. (See also Humane washing and Vegan washing, section 6.)

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Gradualism, Reformist position
Antonyms
Abolitionism, Radicalism
See also
Abolitionism, Welfarism, Humane washing, Vegan washing, Incremental reforms
Example
“For reformists, pressuring companies to improve farming conditions is a realistic step; for abolitionists, it is not enough.”

Religious rituals involving animals

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Practices of sacrifice or ritual use, a sensitive topic at the intersection of ethics and religion.

The rituals vary widely: they include religious slaughter for food, such as halal and kosher, and sacrifices at festivals and ceremonies of many religions worldwide. In Brazil, the Supreme Federal Court ruled in 2019 that the Rio Grande do Sul law allowing animal sacrifice in Afro-Brazilian religious ceremonies is constitutional. Critics point out that outrage at these rituals is often directed at religious minorities, while the slaughter of billions of animals in ordinary livestock farming receives little attention; from a sentientist point of view, the criterion should be the same in every case: the animal's suffering and death.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Religious speciesism, Selective outrage, Cultural relativism, Slaughter
Example
“The debate over religious rituals involving animals pits freedom of worship against the duty to avoid unnecessary suffering.”

Religious speciesism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A form of speciesism justified or reinforced by religious doctrines and traditions that attribute human dominion over animals.

Because it grounds human superiority in religious authority rather than in morally relevant characteristics, antispeciesists see this form of speciesism as particularly resistant to rational revision.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
theological speciesism, religious anthropocentrism
See also
Speciesism, Dominionism, Theocentrism, Religious rituals involving animals
Example
“A doctrine claiming that animals exist to serve humankind can be criticized as religious speciesism.”

Religious veganism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

Veganism or vegetarianism motivated by a religious tradition that asks for compassion and nonviolence toward animals, such as ahimsa in Jainism, Hinduism and Buddhism.

It includes Christian, Jewish and Muslim groups that argue for care for animals. It is veganism in the strict sense only when the reason includes animals and the refusal to exploit them.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Faith-based veganism
See also
Religious speciesism, Theocentrism, Religious rituals involving animals, Veganism
Example
“Some Jains avoid all animal products for religious reasons, while other groups do so for fasting, which is not always veganism in the strict sense.”

Rennet

noun · Animal-Derived Products

An enzyme extracted from the stomach of young calves, lambs or kids, used in traditional cheese production to coagulate milk.

Traditional rennet comes from the stomachs of calves, and also of lambs and kids, killed while young, which is why many cheeses are not even vegetarian. Today most industrial cheese in the United States and the United Kingdom uses chymosin produced by fermentation with microorganisms, but protected traditional cheeses such as Parmigiano Reggiano still require animal rennet. Labels do not always state where the rennet comes from.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal rennet, Calf rennet
See also
Cheese, Dairy products, Vegetarianism, Veal
Example
“Many traditional cheeses, such as Parmesan, use animal rennet taken from calves' stomachs, and the label does not always say so.”

Replaceability (replaceability argument)

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The thesis that killing a being who has a good life may not be wrong if they are replaced by another, who would not otherwise exist, with an equally good life.

The idea goes back to the nineteenth-century philosopher Leslie Stephen, for whom the pig would have the strongest interest in the demand for bacon, since without it the pig would not exist at all; the vegetarian Henry Salt replied that it is a mistake to compare existence with non-existence, as if being born were a favour done to someone. Peter Singer accepted Salt's reply in the first edition of Animal Liberation (1975), but in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993) he came to doubt it and accepted replaceability for beings who are conscious but not self-conscious, while granting that this is the most criticized point of the book and that no answer to the problem is fully satisfactory. Even for him, the argument does not justify factory farming, where the animals' lives are not good, nor hunting, where the animal killed is usually not replaced, and in everyday life he recommends not killing animals for food. Tom Regan rejects the idea that an individual is a receptacle of well-being exchangeable for another, and Gary Francione holds that every sentient being has an interest in continuing to live. Critics from the disability rights side point out that Singer extended the same logic to newborns with disabilities, which shows how dangerous it can be.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Replaceability argument, Replaceability thesis
Antonyms
Irreplaceability of the individual
See also
Total view and prior existence view, Self-conscious and merely conscious beings, Harm of death, Happy meat, Subjects-of-a-life
Example
"To defend free-range farming, the producer appealed to replaceability, saying that each animal slaughtered would make room for another with an equally good life."

Replacement methods

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Alternative techniques to animal experimentation (cell cultures, computer models) developed under the principle of the 3Rs.

They include human cell and tissue cultures, organs-on-chips, computer models and studies with human volunteers at safe doses. In 2022 a US law, the FDA Modernization Act 2.0, removed the legal requirement for animal tests to approve new drugs, without banning them, and in 2025 the FDA announced a plan to reduce these tests, starting with monoclonal antibodies. In Brazil, CONCEA, the federal council that regulates animal use in research, recognizes validated alternative methods and sets deadlines for their adoption. Even so, validated methods replace only part of the tests, and validation tends to be slow.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Alternatives to animal testing, Non-animal methods
See also
3Rs, Animal experimentation, Arouca Law, Animal model
Example
"The institute adopted replacement methods, such as lab-grown tissue, to assess the safety of new cosmetics."

Representation

noun · Intersectionality and Social Justice

The presence of people from different social groups in spaces of decision-making, visibility and voice, such as governments, companies, media and social movements.

A movement with broader representation tends to hear more experiences and reach more people; in the animal movement, there are criticisms that in some countries it is still dominated by certain social groups. There is also an issue specific to the cause: animals can't represent themselves or vote, and depend on humans to defend their interests. That is why there are proposals for the political representation of animals, and parties devoted to them, such as the Party for the Animals in the Netherlands, which first won seats in parliament in 2006.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Political voice, Institutional presence
See also
Lobby, Affirmative action, Intersectionality, Animal rights
Example
“Representation of animal issues in Congress grows when lawmakers make public commitments to the cause.”

proper noun · Plant-Derived Products

A Brazilian brand (Life Co) of plant-based creamy requeijão, a spreadable cheese similar to cream cheese, made from soy.

Extending respect to a being implies recognizing its interests as morally relevant, regardless of its usefulness or its similarity to humans.

Restraint chute (tronco de contenção)

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A structure, usually of metal, used in livestock farming to immobilize the animal, mainly cattle, during procedures such as vaccination, exams, treatments and insemination.

Activists call the structure used to immobilize females for forced insemination a "rape rack". See Brete.

Synonyms and related uses
Squeeze chute, Cattle chute
See also
Brete (handling chute), Rape rack, Artificial insemination, Forced mating
Example

Restrictive diet

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A diet that deliberately excludes certain foods or food groups, for reasons of health, ethics, religion or others.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Antonyms
Varied diet
See also
Diet, Food intolerance, Healthy diet
Example
"Because of her peanut and gluten allergy, she follows a restrictive diet, which requires extra attention to labels and meal preparation."

Reverence for life

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

An ethical principle formulated by the Alsatian physician, theologian and musician Albert Schweitzer, according to which it is good to preserve and promote life and bad to destroy or harm it, whatever the living being.

Schweitzer said the phrase, Ehrfurcht vor dem Leben in German, came to him in 1915 on a boat trip along the Ogooué river, in Gabon, where he ran a hospital at Lambaréné, and he developed it in Kultur und Ethik (1923); he received the 1952 Nobel Peace Prize. The idea comes close to animal ethics in refusing to let a being's value depend on its usefulness to humans. But the criterion is life, not sentience: a leaf or a flower counts, and Schweitzer himself admitted that living requires killing, without offering a clear method for deciding whom to sacrifice. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), notes that Schweitzer describes plant life with words such as longing, pleasure and dread, which only make sense for conscious beings, and that without consciousness there is no reason to respect a tree more than a stalactite. From a sentientist point of view, the question that separates the cases is what it means, for the being itself, to have an interest frustrated, and it only has an answer for those who feel.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Respect for life, Ehrfurcht vor dem Leben
Antonyms
Anthropocentrism
See also
Biocentrism, Biocentric egalitarianism, Deep ecology, Sentientism
Example
"She quoted Schweitzer's reverence for life, but sentientism asked her what a flower loses when it is picked."

Rice

noun · Plant-Derived Products

A widely cultivated staple cereal, the basis of diets in many cultures and an ingredient in plant-based drinks (rice milk).

Example

Riding

The use of an animal (usually a horse) to be ridden by humans.

Animal traction, Animal-drawn cart (carroça, Brazilian usage), Animal entertainment, Halter

"The horse-riding ride along the beach was criticised by activists, who regard it as a form of using animals."

Rights

noun · Animal Law and Legislation

Morally or legally recognized prerogatives that protect the interests of a subject.

Extending rights to animals does not require them to be identical to human rights: animal rights theorists mainly defend basic negative rights, such as not being killed or tortured, and not complex positive rights, such as the vote.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
entitlements, prerogatives
See also
Animal rights, Human rights, Fundamental rights, Interest
Example
“A person’s rights do not vanish just because the majority prefers to ignore them, and the debate is whether some of them extend to other animals.”

Rodeo

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A spectacle in which horses or bulls are ridden or chased by competitors, involving methods that induce stressful behavior in the animal.

In Brazil, Law 10,519/2002 requires cinches and girths of natural wool and bans pointed spurs and electric shocks, but allows the flank strap; in 2016 another law declared rodeo and vaquejada intangible cultural heritage. Animals can suffer fractures and other injuries, and calf-roping events, in which calves are brought down at high speed, are among the most criticized.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Flank strap, Vaquejada, Bullfighting, Animal entertainment
Example
“At the rodeo, tight ropes and straps make the animal frantic, and the crowd applauds while the rider tries to stay on.”

S-risks

noun · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

Risks of suffering on an astronomical scale ("s-risks"), a concept tied to concern about massive future suffering, including that of animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Suffering risks, Astronomical suffering risks
See also
X-risks, Longtermism, Expected impact, Suffering
Example
“S-risk researchers worry about scenarios in which future technologies multiply the suffering of sentient beings on an enormous scale.”

Sadism

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Pleasure in causing others to suffer or in watching them suffer; the term comes from the name of the French writer the Marquis de Sade and was popularized by the psychiatrist Richard von Krafft-Ebing in 1886.

Psychology studies everyday sadism as a personality trait, present to different degrees in people: in a 2013 study, Erin Buckels, Daniel Jones and Delroy Paulhus found that some participants chose, and even enjoyed, grinding up insects in a machine that in fact didn't harm them. Animal cruelty is also tracked by authorities as a warning sign of violence against people; since 2016, the FBI has recorded these crimes separately. But most of the suffering imposed on animals doesn't come from sadism, but from indifference, habit and profit: people who eat meat almost never take pleasure in the animal's suffering, and would rather not think about it. That's why calling meat eaters sadists is as inaccurate as calling them psychopaths. There are exceptions where suffering is part of the spectacle, such as bullfights and animal fights, and there the word may fit better.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Gratuitous cruelty, Pleasure in hurting
See also
Animal cruelty, Bullfighting, Rodeo, Zoosadism
Example
“The abuser filmed the act and enjoyed the cat's pain, behaviour that the investigators described as sadism.”

Safari

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A tourist activity of observing (or hunting) wild animals in their habitat, with debates about its impact on welfare and conservation.

Synonyms and related uses
Hunting expedition, Savanna tour
See also
Sport hunting, Hunting, Zoo, Animal trafficking
Example

Sanctity of life

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The doctrine that human life has a special and inviolable value, so that it is always wrong intentionally to take the life of an innocent human being, whatever their condition.

It has religious roots, in the idea that only humans have an immortal soul and were made in the image of God; Thomas Aquinas treated killing a human as an offense against God. In medical ethics it underpins the prohibition of euthanasia and abortion, and today it is defended, for example, by the Catholic Church and by legal scholars such as John Keown. Peter Singer, in Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), and Helga Kuhse, in The Sanctity-of-Life Doctrine in Medicine (1987), criticize it for protecting life by species rather than by the characteristics of whoever is living it, and for already being contradicted in medical practice, for example when treatment is withdrawn from someone who will not recover. From an antispeciesist point of view, the problem is not valuing life but restricting that value to humans: traditions such as Jainism and Albert Schweitzer's reverence for life extend respect to all living beings. Disability rights activists fear that abandoning the doctrine would expose the most vulnerable, which is why many antispeciesists argue for raising the protection of animals rather than lowering that of any human.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Sanctity-of-life doctrine, Inviolability of life
Antonyms
Quality of life (as a criterion)
See also
Religious speciesism, Dominionism, Theocentrism, Harm of death
Example
“Those who defend the sanctity of life need to explain why it ends at the species boundary.”

Sanctuary

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A nonprofit institution dedicated to taking in and caring for rescued animals, with no purpose of exploitation or commercial breeding.

Sanctuaries differ from zoos and breeding facilities because they do not buy, sell or breed the animals, and seek to give them the best possible life until natural death. Because the name is not protected and is also used by places that exploit animals for tourism, with elephant rides or contact with big-cat cubs, organizations such as the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries (GFAS) accredit sanctuaries that meet care standards. Farmed animal sanctuaries also play an educational role, showing pigs, cows and chickens as individuals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal refuge, Permanent haven
See also
Rescue, Zoo, Adoption, Farmed animal
Example
“At the sanctuary, cows rescued from slaughterhouses live on wide pastures, where they receive names and individual care until the end of their lives.”

Science

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A systematic body of knowledge obtained through observation, experimentation and the empirical method; the basis for studies of sentience, cognition and animal welfare.

The scientific method has been the main tool for dismantling, with evidence, anthropocentric assumptions about the animal mind and the capacity to suffer that were historically accepted.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
scientific knowledge
Antonyms
Pseudoscience, Obscurantism
See also
Evidence, Pseudoscience, Epistemology, Skepticism
Example
"Science has shown that fish have pain receptors, which led researchers to reconsider how these animals are treated in farms and fisheries."

Seafood

noun phrase · Animal-Derived Products

A generic term for aquatic animals other than fish used as food (mollusks, crustaceans).

The expression, like "fruits de mer" or the Portuguese "frutos do mar" (fruits of the sea), makes animals sound like a harvest. It groups shrimp, lobsters, crabs, octopuses, squid, mussels and oysters, animals with very different capacities: there is good evidence of sentience in decapod crustaceans and cephalopods, and the United Kingdom recognized them as sentient in law in 2022. Shrimp trawling catches many other animals by accident, and octopus farming was banned in the US states of Washington and California in 2024. See Crustacean-vegetarianism (crustovegetarianismo, Brazilian usage), Ostroveganism and Pescatarianism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
shellfish and crustaceans, sea food
See also
Ostroveganism, Pescatarianism, Crustacean-vegetarianism (crustovegetarianismo, Brazilian usage), Fishing
Example
“A seafood dish with shrimp and mussels is considered vegetarian by some and not by others, depending on the criterion.”

Seaweed (kombu, nori)

noun · Plant-Derived Products

A marine plant used in cooking, especially in Asian cuisine, and also a source of iodine and other nutrients.

Seaweeds such as nori are sometimes cited as a source of vitamin B12, but many contain forms of the vitamin that the body cannot use, and the content varies greatly between samples. For this reason, nutritionists recommend supplements or fortified foods as a reliable source. Some seaweeds, such as kombu, are also very high in iodine, and excess can be harmful.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
sea vegetable, marine algae
See also
Vitamin B12, Agar, Nutrition, Vegan diet
Example
"The nutritionist reminded him that eating nori does not guarantee vitamin B12 and that people who eat no animal products need a supplement or fortified foods."

Selective outrage

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Outrage at some cases of harm or injustice and indifference to similar, or even greater, ones that are routine or involve those close to us.

With animals, it is very common. The Yulin festival in China, where dogs are killed for food, draws protests worldwide, while billions of pigs and chickens are killed every year without drawing attention. The killing of Cecil the lion by a hunter in Zimbabwe in 2015 moved millions of people who eat animals every day. Outrage tends to follow the beloved species, the rarity of the case or cultural distance, not the size of the harm. That is why it is so often aimed at the practices of other peoples or of minorities, such as religious sacrifice, while the majority's practices are left out. Outrage itself isn't the problem, since it shows the person cares; the problem is the selectivity, which reveals a double standard. The same yardstick applies to animal advocates: being outraged only at what others do, and not at one's own choices, repeats the mistake.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Selective moral outrage
See also
Double standard, Speciesism, Instrumentalization, Moral consistency
Example
"He was outraged by news of dogs being abused, yet ate pork for lunch without a thought, a case pointed to as selective outrage."

Argument in the guide →

Self-conscious and merely conscious beings

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

Peter Singer's distinction between a being who is aware of itself as a distinct entity with a past and a future, whom he calls a person, and a being who feels pleasure and pain without that self-awareness.

The criterion of personhood comes from John Locke, who defined a person as a thinking being able to consider itself as the same thing in different times and places, and Singer uses it to separate being a person from being a member of the human species: some animals would be persons, and some humans would not. For him, pain counts equally in both cases, but killing a person frustrates desires about the future and is therefore generally more serious, while a merely conscious being is open to the replaceability argument. In Practical Ethics (2nd ed., 1993), Singer is categorical only about the great apes, speaks of varying degrees of confidence for many mammals and treats fish as the clearest case of a merely conscious animal; about hens and ducks, he himself calls the assumption that they lack self-consciousness doubtful. Sentientists criticize the hierarchy between lives that the distinction creates, Tom Regan adopts the broader criterion of being a subject of a life, and disability scholars such as Eva Feder Kittay dispute that cognitive capacities should decide who has a full right to life. Studies of memory, planning and self-recognition in many species, still debated, make the line less certain than it seemed.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Persons and merely conscious beings, Self-aware and merely sentient beings
See also
Animals as persons, Subjects-of-a-life, Animal consciousness, Replaceability (replaceability argument), Argument from marginal cases
Example
"In the seminar, the class discussed whether the distinction between self-conscious and merely conscious beings holds up against studies of octopuses and crows."

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The capacity to examine and question one's own beliefs and practices.

It is especially relevant for recognizing inconsistencies between declared values, such as rejecting cruelty, and everyday consumption behavior.

Self-defense

noun · Animal Law and Legislation

The right or justification of an agent to react to a threat in order to protect their integrity.

Self-defense arguments rarely apply to the routine killing of animals for consumption, since they presuppose a real and proportionate threat, which is absent in most of these practices.

The capacity to feel, to have positive or negative subjective experiences such as pain, pleasure and fear.

For sentientism, it is sentience, and not species, intelligence or a being's usefulness to others, that is the only morally relevant criterion for determining who deserves consideration.

Sentience in extraterrestrial life

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The speculative extension of the moral circle to hypothetical sentient life forms beyond Earth.

From a sentientist standpoint, a being's cosmic origin is morally irrelevant: what matters is solely its capacity to suffer or feel pleasure.

See also

Beyond veganism →

Sentience in law

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

The recognition, in laws and treaties, that animals are sentient beings and not mere things.

In the European Union, Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, in force since the Treaty of Lisbon (2009), requires paying regard to the welfare of animals as sentient beings, but makes exceptions for religious rites, cultural traditions and regional heritage. France began defining animals in its Civil Code as living beings endowed with sensitivity in 2015, and the United Kingdom passed an animal sentience law in 2022. The recognition is a symbolic step forward, but on its own it bans no practice: animals are still treated as property.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Legal recognition of sentience
See also
Animals as property, Animal legal personhood, Sentience, Animal protection legislation
Example
“The legal reform began to recognize animals as sentient beings, which in practice requires courts to consider their suffering in legal disputes.”

Sentience in robots

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

A variant of the previous discussion applied to artificial physical bodies; a frontier question in machine ethics.

(see the note under Sentience in AI and digital systems)

Synonyms and related uses
Robot sentience
See also

Sentient being

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

Any being capable of having subjective experiences, positive or negative.

It is this category, and not that of "human being" or "intelligent being", that for sentientism correctly delimits the circle of those who deserve moral consideration.

Synonyms and related uses

Sentientism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A position that takes sentience, not species, as the criterion of moral inclusion; also called sentiocentrism.

It is the criterion adopted, explicitly or implicitly, in most of the critical remarks in this dictionary.

Sentientist

noun / adjective · Currents of Animal Ethics

A person who holds sentientism, that is, who takes sentience, rather than species, substrate or intelligence, as the criterion for moral consideration.

For a sentientist, every being able to feel, to have good and bad experiences, deserves to have their interests taken into account, whether a human, another animal or, if one ever exists, a sentient artificial mind. Since the late 2010s, the term has also named a worldview that joins reason and evidence with compassion for all sentient beings. A sentientist isn't necessarily vegan, and a vegan isn't necessarily a sentientist: one starts from a criterion of moral consideration, the other from a commitment not to exploit animals, and the two usually go together.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Follower of sentientism
Antonyms
Speciesist
See also
Sentientism, Sentience, Antispeciesism, Substratism
Example
“A sentientist holds that any being capable of feeling pain or pleasure deserves consideration, whether a pig, a fish or, in theory, a machine.”

Sentientist environmentalism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A view that protects the environment because of the sentient beings who depend on it, human or not.

It keeps the individual at the center: when an environmental goal conflicts with the interests of beings who feel, what weighs is what happens to those who feel. The chapter on the divergence over ends in the Questão de Ética collection discusses the difference between animal defense and environmentalism that values species and ecosystems.

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A proposal for political and social organization guided by the interests of all sentient beings.

It represents the broadest institutional and political application of sentientism, proposing to extend representation and political participation, today restricted to humans, to all beings capable of having interests.

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

An expression by the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess (1973) for ecology that protects the environment for its value to humans, fighting pollution and resource depletion without questioning anthropocentrism.

It is opposed to deep ecology. Those who start from sentientism propose protecting the environment because of all the beings who feel.

Silk

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A textile fiber produced by silkworm larvae, whose traditional extraction usually involves killing the larvae inside the cocoon.

In conventional production, cocoons are boiled or steamed with the pupa still alive inside, so that the thread can be unwound whole; estimates, mostly from animal protection organizations, range from 5,000 to 7,000 larvae per kilogram of silk. So-called "ahimsa" or "peace" silk waits for the moth to leave the cocoon, but it also draws criticism, for example about rearing conditions. Insect sentience is still debated, but there is growing evidence that some insects can feel pain.

Sizeism

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The tendency to give less consideration to small animals, or to young ones, than to large animals, for example by accepting painful procedures on them that would not be done without anesthesia on a larger animal.

It shows up in the castration and tail docking of piglets and lambs without anesthesia, in procedures performed on mice and in the disregard for fish and insects. Body size doesn't say how much an animal feels, and there are indications that young animals can feel pain intensely. It is a form of bias that leads to inconsistent decisions.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses

See also
Speciesism, Bias, Castration, Temporal bias
Example
“Paying less attention to a mouse's pain than to a horse's, just because it is small, is an example of sizeism in veterinary practice.”

Slaughterhouse

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A facility where animals are slaughtered for consumption.

Slaughterhouses run fast lines, with thousands of birds per hour, which makes it hard to correct stunning failures. They are generally closed to the public, which keeps slaughter out of consumers' sight. The work has high injury rates, and research points to psychological effects on workers; a 2009 study by Amy Fitzgerald and colleagues found in the United States an association between the presence of slaughterhouses and higher rates of some crimes, without establishing causation.

Soundness

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The property of an argument that is valid and has all true premises, which guarantees that its conclusion is also true.

It is the standard an argument must meet to compel anyone who accepts its premises to accept its conclusion. An argument can be invalid, valid but unsound, because some premise is false, or sound. Many objections to animals become valid once reconstructed and fail on soundness: "only those who are rational deserve moral consideration; animals are not rational; therefore, they do not deserve consideration" is valid, but the first premise is false, since babies and people with severe cognitive disabilities deserve consideration without being rational in the required sense. Showing that an argument is unsound does not prove its conclusion false, only that that argument does not support it. The same test applies to arguments for animals, which also need true premises backed by evidence.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
sound argument
Antonyms
unsound argument
See also
Validity, Counterexample, Argument from marginal cases, Logic
Example
“The reasoning is valid but lacks soundness: the premise that only those with duties have rights is false.”

Soy

noun · Plant-Derived Products

A versatile legume, the basis of countless vegan products (tofu, milk, soy meat).

It is common to hear that vegans' soy destroys forests, but according to Our World in Data, based on FAO data, more than three quarters of the world's soy becomes feed for farmed animals, and only a small part is eaten directly by people, as tofu, soy milk or tempeh. In Brazil, one of the largest producers, soy expansion is linked to deforestation in the Cerrado and the Amazon. People who eat meat generally consume more soy indirectly than people who eat tofu.
