“Soy protein isolate is highly purified and often appears on the labels of vegan bars and shakes.”

Specialist

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A person with in-depth, recognized knowledge in a field, acquired through training, research or long experience.

Trusting specialists is reasonable, because no one can check everything alone. But there are cautions: authority holds within each person's field, and a doctor isn't an expert in ethics nor a philosopher in nutrition; the consensus of many specialists weighs more than the opinion of one; and specialists also have biases and conflicts of interest, as when research is funded by those who profit from the result. Citing a specialist outside their field, or a lone one against the consensus, is what is called an appeal to authority.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
expert, authority
Antonyms
layperson, generalist
See also
Generalist, Evidence, Ethicist, Critical thinking
Example
“The nutrition specialist clarified that well-planned vegan diets are adequate, citing positions of professional associations.”

Fallacies →

Species

noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The basic taxonomic unit of biology, grouping organisms capable of reproducing with one another and producing fertile offspring.

Using species as a criterion of moral value is, for antispeciesist currents, a form of arbitrary discrimination (speciesism), since mere biological membership in a group is not, in itself, morally relevant.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Speciesism, Animal, Living being, Biology
Example
“Each species has its own characteristics, but that alone does not answer the question of whether what it feels matters morally.”

Speciesism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

Moral discrimination based solely on species, without any relevant justification.

It is the central concept that gives its name to the opposing position, antispeciesism, and many animal ethics philosophers compare it to racism and sexism as a morally arbitrary form of discrimination.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
species discrimination, species chauvinism
Antonyms
antispeciesism
See also
Antispeciesism, Anthropocentric speciesism, Speciesist term, Equal consideration
Example
“Valuing a cat more than a cow solely because of species is, according to the critique, a form of speciesism.”

Beyond veganism →

Speciesist term

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A word or expression that treats animals as things, uses animal names as insults or makes exploitation seem normal.

In English there are several kinds: calling animals "it", "stock" or "head"; using "pig", "cow", "chicken", "rat", "snake" or "dumb animal" as insults, which assumes those animals are inferior; calling people in experiments "guinea pigs"; and idioms that normalize violence, such as "kill two birds with one stone", "beat a dead horse", "there's more than one way to skin a cat" or "like lambs to the slaughter". Simple alternatives exist, such as "solve two problems at once", "go over old ground" or "there's more than one way to do it". In 2018, PETA proposed playful swaps such as "feed two birds with one scone", and was widely mocked, which shows how easily the subject can backfire. Language reflects and reinforces attitudes, and noticing these terms helps us see how common speciesism is. But changing words doesn't change practices by itself, and constantly correcting other people's speech can push away those who are just starting to think about the subject.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Speciesist language, Speciesist expression
See also
Euphemism, Absent referent, Objectification, Beast of burden, Guinea pig
Example
“Calling someone a ‘pig’ or an ‘ass’ as an insult is a speciesist term, because it uses a species as a symbol of stupidity.”

Speciesist vegan

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A vegan who rejects animal exploitation but still gives less weight to the interests of some sentient beings just because of their species.

Veganism starts from the principle of not exploiting animals. Antispeciesism goes further: it asks that similar interests of any sentient being weigh equally, whatever the species, including in situations that don't involve exploitation. A vegan can be speciesist in two ways. The first is discriminating among animals by species without justification, such as caring about dogs, cows and dolphins while dismissing fish, insects and other invertebrates who may also feel, which the glossary calls xenospeciesism. The second is ignoring sentient beings in scenarios beyond exploitation: wild animal suffering, treated as "just nature" even when helping would be possible; animals seen as pests, killed without need or in cruel ways; animals hit by disasters, road traffic or pollution, who get attention only when they belong to favored species. Dismissing possible new minds, such as sentient AIs, in advance is a similar mistake, but it isn't speciesism, because they belong to no species: the name for that bias is substratism, or carbonism when it favors organic bodies. The critique works as self-criticism, to carry the principle all the way through, not to invalidate veganism: pointing out that some vegans are speciesist doesn't show that exploiting animals is acceptable.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Vegan with species bias
Antonyms
Antispeciesist vegan
See also
Speciesism, Xenospeciesism, Antispeciesism, Wild animal suffering, Substratism
Example
“Someone who does not eat animals but ignores the suffering of insects or digital beings simply because they are different may be called a speciesist vegan.”

Argument in the guide →

Sport hunting

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A form of hunting for leisure or trophies, with no subsistence purpose.

It includes trophy hunting, in which the hunter pays to kill large animals, such as lions, elephants and rhinoceroses, and takes body parts as a souvenir. Supporters say the fees fund conservation and local communities; critics, including some conservationists, question how much of that money actually reaches those ends. The killing of Cecil the lion in Zimbabwe in 2015 caused protests worldwide and led airlines to stop carrying trophies. From a sentientist point of view, conserving a species does not justify killing an individual for fun.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
recreational hunting, trophy hunting
Antonyms
Subsistence hunting
See also
Hunting, Safari, Selective outrage
Example
"The tourist paid a fortune to join a sport hunt and came home with an antelope's head as a trophy for his wall."

Spur

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An instrument attached to a rider's heel and used to urge the mounted animal on through pressure or pain.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
riding spur
See also
Riding, Halter, Rodeo, Harness
Example
“At the rodeo, the rider drove the spur into the horse’s flank to urge it on, which animal advocates consider a form of pain.”

Status quo

Latin expression · Criteria and Moral Status

The current state of things.

Invoking it to justify maintaining practices of animal exploitation is considered by antispeciesists to be a fallacy: the fact that something is customary does not imply that it is morally right.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Established order, The way things are
See also
Fallacies, Paradigm shift, Moral progress, Reformism
Example
“Defending animal farming just because it has always existed is an appeal to the status quo, not a moral reason to keep it.”

Statute

noun · Animal Law and Legislation

A written, general and binding rule passed by the legislature through the process set out in the constitution.

Statutes sit within a hierarchy: below the constitution and above decrees and regulations. In Brazil, the Constitution itself prohibits practices that subject animals to cruelty (art. 225), and laws such as the Environmental Crimes Law and the Arouca Law deal with cruelty and the use of animals in research. A statute can protect animals or allow their exploitation, and something being legal doesn't settle whether it is just.

Act

Law, Jurisdiction, Animal protection legislation, Legality

Steelman

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Presenting the strongest and most honest version of an argument before answering it, the opposite of the straw man.

It is the guide's method: each chapter presents the strongest version of the objection, shows what it gets right and only then where it fails.

Antonyms

See also

Example

Stereotypic behavior

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A repetitive, invariable behavior pattern with no apparent function, an indicator of psychological suffering in confined animals.

Common examples are sows biting the bars of their crates, cattle rolling their tongues, horses biting their stalls and zoo animals pacing back and forth. Ethologists treat stereotypy as a sign that the current or past environment does not meet the animal's needs, although its absence does not prove that the animal is doing well.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
stereotypy, abnormal repetitive behavior, cage neurosis
See also
Stereotypy, Environmental enrichment, Zoo
Example
"The zoo bear paced back and forth without stopping, a stereotypic behavior that veterinarians link to boredom and lack of stimulation."

Stereotypy

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

Repetitive behavior with no apparent function, such as pacing back and forth, head swaying or bar biting, an indicator of psychological suffering or frustration in animals kept in inadequate conditions.

It appears in sows confined in crates, horses in stalls, elephants and bears in zoos and laboratory animals. A stereotypy can be the scar of a poor past environment and may continue even after conditions improve. On the other hand, the absence of stereotypies doesn't prove that the animal is well: some become apathetic.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
abnormal repetitive behavior, stereotypic behavior
See also
Stereotypic behavior, Environmental enrichment, Stress, Animal confinement
Example
“The mare that sways her head nonstop in the stall shows stereotypy, a known sign of frustration and boredom.”

Sterile insect technique

noun phrase · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

A method of controlling insect populations that consists of rearing and sterilizing large numbers of males, usually by radiation, and releasing them into the wild so that they mate without producing offspring.

It was developed by the entomologists Edward Knipling and Raymond Bushland in the 1950s against the New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax), whose larvae eat the living flesh of mammals and birds, and it eliminated the pest from the United States and later from Mexico and Central America down to Panama. The fly began spreading again in 2023 and reached Mexico in 2024, which led the United States to open a base in Texas in 2026 for releasing sterile flies. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) cites the technique as proof that humans have been interfering with the reproduction of wild animals for decades, for economic and environmental reasons, and as a model of intervention that reduces births without killing; in the case of the screwworm, it also spares many animals, including wild ones, a slow death. From a sentientist point of view, the technique raises its own questions, such as the welfare of the insects reared and irradiated and the effects of reducing one population on other species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
SIT, Sterile male technique
See also
Animal population control, Pests, Parasitism, Wild animal suffering
Example
“Instead of using insecticide, the program released sterilized males to reduce the mosquito population without poisoning the environment.”

Straight edge

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A subculture that emerged from US hardcore punk in the early 1980s, whose followers abstain from alcohol, tobacco and other drugs; the vegan straight edge strand, which spread in the 1990s, adds the refusal of animal products.

The name comes from the song "Straight Edge" by the band Minor Threat (1981). Not every straight edger is vegan, and veganism doesn't require abstaining from alcohol: the two choices met in part of the hardcore scene, which helped spread veganism among young people.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Straightedge, sXe
See also
Vegan movement, Veganism, Activism, Boycott
Example
“Many young people in the hardcore scene came across veganism through the straight edge movement, which rejects alcohol, drugs and, among some followers, animal products.”

Street activism

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

A direct, public approach (leafleting, demonstrations, exhibitions).

street outreach, grassroots outreach

Protest, Vigil, Digital activism, Guerrilla marketing, Vegan witness (bearing witness)
Example
"On Saturdays, volunteers do street activism in the square: they hand out leaflets and show short videos about animal farming to passers-by."

Stress

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

The set of bodily and behavioral responses to a threat or challenge, such as the release of hormones like cortisol, a faster heart rate and flight.

Short-term stress is part of life and helps an animal react to danger. The problem is intense or prolonged stress, sometimes called distress, when the animal can no longer adapt and their health and behavior deteriorate, as in many confinement systems. Measuring hormones helps but is not enough: cortisol also rises in good situations, such as mating, so scientists combine several indicators.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
tension, stress response
Antonyms
relaxation
See also
Coping, Suffering, Stereotypic behavior, Learned helplessness
Example
“The long, overcrowded transport caused stress in the animals, with rising cortisol and injuries.”

Strict vegetarianism

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A diet free of all animal products: no meat, fish, seafood, milk and dairy, eggs or honey.

It corresponds to the strict sense of vegetarianism and is the expression used in Brazil, for example by the Brazilian Vegetarian Society. It describes only the diet: veganism includes the same diet, but goes further and rejects animal exploitation also in clothing, entertainment and other uses.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Strict vegetarian diet, Pure vegetarian diet
Antonyms
Omnivorism
See also
Vegetarianism, Vegan diet, Veganism
Example
“She follows strict vegetarianism: no meat, eggs or dairy, but she still uses leather and wool, so she does not consider herself vegan.”

Stunning of animals

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A procedure that seeks to render an animal unconscious before slaughter, reducing (but not always eliminating) the perception of pain.

The most common methods are the captive bolt gun, electric shock and, for pigs and poultry, gases such as carbon dioxide. At high concentrations, carbon dioxide is aversive to pigs, who show signs of panic and breathlessness before losing consciousness. Failures happen, and some animals reach the bleeding stage conscious.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Stunning, Pre-slaughter stunning
See also
Humane slaughter, Slaughterhouse, Slaughter
Example
"The law requires animals to be stunned before slaughter, but inspectors report that failures in the procedure leave some of them conscious."

Subjective experience

noun phrase · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

What is felt from the point of view of the one living through something: there being "something it is like to be" that being, in the words of the philosopher Thomas Nagel.

It is what distinguishes a sentient being from an object or a system that only reacts to stimuli: a stone has no experience, and a dog does. Sentience is the capacity to have good or bad subjective experiences, which is why it is the guide's moral criterion. The 2024 New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness states that there is strong scientific support for conscious experience in mammals and birds, and a realistic possibility in all vertebrates and many invertebrates, such as octopuses, crabs and insects.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
qualia, inner life, phenomenal consciousness
See also
Consciousness, Subjectivity, Sentience, Philosophy of mind
Example
“When a lobster is boiled, the question is whether there is a subjective experience of pain, something it is like to be it.”

Subjectivity

noun · Sentience, Consciousness and Cognition

The condition of being a "subject-of-a-life", with one's own perspective on what happens to one (a central concept in Tom Regan, cited only as a reference).

Recognizing a being's subjectivity implies recognizing it as someone, and not as something, a shift in perspective central to overcoming speciesism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Own point of view, Subjective perspective
Antonyms
Objectivity
See also
Subjective experience, Sentience, Subjects-of-a-life, Consciousness
Example
“Recognizing a hen’s subjectivity is admitting that someone is there, with a point of view on what happens to her, and not merely a body.”

Subjects-of-a-life

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

A concept from Tom Regan (cited only as a reference) designating beings with a unified psychophysical existence, memory, preferences and a well-being of their own, who deserve basic rights.

This concept underpins the defense of basic rights, to life and to liberty, for various nonhuman species, and not only for humans.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Subject-of-a-life
Antonyms
Mere resource
See also
Animal rights, Intrinsic value, Subjectivity, Moral patient, Rights
Example
“In animal rights theory, adult mammals are subjects of a life: they have beliefs, desires and memory, and what happens to them matters to them.”

Subsidies

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Public resources given to a sector or product, such as direct payments, cheap credit, insurance or price guarantees, to lower its costs or sustain its production.

According to a 2021 report by FAO, UNDP and UNEP, support to agricultural producers worldwide amounts to about 540 billion dollars a year, and 87% of it distorts prices or causes environmental and social harm. Much of it goes to animal farming and feed grains, which helps keep meat, milk and eggs artificially cheap. The environmentalist critique asks for prices to include costs to the environment and health, but the animal-centered critique goes further: the gravest cost, the suffering and death of animals, isn't counted at all. And a caution: a policy that charged only for environmental impact could make chicken and fish cheaper, since they emit less per kilo, and increase the number of animals killed. Well-justified subsidies would be those supporting plant proteins, fermentation and cultivated meat.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Subventions, Public incentives, State aid
See also
Tax incentive, Agribusiness, Externality, Meat industry
Example
“Public subsidies for livestock make meat and milk cheaper, while plant proteins receive far less support, which distorts the market.”

Argument in the guide →

Subsistence

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The use of animals out of a need for direct survival, a recurring argument in debates about ethical exceptions.

The argument applies to real situations, such as peoples living in regions without viable alternatives, and many advocates of veganism recognize these exceptions; the Vegan Society's definition speaks of avoiding exploitation "as far as is possible and practicable". Most consumption of animal products in the world, however, takes place where alternatives exist, and the argument does not extend to those cases.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Basic survival, Livelihood
See also
Necessity, Hunting, Veganism, Needs principle
Example
“An isolated community that depends on fishing to survive is not in the same situation as someone with a supermarket and plant options at hand.”

Substratism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

Giving different weight to the good of a sentient being according to the substrate its body is made of, biological or digital, for example.

The parallel is direct: just as speciesism uses species as the criterion, and species says nothing about the capacity to suffer, substratism uses the material of the body, which says nothing either. The legitimate question is a different, empirical one: is that being sentient?

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Substrate chauvinism
See also
Carbonism, Speciesism, Sentience in robots, Sentience in AI and digital systems
Example
“Saying that a system cannot feel just because it is made of silicon rather than carbon would be substratism, not a conclusion based on evidence.”

Biases →

Suffering

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

A negative state experienced by a sentient being, which can include pain, fear, stress, frustration, hunger, boredom or isolation, especially when intense or prolonged.

Suffering is broader than physical pain: an animal confined without room to move, separated from their mother or prevented from natural behaviors can suffer without being injured. So the moral question is not only "does it hurt?" but "what is this animal's life like?".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Distress, Affliction, Anguish
Antonyms
Well-being, Pleasure, Happiness
See also
Pain, Animal welfare, Sentience, Negative experiences
Example
“More than momentary pain, the prolonged suffering of a cow separated from her calf is what many activists point to as a central problem in the dairy sector.”

Suffering from natural causes

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

Pain and death that occur without human intervention (disease, predation, disasters).

Most wild animals are born into species that have many offspring, and most of these die shortly after birth from hunger, disease, cold or predation. For this reason some philosophers, such as Oscar Horta, argue that suffering in nature is enormous and deserves moral attention, even without human fault. Others answer that intervening in nature may cause more harm than it prevents; the most common position among those who study the subject is to research before acting. It is also disputed that suffering predominates in nature: Zach Groff and Yew-Kwang Ng (2019) found an error in Ng's 1995 model and concluded that the balance is uncertain, and Heather Browning and Walter Veit (2023) argue that wild lives may be considerably more positive than assumed; Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that, even with a positive balance, there would still be reasons to help the animals who suffer.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Natural harm, Natural suffering
Antonyms
Human-caused suffering
See also
Wild animal suffering, Idyllic nature, Predation, Natural harms
Example
“Hunger, disease and parasites cause enormous suffering from natural causes, and some argue we should help these animals when it is feasible.”

Sufficient condition

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A condition that is enough for something to occur or hold: A is a sufficient condition of B when, given A, there is B.

In conditional form, it is written "if A, then B". A condition can be sufficient without being necessary: being a mammal is enough to be an animal, but some animals are not mammals. Animal advocates tend to argue from sufficient conditions: for Peter Singer, being sentient is enough to have interests that count morally; for Tom Regan, being the subject of a life is enough to have inherent value and rights. This strategy does not require showing that only sentient beings matter, only that sentience is enough and that animals have it; to defeat it, one would need a counterexample, a sentient being whose suffering did not count. That is why showing that animals lack reason, language or duties does not refute the argument, which never claimed those capacities were necessary.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Necessary condition, Sentience, Subjects-of-a-life, Counterexample
Example
“The argument doesn't say that only sentient beings matter: it says sentience is a sufficient condition for someone's suffering to count.”

Sufficientarianism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

The position that what matters morally is ensuring that all individuals reach a sufficient minimum threshold of well-being, prioritizing those below that threshold.

From this standpoint, ensuring that no animal has its well-being reduced below a minimally acceptable threshold would be morally more urgent than maximizing aggregate well-being or seeking full equality.

Synonyms, example and related terms

Doctrine of sufficiency
See also
Prioritarianism, Egalitarianism, Utility maximisation, Justice
Example
“By sufficientarianism, what matters is that each animal has enough for a decent life, not that all have exactly the same.”

Superbug

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A bacterium resistant to several antibiotics, sometimes to almost all those available, which makes the infections it causes hard or impossible to treat.

The name is popular, not technical: specialists speak of multidrug-resistant bacteria. They emerge and spread through excessive or inappropriate antibiotic use, in human medicine and in animal farming, where drugs are often given to healthy animals. One example is the mcr-1 gene, which confers resistance to colistin, a last-resort antibiotic, identified in 2015 in pigs and chickens in China.

See also

Stop saying →

Supererogatory

adjective · Normative Ethical Theories

Describes a morally good and praiseworthy act that goes beyond duty, so that not doing it is not wrong.

The modern discussion begins with J. O. Urmson's article "Saints and Heroes" (1958), which drew attention to heroic acts that no one is obliged to perform. The notion only fits some non-consequentialist theories: for consequentialism, there is always a duty to choose the best possible outcome, however difficult. In the debate about wild animals, it is common to accept that helping them is admirable but optional; Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers that, even granting the category, the natural harms at stake are so great that helping when the cost is low could hardly be merely praiseworthy. Defenders of the supererogatory argue that a morality with no room for personal choices would be too demanding.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Beyond duty, Above and beyond
Antonyms
Obligatory, Required
See also
Demandingness objection, Positive and negative duties, Consequentialism, Deontology
Example
“A person who spends weekends rescuing abandoned animals performs a supererogatory act: it is praiseworthy, but no one has a duty to do it.”

Surface learning

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A way of studying aimed at memorizing and reproducing information, without seeking to understand its meaning or connect the ideas.

The distinction between surface and deep learning comes from the Swedish researchers Ference Marton and Roger Säljö in the 1970s. Memorizing has its place: knowing the short answer to an objection by heart helps in a quick conversation. The problem is stopping there. Someone who memorized an answer often gets stuck when the objection comes in another form, or when the other person makes the next reply.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
rote learning, rote memorization, cramming
Antonyms
Deep learning
See also
Deep learning, Declarative (or explicit) knowledge, Critical thinking, Steelman
Example
"The night before the exam he memorized definitions without grasping how they connected, and had forgotten almost everything a week later, typical of surface learning."

Flashcard practice →

Sustainable livestock farming

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A model of animal farming that seeks to reduce environmental impacts and increase resource efficiency, without necessarily changing the paradigm of using animals as a resource.

Measures such as improving pastures, reducing losses and using feed additives can lower emissions per kilogram of meat or milk. Even so, a 2018 study by Joseph Poore and Thomas Nemecek, which analysed about 38,000 farms in 119 countries, concluded that the lowest-impact animal products typically exceed the impacts of plant-based substitutes. The term also says nothing about the animals' welfare or their death.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Livestock farming, Sentientist environmentalism, Plant protein, Happy meat
Example
“The sustainable livestock label speaks of restored pastures, but does not mention that the animals are still killed well before old age.”

Synanthropic animals

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Species that have adapted to live in urban environments or near humans (rats, pigeons, cockroaches), often treated as pests.

Rats, pigeons and cockroaches live near humans because cities offer abundant food, shelter and waste; to a large extent, their presence is a consequence of how humans organize space. For that reason, measures such as waste management and sealing entry points tend to reduce populations more lastingly than killing, which can be followed by recolonization. Living close to humans does not change these animals' capacity to feel.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
urban wildlife, commensal animals, urban animals
See also
Pests, Animal population control, Liminal animals and animal sovereignty, Wild animal suffering
Example
"Possums, pigeons and rats are synanthropic animals: they thrive in cities because they find shelter and food on roofs, in drains and in rubbish."

Tacit knowledge

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

Knowledge we have and use but can't fully explain in words, such as recognizing a face or sensing that an animal isn't well.

The concept comes from the philosopher and chemist Michael Polanyi, in The Tacit Dimension (1966), summed up in the phrase "we can know more than we can tell". It is learned by living and practising alongside those who already know. Sanctuary caretakers, for example, often notice that an animal is ill from their posture or the way they move before any test. This knowledge is valuable, but it is worth confirming with systematic observation, because intuition can also be wrong.

Tail docking

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The partial or total amputation of an animal's tail, a common practice in pigs and some dog breeds.

In piglets, the tail is cut to prevent pigs from biting each other's tails, a behaviour linked to stress and lack of stimulation. In the European Union routine docking is prohibited, but it is still done on most farms, with exceptions such as Sweden and Finland; in Brazil, the 2020 pig welfare rule tolerates cutting the last third of the tail and requires anaesthesia only after the third day of life. In dogs, cosmetic docking is banned in several European countries and, in Brazil, by the Federal Council of Veterinary Medicine since 2013. Tails are also docked in sheep and, in some countries, in dairy cows.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
tail amputation, tail cutting
See also
Cannibalism (in confinement), Ear cropping, Anesthesia
Example
"On the farm, piglets had their tails docked in the first days of life, a procedure meant to prevent bites caused by the stress of confinement."

Tallow

noun phrase · Animal-Derived Products

Solid fat extracted from animal tissues, used to make candles, soaps and some foods.

Tallow is a by-product of slaughter and appears in little-noticed uses, such as soaps, candles, lubricants and industrial additives. In 2016, the Bank of England confirmed that the new polymer £5 notes contained traces of tallow; a petition against this passed 130,000 signatures, but the bank kept the notes, citing cost. The case shows how animal derivatives circulate in products almost no one associates with animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Rendered fat
See also
Gelatin, Lanolin, Vegetable fat, Meat
Example
“Traditional candles and soaps often contain animal tallow, even without saying so on the label, which surprises many people.”

Tax incentive

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A reduction of or exemption from taxes granted by the government to encourage an activity, a sector or the consumption of a product.

Tax incentives usually apply to products considered essential or strategic. In Brazil's tax reform, for example, meats were included in the national basic food basket with a zero tax rate, alongside foods such as rice and beans. From the animals' point of view, the problem is that the tax doesn't account for the cost production imposes on them: a product that requires confining, causing suffering to and killing sentient beings gets the same treatment as, or better than, alternatives that don't. Being strategic or profitable for the economy doesn't make a practice just. A tax policy that took animals seriously would favor plant proteins and new food technologies, not exploitation.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Tax break
See also
Subsidies, Externality, Lobby
Example
"The government offered a tax incentive to companies producing plant-based foods, to make those products cheaper."

Technological veganism

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A position that sees technology, such as plant-based meat, cultivated meat and precision fermentation, as the fastest route to ending large-scale animal exploitation.

It is not an established label: the name describes a position that exists. Jacy Reese Anthis, in The End of Animal Farming (2018), and the Good Food Institute are examples.

Telos

noun · Criteria and Moral Status

A Greek term for purpose or proper nature; in animal ethics, used by the philosopher Bernard Rollin for the set of needs and interests characteristic of each species, such as a pig's need to root or a hen's need to scratch and dust-bathe.

Rollin argued that respecting an animal includes letting it live according to its nature, not only avoiding pain. The idea helps explain why confinement causes suffering even without injuries. Critics point out that genetic engineering can alter the telos itself, for instance by creating animals that tolerate confinement better, which shows the concept needs to be combined with attention to what the individual feels.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Own nature, Species-typical nature
See also
Psychological integrity, Animal confinement, Genetic engineering, Interest
Example
“Those who speak of a cow's telos mean grazing, walking and living with the herd, and confinement frustrates it even when the animal is well fed.”

noun · Plant-Derived Products

A fermented soy-based food of Indonesian origin, rich in protein.

Temporal bias

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The tendency to give more weight to what is near in time, treating future suffering as less important merely for being future; the position that adopts it as a principle is called temporalism.

The parallel is with distance in space: someone's pain ten thousand kilometres away is no smaller for it. Parfit distinguished discounting for uncertainty, which is legitimate, from pure discounting, merely for being later.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Temporal partiality, Time preference
Antonyms
Temporal impartiality
See also
Impartiality, Temporal impartiality, Longtermism, Bias
Example
“Giving less weight to suffering just because it will occur a hundred years from now is a temporal bias that many philosophers reject.”

Temporal impartiality

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Unbiased consideration of those affected by our decisions, whatever time they exist in.

It is impartiality applied to time, as spatial impartiality is applied to distance. Accepting it while excluding future animals adds two kinds of neglect together: temporal bias and speciesism.

Time neutrality, Temporal neutrality
Antonyms

The Link

noun phrase · Animal Law and Legislation

A body of research that finds an association between animal abuse and other forms of violence, such as domestic violence, child abuse and violent crime.

Because of this research, some protection services began cross-reporting animal abuse and domestic violence, and the FBI began recording animal cruelty crimes in their own category from 2016. Overstatement should be avoided: the association is statistical, and most people who mistreat an animal do not go on to commit serious crimes against people. Nor should the argument be the only reason to protect animals, who matter in themselves.

Synonyms and related uses
Link theory, Cruelty–violence link
See also
Animal cruelty, Empathy, Sadism, Zoosadism
Example
“Supporters of the link theory point out that many violent offenders had a prior history of abusing animals, and so they take animal cruelty seriously.”

Theocentrism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

The view that God or the divine is the center of reality and morality.

Theocentric traditions vary: some see animals as created to serve humans, while others call for compassion and care toward them, as in ahimsa and tza'ar ba'alei chayim.

God-centered worldview

Anthropocentrism

Tokenization (using others as a shield)

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

In debate, using people who live in very different situations as a shield to justify one's own choices, such as Indigenous peoples, the species' ancestors or people in extreme poverty.

It shows up in lines like "what about Indigenous people who hunt?", "our ancestors ate meat" or "what about people who go hungry?", said by someone who lives in none of those situations. The other person's circumstances, which may involve a lack of alternatives, survival or a culture of their own, are used to justify a choice made in very different conditions, such as buying meat at the supermarket. This has two problems: it changes the subject, because the question was about the person deciding, and it uses those people as a tool for the argument, without really considering their lives. The guide answers these cases on their own terms, in arguments such as "Indigenous and traditional peoples eat animals", "Poor people have no access" and "Eating meat made us evolve". The name comes from "token", a symbol, and recalls tokenism, the merely symbolic inclusion of members of a group; not to be confused with tokenization in computing, the replacement of data with a code.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Tokenism
See also
Instrumentalization, Double standard, Fallacies, Oppression
Example
“When someone cites an isolated people to justify their own barbecue, they are using tokenization: that people’s situation is nothing like theirs.”

Argument in the guide →

Total liberation

noun phrase · Currents of Animal Ethics

A perspective that unites animal liberation with other social liberation struggles (racial, gender, class) under a single political horizon.

It reflects the view that speciesism shares structural roots with other forms of oppression, and that fighting them in isolation would be strategically and ethically insufficient.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Integral liberation
See also
Intersectionality, Animal liberation, Intersectional veganism, Ecofeminism
Example
"The collective adopts total liberation as a principle and joins both animal campaigns and struggles for housing and racial equality."

Beyond veganism →

Total view and prior existence view

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

Two ways of counting well-being in utilitarianism: the total view adds up everyone's pleasure, including that of beings who may come to exist, while the prior existence view counts only beings who already exist or will exist anyway.

Peter Singer set out the distinction in Practical Ethics. On the total view, creating beings with pleasant lives is good, and the loss caused by a death can be made up for by bringing another being into existence, which is the basis of the replaceability argument; on the prior existence view there is no such compensation, and killing animals for food is normally wrong when they could have lived more months or years of good life. Each has costs: the total view seems to oblige us to have happy children and, pushed further, leads to what Derek Parfit called the repugnant conclusion, a vast world of lives barely worth living; the prior existence view struggles to explain why it is wrong to knowingly bring into the world a being who will have a miserable life. In the first edition (1979), Singer tentatively combined the two, applying the total view to beings without self-consciousness and the prior existence view to those who have it; in the second (1993), he replaced that combination with a single preference utilitarianism. For animal advocates, the debate shows that the answer to so-called painless slaughter does not depend only on avoiding suffering, but on the value we recognize in each individual's life.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Total view and prior-existence view
See also
Replaceability (replaceability argument), Preference utilitarianism, Classical utilitarianism, Harm of death
Example
"On the total view, creating more happy chickens would be good; on the prior existence view, only the chickens who already exist count."

Traces (of allergens)

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

A labeling warning indicating possible cross-contamination of a product with small unintentional amounts of an ingredient (such as milk or egg).

Vegans debate whether a product that "may contain traces of milk" is vegan. The Vegan Society accepts this warning on products with its trademark, as long as the contamination risk is managed, because it signals a risk on the production line, not an ingredient; other certifiers are stricter. The warning exists to protect people with allergies, and avoiding these products does not reduce the use of animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
May contain
See also
Vegan, Cruelty-free, Food intolerance
Example
“The package carried the warning ‘may contain traces of milk’, which matters to people with allergies but does not change the use of animals in production.”

Transhumanism

noun · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

An intellectual movement that advocates using science and technology to overcome biological limits, such as ageing, disease, cognitive limitations and suffering.

The term was popularized by the biologist Julian Huxley in 1957, and the movement organized in the late 1990s, when Nick Bostrom and David Pearce founded the World Transhumanist Association, now Humanity+. The Transhumanist Declaration advocates the well-being of all sentience, including humans, non-human animals and possible artificial intelligences. Pearce goes further and proposes using technology to abolish suffering in all sentient beings, wild animals included. Not every transhumanist thinks this way: many focus only on enhancing humans. The movement also draws criticism, about unequal access to technologies, the risk of new forms of eugenics and speculative promises; the political scientist Francis Fukuyama went as far as calling it "the world's most dangerous idea".

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
H+
Antonyms
Bioconservatism
See also
Transhumanist, Wild animal suffering, Cultivated meat, Sentience in AI and digital systems, Posthumanism
Example
“Some advocates of transhumanism propose using technology to reduce the suffering of all sentient beings, including wild animals.”

Transhumanist

noun / adjective · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

A person who holds transhumanism, that is, who advocates using science and technology to overcome the biological limits of humans and, in some versions, of all sentient beings.

For the animal cause, the difference between versions matters: a transhumanist focused only on humans can be as speciesist as anyone else, while a sentientist transhumanist sees technology as a means of reducing everyone's suffering, for example through cultivated meat or interventions to help wild animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Follower of transhumanism
Antonyms
Bioconservative
See also
Transhumanism, Sentientist, Wild animal suffering, Posthumanism
Example
“A transhumanist might defend gene editing of predators so they no longer need to kill, which raises ethical and ecological debates.”

Trump and greater weight

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

The distinction between a moral factor that beats any other, whatever the quantities at stake (a trump), and a factor that weighs more but can be outweighed by much larger quantities on the other side (greater weight).

The idea of rights as trumps was popularized by Ronald Dworkin, in Taking Rights Seriously (1977), and recalls John Rawls's lexical priority. Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) uses the distinction in several arguments: even if preventing harms caused by humans mattered more than preventing natural harms, only a trump would always give it priority; with greater weight, there would be a point at which preventing a very large amount of natural harm would come first. The same applies to the idea that preventing suffering counts more than promoting happiness, which he accepts as greater weight but not as a trump. The distinction helps to spot arguments that assume, without saying so, that one factor always wins.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Moral trump, Decisive weight
See also
Negative axiology, Natural harms, Rights, Prioritarianism, Maximin
Example
“Those who see rights as trumps say no collective benefit justifies torturing an individual; those who speak of greater weight admit it can be outweighed.”

Truth

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

Correspondence between a statement and reality: a statement is true when things are as it says.

Factual statements are true or false regardless of who defends them. In ethics, philosophers debate whether moral judgments can also be true, the debate between moral realism and anti-realism. The guide doesn't depend on settling that question: it asks for consistency. If a human being's pain matters because it is pain, another sentient being's pain matters too.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Veracity, Factual accuracy
Antonyms
Falsehood, Lie
See also
Moral relativism, Fact, Opinion, Post-truth
Example
“For those who distinguish truth from opinion, saying a pig feels pain is a testable fact, not a matter of taste.”

Tu quoque

Latin expression · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

A fallacy that tries to dismiss an argument by pointing out an inconsistency in whoever makes it, instead of examining the argument.

It is common in charges of hypocrisy against vegans: even if the charge is true, it does not change what happens to animals.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
You too fallacy, Appeal to hypocrisy
See also
Fallacies, Double standard, Critical thinking, Argument
Example

Fallacies →

U↑ A–Z

Utilitarianism

noun · Normative Ethical Theories

A consequentialist strand that seeks to maximize well-being and minimize the aggregate suffering of those affected by a decision (reference: Bentham, Singer, cited only as examples).

Bentham already pointed out, as early as the eighteenth century, that the relevant question about animals is not whether they can reason or talk, but whether they can suffer, a seminal formulation of sentientism.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Antonyms
Deontology
See also
Classical utilitarianism, Negative utilitarianism, Consequentialism, Sentience, Sentientism
Example
“Utilitarianism evaluates actions by their consequences for everyone affected, which includes animals, since they also suffer and feel pleasure.”

Political or ethical objection →

Utility maximisation

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The central principle of utilitarianism, according to which the right action is the one that produces the greatest possible balance of well-being over suffering.

Applied consistently, this principle requires counting the suffering and well-being of all sentient beings affected by an action, not only humans.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Welfare maximisation
See also
Utilitarianism, Classical utilitarianism, Consequentialism, Expected value maximisation
Example
"For those who accept utility maximisation, the right choice is the one that most increases the surplus of pleasure over pain, summing across all affected."

V↑ A–Z

Valence

noun · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

The positive or negative character of an experience, that is, whether it is felt as good or bad by the one living it.

The term comes from the psychology of emotion and is used in animal welfare science to speak of affective states without assuming emotions identical to human ones: pain, fear and hunger have negative valence, while pleasure, play and satiety have positive valence. For many authors, having valenced experiences is what distinguishes sentience from the mere capacity to detect harmful stimuli, nociception. In the debate about wild animals, it is discussed whether the intensity of valence depends on the number of neurons: Heather Browning and Walter Veit suggest that very small young animals might feel less, and Luciano Carlos Cunha (2022) answers with cases such as zebrafish larvae, which have about 100,000 neurons, against some 10 million in the adult, and still show signs of feeling pain. There is still no reliable method for comparing the intensity of experiences across species, the subject of studies on welfare ranges.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Affective tone, Hedonic tone
See also
Sentience, Nociception, Negative experiences, Positive experiences, Welfare range
Example
“Researchers measure the valence of an animal’s experiences, that is, whether what it goes through is pleasant or unpleasant for it.”

Validity

noun · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The property of an argument whose conclusion follows from its premises, so that, if they are true, the conclusion cannot be false.

Validity concerns form, not content: an argument can be valid with false premises, and invalid with true premises and a true conclusion. So, faced with an objection to veganism, there are two separate questions: does the conclusion follow from the premises? And are the premises true? "Animals are not human; therefore, we may eat them" is not valid, because the premise linking the two is missing; once it is added ("we may eat whoever is not human"), the argument becomes valid, and the debate moves to that premise. Nathan Nobis, in Animals & Ethics 101 (2016), recommends this method: make the conclusion and premises precise and add the assumed ones until the argument is valid. Being valid is not enough to accept the conclusion; for that, the argument must also be sound.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
valid argument
Antonyms
invalidity
See also
Soundness, Hidden premise, Logic, Fallacies
Example
“The argument has validity, because the conclusion follows from the premises, but that says nothing about whether the premise ‘only rational beings matter’ is true.”

Vaquejada

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A traditional Brazilian practice in which two cowboys on horseback chase a bull and bring it down by the tail, causing physical injuries to the animal.

In 2016, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court struck down a law from the state of Ceará regulating vaquejada, finding that the practice subjects animals to cruelty, which the Constitution forbids. In 2017, Congress passed Constitutional Amendment 96, which states that sporting practices with animals registered as cultural expressions are not considered cruel. The case shows the conflict between tradition and animal protection, and how the law can be changed to keep a practice going.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Steer tailing, Bull-tailing contest
See also
Rodeo, Bullfighting, Animal cruelty, Cultural relativism
Example
“In vaquejada, two riders on horseback bring down a steer by pulling its tail, a practice that animal protection groups consider cruel.”

Veal

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Meat from calves slaughtered while still young, often raised in intensive confinement (the veal crate).

Veal is a by-product of the dairy industry: male calves of dairy breeds do not produce milk and grow too slowly for beef production, so they are killed young, at days, weeks or a few months of age. Traditional pale meat depends on a low-iron diet and little movement. Even where veal crates have been banned, as in the European Union, separation from the mother and slaughter at a young age continue.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Calf meat
See also
Veal crate, Dairy industry, Premature slaughter
Example
“Veal comes from male calves of dairy cows, slaughtered young, which ties milk consumption to meat consumption.”

Veal crate

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A narrow compartment used to confine calves destined for veal production, restricting their movement to keep the meat tender.

The calf, separated from the mother soon after birth, is kept in a narrow individual pen, often tethered, and fed a low-iron liquid diet to keep the meat pale. The United Kingdom banned these crates in 1990, and the European Union completed its ban in 2007; in the United States, several states have banned them. Veal continues to exist without crates, because it depends on the dairy industry, which produces male calves of no value for milk production.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
veal stall, veal pen, individual veal hutch
See also
Veal, Dairy industry, Premature slaughter
Example
"The restaurant chain announced it would stop buying meat from calves raised in veal crates, after campaigns by animal protection groups."

Vegan

noun / adjective · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A person who follows veganism, that is, who seeks to exclude, as far as is possible and practicable, all forms of exploitation of and cruelty to animals, in food, clothing, entertainment and other uses; also the adjective for products and practices free of animal origin or exploitation.

The word was coined in 1944 by Donald Watson and other founders of the Vegan Society, in England, from the first and last letters of "vegetarian". Being vegan isn't just a diet: someone who eats only plants but wears leather or pays to watch animals in shows follows a vegan diet without being vegan. The phrase "as far as is possible and practicable" acknowledges that living without causing any harm to animals is impossible; the commitment is to avoid what can be avoided.

Follower of veganism

See also

A substitute for traditional cheese made from nuts, soy or starches, without the use of animal milk.

A diet without any animal products: no meat, fish, seafood, dairy, eggs or honey. It is the dietary part of veganism, which also rejects animal exploitation in clothing, entertainment and other uses.

Well planned, it is considered adequate at all stages of life by bodies such as the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, with vitamin B12 supplementation. People who follow it for health, without the ethical motivation, often use the term plant-based.

Vegan pet food

noun phrase · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Feed formulated without ingredients of animal origin, generally intended for dogs and cats.

Dogs are omnivores and, according to the available studies, can do well on nutritionally complete vegan foods; cats are obligate carnivores, but what they need are nutrients, such as taurine, arachidonic acid and vitamin A, which can be synthesized and added to the food. Studies are still few and largely based on guardian reports, such as those by Andrew Knight and colleagues in 2022 and 2023, which found no worse health outcomes in animals on vegan diets. Veterinary associations, such as the British BVA, are more cautious and warn of the risk of poorly formulated diets; the common recommendation is to use foods formulated to be complete and to have the animal followed by a veterinarian.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Plant-based pet food
See also
Animal nutrition, Veterinary ethics, Predation, Feed
Example

Vegan washing

noun phrase · Biases, Fallacies and Rhetoric

The use of vegan or plant-based imagery by brands or companies with no real commitment to the animal cause.

It is criticized for diluting the ethical meaning of veganism, reducing it to a market trend detached from the moral consideration for animals that originally motivates it.

Vegan witness (bearing witness)

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

The practice of publicly documenting animal suffering at sites of exploitation (slaughterhouses, markets).

The practice spread from Toronto Pig Save, founded in Canada in 2010, which inspired hundreds of similar groups known as the Save Movement. In 2017, its founder, Anita Krajnc, was acquitted of charges for giving water to pigs in a truck on the way to slaughter, in a case that drew international attention.

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

A current that joins veganism with anarchism and sees animal exploitation as a form of domination to be abolished along with the others.

The term was coined by Brian A. Dominick in 1995, in the text "Animal Liberation and Social Revolution".

“Veganarchists see the oppression of animals and that of humans as faces of the same system of domination and fight against both.”

Veganism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A philosophy and practice that seeks to exclude, as far as possible and practicable, all forms of animal exploitation.

The most cited definition is that of the Vegan Society, founded in England in 1944. Veganism is not only a diet: it includes clothing, entertainment, testing and other uses. The phrase "as far as is possible and practicable" acknowledges that living without causing any harm to animals is impossible, and also opens debates about where that limit lies, for example with medicines tested on animals. There is disagreement about whether veganism is a moral baseline, as abolitionism holds, or a means of reducing suffering, as pragmatic strands hold.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Vegan lifestyle
Antonyms
Omnivorism, Carnism
See also
Vegan, Vegan diet, Abolitionist veganism, Pragmatic veganism, Vegetarianism
Example
“For those who adopt veganism, the decision goes beyond diet: it includes avoiding leather, animal testing and entertainment that exploits animals.”

Vegetable fat

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

Fat extracted from plant sources (coconut, palm, soy), used as a substitute for animal fats.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
plant fat
See also
Tallow, Margarine, Plant-based cream, Butter
Example
“In the vegan recipe, vegetable fat replaced butter to make the cake tender.”

Vegetarian

noun / adjective · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A person who doesn't eat the meat of any animal, including fish and seafood; in the most common sense, they may consume other animal products, such as milk, eggs and honey.

Many people call someone who eats fish or chicken a vegetarian, but that usage is wrong: someone who eats fish is a pescetarian. Most vegetarians are lacto-ovo vegetarians. That is the broad and most common sense; in the strict sense, a vegetarian is someone who consumes no animal products in their diet, which in Brazil is called a strict vegetarian. It's worth noting that, in most of the industry, producing milk and eggs also involves killing animals, such as the calves separated from cows and the male chicks culled at hatching; so vegetarianism reduces, but doesn't eliminate, participation in the killing.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Follower of vegetarianism
Antonyms
Omnivore
See also
Vegetarianism, Lacto-ovo vegetarianism, Vegan, Reducetarianism
Example
“The restaurant marked vegetarian dishes with a leaf, but warned that some contained cheese or egg.”

J10 · I'm vegetarian for the animals; I already do my part →L29 · Vegans treat vegetarians as enemies →

Vegetarianism

noun · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A diet that excludes the meat of any animal, including fish and seafood; in the strict sense, it also excludes all other animal products, such as milk, eggs and honey.

The word has two senses. In the broad sense (lato sensu), the most common, a vegetarian is someone who doesn't eat meat but may consume milk, eggs or honey; in practice, most are lacto-ovo vegetarians, and that is what most people understand by the term. In the strict sense (stricto sensu), vegetarianism is a diet free of all animal products, which in Brazil is called strict vegetarianism. Those who defend the strict sense often say it was the original meaning, and there is some support for this: some of the first to use the word, in the early 1840s, such as the members of the Alcott House community in England, ate no animal products at all. But the Vegetarian Society, founded in 1847 and responsible for popularizing the term, accepted eggs and dairy from the start, and that usage took hold; historians still debate the exact meaning of the earliest records. It was to name those who consumed no animal products that the word vegan was coined in 1944. Many people think vegetarians eat fish, but they don't, and some products hide ingredients from dead animals, such as gelatin and the rennet in certain cheeses.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Vegetarian diet
Antonyms
Omnivorism
See also
Vegetarian, Strict vegetarianism, Lacto-ovo vegetarianism, Veganism
Example
“In vegetarianism, a person does not eat meat but may consume eggs and dairy, which also involve suffering and slaughter.”

Veterinary ethics

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A current that discusses the moral dilemmas of veterinary practice, such as euthanasia, the use of animals in livestock farming and experimentation.

One of its central dilemmas is the fact that a good part of veterinary professionals work directly in the service of animal exploitation systems, which creates conflict between the duty of care and the economic function of the work.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Ethical veterinary practice
See also
Veterinary medicine, Euthanasia, Animal welfare, Zootechnics (animal science)
Example
“The veterinarian refused to perform a purely cosmetic procedure on a dog and offered to explain to the guardian why it was not advisable, an ethical veterinary stance.”

Veterinary medicine

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The medical science dedicated to the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of diseases, trauma and disorders in animals.

Historically, because much of its practice is oriented toward animal exploitation and productivity, the field is in tension with welfare approaches and non-anthropocentric worldviews.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Veterinary science
See also
Veterinary ethics, Zootechnics (animal science), Animal welfare, Anthropocentrism
Example
“Veterinary medicine looks after animal health, but it also serves industries that exploit animals, which creates ethical tensions in the profession.”

Vicarious trauma (secondary traumatic stress)

noun phrase · Activism and the Movement

Psychological distress in people who are repeatedly exposed to other people's trauma, even without having lived through it directly.

The concepts were first described among therapists and emergency workers: vicarious trauma by McCann and Pearlman (1990), secondary traumatic stress by Charles Figley. In animal advocacy, it mainly affects people who investigate or frequently watch footage of slaughter and abuse, and those who work in rescues and sanctuaries. It can bring intrusive thoughts, insomnia, irritability and avoidance. Limiting exposure and seeking support, including professional help, helps.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Vicarious traumatization
See also
Activist burnout, Vystopia, Activist fatigue, Empathy
Example
“After months of documenting slaughter, the investigator suffered vicarious trauma, with nightmares and trouble sleeping, and sought psychological support.”

Vigil

noun · Activism and the Movement

In animal advocacy, a peaceful gathering outside slaughterhouses, farms or animal markets to bear witness to the animals' suffering, record it and make it visible.

The format became known through Toronto Pig Save, founded in Canada in 2010 by Anita Krajnc, which grew into the Animal Save Movement, now with groups in many countries. At vigils, activists look at the animals arriving in trucks, photograph and film them, and sometimes give them water when drivers stop. In 2015, Krajnc was charged for giving water to pigs in a truck, and she was acquitted in 2017. Vigils usually follow safety and non-violence rules, but they carry risks: in 2020, the activist Regan Russell was killed by a truck transporting pigs during a vigil in Ontario. For many participants, a vigil is also an act of mourning and a refusal to look away.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Animal save vigil, Vigil at slaughterhouse
See also
Vegan witness (bearing witness), Protest, Guerrilla tactics, Slaughterhouse
Example
“Activists held a vigil in front of the slaughterhouse, silently watching the trucks arrive and giving water to the animals.”

Virtue ethics

noun phrase · Normative Ethical Theories

A theory centered on the character of the moral agent, rather than on rules or consequences.

From this standpoint, causing avoidable suffering to an animal can be interpreted as an expression of vices such as cruelty or insensitivity, and avoiding it as an expression of virtues such as compassion and justice.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
aretaic ethics
See also
Normative ethics, Deontology, Consequentialism, Ethics of care
Example
“Under virtue ethics, asking whether an action shows compassion or cruelty matters more than following a rule.”

Political or ethical objection →

Vitamin B12

noun phrase · Plant-Derived Products

An essential nutrient produced by microorganisms, not reliably present in plant sources, whose supplementation is usually recommended in vegan diets.

B12 is not produced by animals or plants, but by bacteria. In livestock farming, farmed animals are usually given cobalt or B12 itself in their feed, so part of the B12 in meat also comes from supplements. For this reason, the need to supplement does not show that a vegan diet is unnatural, only that the source of the vitamin has changed.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Cobalamin, B12
See also
Vegan diet, Nutritional yeast, Nutrition, Healthy eating
Example
“People on a vegan diet should supplement vitamin B12, since plants do not produce it in reliable amounts.”

Vivisection

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Experimentation on live animals, a historically loaded term used by antivivisection movements.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Live animal experimentation, Dissection of living animals
See also
Animal experimentation, Antivivisectionism, Replacement methods, Guinea pig
Example
“Students asked for vivisection to be replaced by simulators and digital models in biology classes.”

Vystopia

noun · Activism and the Movement

The existential anguish of being vegan in a world that normalizes animal exploitation: constant awareness of that exploitation, isolation and frustration at seeing that most people don't notice it.

The term was coined by the Australian psychologist Clare Mann in her book Vystopia: The Anguish of Being Vegan in a Non-Vegan World (2018). It is not a clinical diagnosis: the author describes it as an understandable response to what one knows about animals. The prevalence figures in circulation come from the author's own surveys. See Activist burnout and Vicarious trauma.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Activist burnout, Vicarious trauma (secondary traumatic stress), Empathy, Activist fatigue
Example
“The author described how vystopia left her feeling isolated in a world where violence against animals is normal and invisible.”

W↑ A–Z

Weakness of will

noun phrase · Criteria and Moral Status

The phenomenon of acting against one's own moral judgment.

In the context of animal consumption, it appears when someone intellectually recognizes that animal exploitation is ethically problematic but keeps consuming its products out of habit, convenience or social pressure.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
akrasia, moral weakness
Antonyms
willpower, self-control
See also
Cognitive dissonance, Moral consistency, Dietary transition, Choice
Example
“He knows that cheese involves suffering and eats it anyway: weakness of will, not lack of information.”

Weaning

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The end of a young animal's nursing; in dairy farming, calf and mother are separated within the first hours or days, long before natural weaning, which in cattle happens at around 9 to 11 months.

In dairy cattle, the calf is usually separated from the mother within the first hours or days of life so that the milk can be sold, and mothers and young may call and search for each other for days. In pig farming, piglets are weaned at three to four weeks, while in semi-natural conditions weaning ends at around three to four months. In beef cattle, weaning usually happens at around seven months, closer to the natural age, which ranges from seven to fourteen months.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Dairy industry, Veal, Milk
Example
"In dairy farming, the calf is taken from its mother shortly after birth, long before natural weaning, so that the milk can be sold."

Welfare biology

noun phrase · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A proposed field of research to study how animals, especially those living outside human control, are positively and negatively affected in their well-being.

The expression comes from the economist Yew-Kwang Ng, in the article "Towards Welfare Biology" (1995), and was developed by Catia Faria and Oscar Horta in the chapter "Welfare Biology" of the Routledge Handbook of Animal Ethics (2020). It would be an interdisciplinary field, bringing together ecology, animal welfare science, zoology and veterinary science, to study what is better or worse for each animal as a sentient individual, not as a member of a species, including the natural harms that most wild animals suffer. It is not the same as animal welfare science, which measures physiological and behavioural indicators mainly in animals under human control, such as farmed and laboratory animals, nor as conservation biology, compassionate conservation and conservation welfare, which look at welfare only within conservation goals, a distinction drawn by Luciano Carlos Cunha in Razões para ajudar (2022, in Portuguese). Ng's conclusion that suffering predominates in nature was revised by Zach Groff and Ng himself in 2019, who found an error in the model and concluded that the balance is uncertain, and Heather Browning and Walter Veit (2023) dispute the evidence that wild lives are predominantly bad; it is precisely to answer these doubts that the field proposes empirical research, now funded by organizations such as Wild Animal Initiative.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Wild animal suffering, Animal welfare, Conservation biology, Compassionate conservation, Conservation welfare
Example
"Welfare biology aims to measure how animals live in nature, for instance how many young of a species survive and how the others die."

Beyond veganism →

Welfare range

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

An estimate of how well or badly a being's life can go, from the worst to the best possible experience, compared with that of other beings.

It is not a moral weight by itself, and the estimates for insects and other invertebrates are provisional. The Moral Weight Project, from Rethink Priorities, is the reference.

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Animal welfare, Sentience, Positive experiences, Negative experiences
Example
“Comparing species, researchers estimated the welfare range of chickens and fish, still with much uncertainty.”

Welfarism

noun · Movement Strategy: Reformism, Abolitionism and Ethical Washing

A position that accepts the use of animals as long as high welfare standards are met, often set against abolitionism in the movement's strategic debate.

The best-known criticism comes from the legal scholar Gary Francione, who argued in Rain Without Thunder (1996) that welfare reforms make the use of animals more acceptable and prolong it. Supporters of reforms answer that they reduce suffering now, for animals who cannot wait for abolition. Welfarism, as a political position, is not the same as animal welfare, the science that assesses how animals are doing.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
animal welfarism, welfare reformism
Antonyms
Abolitionism
See also
Abolitionism, Neo-welfarism, Incremental reforms, Reformism, Animal welfare
Example
"For welfarism, using animals is acceptable as long as they are well treated, which is why the movement asks for larger cages, not the end of farming."

Beyond veganism →

Wild animal suffering

noun phrase · Experiences (Welfare, Pain and Affective States)

A philosophical debate over whether and how humans would have an obligation to intervene to reduce suffering in nature.

In nature, most species have many offspring, and almost all of them die young, from hunger, cold, disease or predation. If suffering matters wherever it occurs, this is also a moral problem. Most of those who study the subject don't propose intervening on a large scale today, for lack of knowledge and the risk of making things worse, but rather researching and acting in safe cases, such as vaccinating wild animals against rabies, rescue in disasters and contraception.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Suffering in nature, Wild animal welfare
See also
Suffering from natural causes, Idyllic nature, Predation, Animal population control, Sterile insect technique
Example
“Researchers study wild animal suffering, such as that of young animals that starve soon after birth, and discuss safe interventions.”

Wool

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

A fiber obtained from the shearing of sheep and other animals, whose production can involve injuries and stress (e.g., mulesing).

Merino sheep were selected to produce far more wool than they need and to have wrinkled skin, which makes them dependent on shearing and vulnerable to flystrike, the reason for mulesing. Shearing at industrial pace can cause cuts and stress, as investigations by animal protection organizations in several countries have shown. In much of the world, wool and meat come from the same flocks, and wool sheep are also slaughtered when production falls.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Fleece, Sheep fibre
See also
Mulesing, Lanolin, Fur and leather, Silk
Example
"She swapped her wool coat for one of recycled cotton after learning that shearing can injure sheep."

Working-class veganism (veganismo popular, Brazilian usage)

noun phrase · Diet and Vegetarianism: Variants

A strand aimed at the economic and cultural accessibility of veganism for working-class communities.

Affordable veganism
Antonyms
Elitist veganism
See also

X-risks

noun · Applied Ethics, the Future and Technology

Existential risks, capable of extinguishing human life and sentient life or its future potential.

Synonyms, example and related terms

Existential risks
See also
S-risks, Longtermism, Extinction, Expected impact
Example
“X-risk researchers study threats like pandemics and nuclear war, which could wipe out humanity or compromise its future.”

Xenospeciesism

noun · Currents of Animal Ethics

Moral discrimination among different nonhuman species, privileging some (e.g. dogs, dolphins) over others (e.g. insects, fish) without a morally relevant justification. It is pointed out by sentientists as a "second-degree" form of speciesism: even among those who already reject human superiority, aesthetic preferences or preferences based on similarity end up recreating morally arbitrary hierarchies among nonhuman species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Speciesism among nonhuman species
Antonyms
Equal consideration
See also
Speciesism, Speciesist vegan, Antispeciesism, Substratism
Example
“Those who care only about mammals and ignore fish and insects end up reproducing a hierarchy known as xenospeciesism.”

Xenotransplantation

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The transplantation of organs or tissues between different species (e.g. from pigs to humans), raising ethical questions about the use of animals as "organ banks".

The organs come from genetically modified pigs, raised in isolated facilities and killed to remove their organs. The first pig heart transplants into living patients, in the United States in 2022 and 2023, gave survival of at most about two months; pig kidney transplants performed since 2024 have had better results, and the FDA authorized clinical trials in 2025. The shortage of human organs is real, but critics argue that the technique expands the use of animals as a source of spare parts and advocate strengthening human organ donation and other alternatives.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Cross-species transplant
Antonyms
Allotransplantation
See also
Genetic engineering, Animal experimentation, Instrumentalization, Animal model
Example
“Genetically modified pigs are bred to supply organs for xenotransplants, which raises questions about the use of these animals.”

Yuba

noun · Plant-Derived Products

A film that forms on the surface of heated soy milk, used as food in Asian cuisine.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Tofu skin, Soy skin
See also
Tofu, Soy, Soy protein, Plant protein
Example
“Yuba, the thin film that forms on the surface of soy milk, was used as a wrapper for rolls in a vegan dish.”

Z↑ A–Z

Zoo

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An institution that keeps wild animals in captivity for display, education or research; a central target of criticism by the animal liberation movement.

Zoos are justified by conservation and education, but many of the species on display are not threatened, and it is hard to show that visits change the public's behavior. Animals that range over large areas in the wild, such as elephants, polar bears and big cats, tend to suffer more in captivity, with stereotypies and higher mortality. Zoos differ, and some are closer to rescue centers or sanctuaries.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Zoological garden, Zoo park
See also
Captive breeding, Environmental enrichment, Sanctuary, Animal entertainment
Example
“The zoo justifies keeping animals in captivity with education and conservation, which critics question given the confinement.”

Zoology

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

The branch of biology dedicated to the scientific study of animals.

Like ethology, zoology has helped dismantle traditional hierarchies among species by revealing the biological and behavioral complexity of organisms once considered "inferior".

Synonyms, example and related terms
See also
Ethology, Biology, Animal cognition, Zootechnics (animal science)
Example
“Zoology, by describing the behavioral complexity of species once considered simple, has helped topple myths about ‘inferior’ animals.”

Zoonosis

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

An infectious disease that passes from other animals to humans, or the other way round.

Most infectious diseases that emerge in humans originate in animals: a study published in Nature in 2008 found that 60% of emerging disease events between 1940 and 2004 were zoonoses, and that 72% of these came from wildlife, such as HIV and Ebola. Intensive farming, with thousands of genetically similar animals kept close together, favours the circulation and mutation of viruses, such as those of bird flu and swine flu; the wildlife trade, hunting and deforestation also increase contact between species.

Synonyms, example and related terms
Synonyms and related uses
Zoonotic disease
See also
Pandemic, Antimicrobial resistance, Industrial livestock farming, Animal trafficking, One Health
Example
“Avian influenza is a zoonosis: a virus that jumps from birds to humans, and intensive farming raises the risk of such a leap.”

Zoophilia

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

The practice of sexual activity between humans and animals; a crime and a serious form of animal abuse.

Zoosadism

noun · Livestock, Exploitation and Related Practices

Pleasure derived from inflicting suffering or death on animals; a form of cruelty associated with behavioral disorders.

Zootechnics (animal science)

noun · Technical Fields Related to Animals

A science applied to the breeding and management of animals for production, historically oriented toward productivity and economic yield. Because it defines animals primarily as productive resources, zootechnics is often pointed to by abolitionist currents as a structurally speciesist discipline, even when it incorporates welfare parameters.

See also
